scenes.text: A private company has paid-up capital plus reserves of ₹80 lakh, borrowings ₹1.4 crore and revenue ₹6 crore.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: CARO 2020 applicability
steps.body: Applies to every company including foreign companies, except: banking companies, insurance companies, section 8 companies, One Person Companies, small companies, and private companies (not holding or subsidiary of a public company) whose paid-up capital and reserves do not exceed ₹1 crore, borrowings from banks/financial institutions do not exceed ₹1 crore at any time in the year, and total revenue does not exceed ₹10 crore — all three conditions must be satisfied for exemption. Also not applicable to the consolidated report except clause (xxi).

steps.title: Main clauses (21)
steps.body: Property, plant and equipment (records, physical verification, title deeds); inventory (physical verification, discrepancies ≥ 10%); loans, investments, guarantees; deposits; cost records; statutory dues; unrecorded income surrendered in tax assessments; loan defaults and wilful defaulter status; use of funds raised; fraud and whistle-blower complaints; Nidhi companies; related party transactions; internal audit; non-cash transactions with directors; RBI registration; cash losses; resignation of statutory auditors; material uncertainty on meeting liabilities; CSR unspent amount; qualifications in group companies' CARO reports.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Paid-up + reserves ₹80 lakh (≤ 1 crore ✔); borrowings ₹1.4 crore (> 1 crore ✘); revenue ₹6 crore (≤ 10 crore ✔). Step: Since one condition fails, the exemption is lost → CARO 2020 applies.

steps.title: Liabilities
steps.body: Civil: negligence (London and General Bank 1895 — auditor is 'a watchdog, not a bloodhound'; Kingston Cotton Mill 1896), misfeasance. Criminal: s.147 — contravention of ss.139–146 attracts fine; wilful intent to deceive attracts imprisonment and fine; s.448 false statements; s.447 fraud. Professional misconduct under the Chartered Accountants Act 1949. NFRA (s.132) oversees auditors of listed and large companies and can impose penalties and debar.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating the exemption conditions as 'any one' instead of 'all'; applying CARO to OPCs.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Corporate Governance, Committees, SEBI LODR & CSR
courses.summary: Concept, theories and history of corporate governance; landmark committees and scandals; board structure and independent directors; audit, nomination and remuneration, stakeholders' relationship and CSR committees; SEBI (LODR) Regulations 2015; vigil mechanism; and CSR under s.135.
outcomes: Explain agency, stewardship and stakeholder theories
Summarise major governance reports and the lessons of corporate failures
State board composition and independent director rules under the Act and LODR
Describe the composition and role of key board committees
Compute CSR obligation under s.135

scenes.text: In January 2009, Satyam's chairman confessed in a letter that the company's cash balances had been inflated for years.
India responded with stronger rules on boards, audit and disclosure — many found in the Companies Act 2013.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Corporate governance is the system by which companies are directed and controlled (Cadbury Report 1992). It balances the interests of shareholders, management, customers, suppliers, financiers, government and the community. Pillars: accountability, transparency, fairness, responsibility, independence.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body: Agency theory: managers (agents) may not act in the interest of shareholders (principals); governance reduces agency costs through monitoring, incentives and disclosure. Stewardship theory: managers are trustworthy stewards; empower them. Stakeholder theory: firms owe duties to all who affect or are affected by them. Resource dependence theory: boards provide links to critical resources.

steps.title: Landmark reports and failures
steps.body: UK: Cadbury (1992), Greenbury (1995), Hampel (1998), Higgs (2003). USA: Sarbanes–Oxley Act 2002 after Enron and WorldCom. India: CII Desirable Code (1998), Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee (1999, led to Clause 49 of the Listing Agreement), Naresh Chandra Committee (2002), N. R. Narayana Murthy Committee (2003), J. J. Irani Committee (2005, company law), Uday Kotak Committee (2017, LODR amendments). Failures: Enron, WorldCom, Satyam, IL&FS.

steps.title: Worked example: what failed at Satyam
steps.body: Step 1: Board — independent directors did not question a related acquisition proposal (Maytas, 2008). Step 2: Audit — bank balances not independently confirmed. Step 3: Promoter dominance and pledged shares. Responses: mandatory rotation of auditors, NFRA, stricter independent director rules, audit committee powers, fraud reporting by auditors.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Equating governance with compliance only; attributing Clause 49 to the Narayana Murthy Committee alone (it originated from the Birla Committee and was revised later).

activity.prompt: Match the item to its country.

quiz.q: 'The system by which companies are directed and controlled' is from
quiz.why: The Cadbury Report of 1992 gave this widely used definition.

quiz.q: Agency theory focuses on
quiz.why: It studies conflicts and costs arising when agents act for principals.

quiz.q: Clause 49 of the Listing Agreement originated from
quiz.why: SEBI introduced Clause 49 in 2000 based on the Birla Committee's recommendations.

scenes.text: A listed company has an executive chairman and a board of 11 directors.
How many must be independent?

steps.title: Companies Act 2013
steps.body: Listed public companies: at least one-third of directors independent (s.149(4)); prescribed public companies (paid-up capital ≥ ₹10 crore, or turnover ≥ ₹100 crore, or outstanding loans/debentures/deposits ≥ ₹50 crore): at least two independent directors. Independent director: not a promoter or related to promoters, no material pecuniary relationship, not a KMP or employee in last 3 years, holds less than 2% voting power with relatives, registered in the IICA databank. Tenure: up to two terms of five consecutive years; second term by special resolution; cooling-off of three years. Code for Independent Directors in Schedule IV; at least one separate meeting a year without non-independent directors.

steps.title: SEBI LODR Regulation 17
steps.body: At least one woman director (top 1,000 listed: one woman independent director). At least half the board non-executive. If the chairperson is non-executive, at least one-third independent; if the chairperson is executive or a promoter-related non-executive, at least half independent. Top 2,000 listed entities: at least six directors. Board meets at least four times a year, gap not more than 120 days.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Board of 11, executive chairman. Step 1: Requirement = at least half independent → 11 ÷ 2 = 5.5 → 6 independent directors (round up). Step 2: Non-executive directors must be at least 6 as well — independents count. Step 3: At least one woman (independent if in top 1,000).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Rounding down fractions; counting a nominee director of a lender as independent.

activity.prompt: A listed company has a non-executive chairperson (not related to promoters) and a board of 13. Minimum number of independent directors under LODR.

options: up to 5 consecutive years per term, max two terms
quiz.why: Section 149(10)–(11) allows two terms of up to five consecutive years each.

quiz.why: Section 149(6)(c) bars holding two percent or more of total voting power.

quiz.why: Regulation 17(1)(b) requires at least half the board to be independent in that case.

scenes.text: An employee emails the audit committee chair about inflated invoices from a vendor owned by a director's relative.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Audit committee (s.177; LODR Reg 18)
steps.body: Act: minimum three directors with independent directors forming a majority; majority including chairperson able to read and understand financial statements. LODR: at least two-thirds independent, chairperson independent, all financially literate and at least one with accounting or financial management expertise; at least four meetings a year with not more than 120 days gap; quorum two members or one-third, with at least two independents. Role: recommend auditor appointment and fees, review financial statements and auditor's report, approve related party transactions, scrutinise inter-corporate loans, evaluate internal financial controls, oversee the vigil mechanism.

steps.title: Other committees
steps.body: Nomination and Remuneration Committee (s.178): three or more non-executive directors, at least half independent; criteria for appointment, remuneration policy, evaluation of directors. Stakeholders Relationship Committee: companies with more than 1,000 shareholders/security holders; chaired by a non-executive director; resolves grievances on transfer, dividends, annual reports. CSR Committee (s.135): three or more directors with at least one independent (where required). Risk Management Committee: top 1,000 listed entities (LODR Reg 21).

steps.title: Vigil mechanism (s.177(9)–(10), LODR Reg 22)
steps.body: Listed companies and companies accepting public deposits or borrowing above ₹50 crore from banks must establish a vigil mechanism for directors and employees to report genuine concerns, with safeguards against victimisation and direct access to the audit committee chairperson in exceptional cases.

steps.title: Worked example: route the complaint
steps.body: Step 1: Complaint reaches the vigil officer / audit committee chair. Step 2: The committee orders an independent investigation (internal audit or external forensic firm). Step 3: The related-party contract is reviewed for approval under s.188 and Reg 23. Step 4: Whistle-blower's identity protected; outcome reported to the board.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying an executive director can chair the audit committee under LODR (chair must be independent); forgetting the 1,000-holder trigger for the Stakeholders Relationship Committee.

scenes.text: A company's net profits for the last three years were ₹6 crore, ₹8 crore and ₹10 crore.
How much must it spend on CSR this year?

steps.title: Applicability
steps.body: Every company with, in the immediately preceding financial year, net worth of ₹500 crore or more, or turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or net profit of ₹5 crore or more. It must constitute a CSR Committee (not required if CSR obligation does not exceed ₹50 lakh — the board then discharges its functions).

steps.title: Spending and unspent amounts
steps.body: Spend at least 2% of average net profits (computed under s.198) of the three immediately preceding financial years (or since incorporation if shorter). Activities as per Schedule VII: eradicating hunger and poverty, health, education, gender equality, environmental sustainability, heritage, armed forces veterans, sports, PM's National Relief Fund and similar, technology incubators, rural development, slum development, disaster management. Unspent amount not related to an ongoing project: transfer to a Schedule VII fund within six months of the end of the FY. Related to an ongoing project: transfer to an Unspent CSR Account within 30 days, to be spent within three years. Excess spending may be set off over the next three years.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Net profits ₹6 crore, ₹8 crore, ₹10 crore. Step 1: Average = 24 ÷ 3 = ₹8 crore. Step 2: 2% × 8 crore = ₹16 lakh. Step 3: Obligation ≤ ₹50 lakh → CSR Committee not mandatory; board approves the policy and spending. Step 4: Spending only ₹10 lakh with no ongoing project → transfer ₹6 lakh to a Schedule VII fund within six months of FY end.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using current year profit instead of the three-year average; counting activities for employees only, or for political parties, as CSR (excluded).

uni-bcom-b.title: B.Com — Corporate Law & Taxation basics, unit by unit
uni-bcom-b.description: B.Com core papers on Company Law (Companies Act, 2013) and Taxation basics (Income-tax and GST) — concepts, sections commonly studied, case-based examples and unit exams. General education, not legal or tax advice.

courses.title: Corporate Law I · company, incorporation, doctrines, capital
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Nature and kinds of companies under the Companies Act, 2013, incorporation with MoA and AoA, the doctrines of ultra vires, constructive notice and indoor management, and prospectus and share capital basics.
outcomes: Learners can explain separate legal entity and when the veil is lifted
Learners can classify companies by type
Learners can describe MoA clauses and apply key doctrines to cases
Learners can explain kinds of share capital and rules on premium, bonus, rights and buy-back

scenes.text: In 1897, Mr Salomon's boot business failed. Creditors argued he and his company were the same person.
The House of Lords disagreed: the company was a separate legal person. That idea underpins all company law.

steps.title: Features of a company
steps.body:
- **Separate legal entity** (Salomon v Salomon & Co Ltd, 1897): the company owns property, sues and is sued in its own name
- **Limited liability** of members (by shares or guarantee)
- **Perpetual succession**: members may change; the company continues
- **Transferability** of shares (restricted in private companies)
- **Lifting the corporate veil**: courts or statute look behind the company for fraud, tax evasion, sham companies, or when it acts as an enemy agent

steps.title: Kinds (Companies Act, 2013)
steps.body:
- **Private company**: restricts share transfer, max 200 members (excluding employee-members), min 2 members and 2 directors
- **Public company**: min 7 members and 3 directors
- **One Person Company (OPC)**: single member (a natural person), min 1 director
- **Small company**: private company within prescribed paid-up capital and turnover limits
- **Section 8 company**: promotes charity, education, art, etc.; profits not distributed
- **Government company**: at least 51% paid-up share capital held by government(s)
- Holding/subsidiary, listed/unlisted, limited by shares/guarantee, unlimited

steps.title: Solved: classify the company
steps.body:
- Four friends, 150 shareholders, shares not freely transferable → **private company**
- A company whose 60% shares are held by the Government of Gujarat → **government company**
- A non-profit set up to run a free library, licensed by the Central Government → **Section 8 company**

steps.title: Solved: lifting the veil
steps.body: A director forms a company only to dodge a non-compete promise he personally made. A court can treat the company as his alter ego and grant relief against both — the veil is lifted because the company is a **sham** to evade a legal obligation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking shareholders own the company's assets directly.
- Saying a private company must have 7 members.
- Confusing limited liability with no liability.
- Treating every company with government shareholding as a government company (it needs ≥ 51%).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Check the current text of the Act and rules for numerical limits.

activity.prompt: Match the company type to its feature.

quiz.q: Separate legal entity was established in:
quiz.why: Salomon v Salomon (1897) established that a company is a separate legal entity from its members.

quiz.q: Minimum directors in a public company:
quiz.why: A public company must have at least 3 directors.

quiz.q: Perpetual succession means:
options: company continues despite change in members
quiz.why: Perpetual succession means the company continues to exist despite changes in its members, even on death.

quiz.q: A Section 8 company:
quiz.why: A Section 8 company is a non-profit company that applies its profits to promoting its objects. It doesn't pay dividends to members.

quiz.q: Veil may be lifted in cases of:
quiz.why: Courts may lift the corporate veil when the company is used for fraud or as a sham, to see the people behind it.

scenes.text: Two engineering graduates want to register 'BrightBytes Private Limited'.
They reserve the name, file the incorporation form online with the MoA and AoA, and receive a certificate with a CIN.

steps.title: Incorporation
steps.body:
- Promoters conceive the company and take steps to form it
- Name reservation and incorporation are filed online with the Registrar of Companies (through the MCA portal's integrated incorporation form)
- Documents include the MoA, AoA, declarations and subscriber/director details
- The **certificate of incorporation** is conclusive evidence that the company is incorporated; it carries the Corporate Identity Number (CIN)
- Minimum paid-up capital requirements were removed by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015

steps.title: MoA and AoA
steps.body:
**Memorandum of Association** (charter; defines scope):
- Name clause, registered office clause, objects clause, liability clause, capital clause, and subscription/association clause

**Articles of Association** (internal rules): management, meetings, transfer of shares, directors' powers. Model articles are in Schedule I (e.g. Table F for companies limited by shares).

The MoA prevails over the AoA if they conflict. Alteration generally needs a **special resolution** (some changes also need approval from the Central Government or Tribunal).

steps.title: Solved: ultra vires
steps.body:
**Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co v Riche (1875)**: a company formed to make railway carriages agreed to finance a railway in Belgium. The contract was outside its objects clause and **void ab initio** — even unanimous shareholder approval could not ratify it.

Today: an act ultra vires the MoA is void; an act ultra vires the directors but within the company's powers can be ratified by members.

steps.title: Solved: which clause?
steps.body:
- Moving the registered office from Pune to Bengaluru → **registered office clause** (inter-state shift needs Central Government approval)
- Adding a new line of business → **objects clause**
- Increasing authorised capital → **capital clause** (ordinary resolution, if the articles permit)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking ultra vires contracts can be ratified by shareholders.
- Saying AoA overrides MoA.
- Forgetting that the certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence.
- Believing a minimum ₹1 lakh capital is still needed for private companies.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to incorporate a company.
items: Promoters decide the business and structure
Apply for name reservation
Draft MoA and AoA
File the incorporation form with documents and fees
Receive the certificate of incorporation with CIN
Commence business after required declarations

quiz.q: The objects clause appears in the:
quiz.why: The objects clause is in the Memorandum of Association (MoA), the company's charter.

quiz.q: Ashbury v Riche concerns:
quiz.why: Ashbury v Riche concerns the doctrine of ultra vires: acts beyond the objects clause are void.

quiz.q: If MoA and AoA conflict:
quiz.why: The MoA is the supreme charter. If the MoA and AoA conflict, the MoA prevails.

quiz.q: Model articles for a company limited by shares:
options: Table A (old Act) / Table F (2013 Act)
quiz.why: Model articles for a company limited by shares were Table A under the old Act and Table F under the Companies Act, 2013.

quiz.q: Certificate of incorporation is:
quiz.why: The certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that the company has been properly incorporated.

story.title: The bank and the borrowing limit

scenes.text: A bank lends to a company on the directors' word. Later the company claims the loan needed a shareholder resolution that was never passed.
Can the bank recover? The doctrine of indoor management protects outsiders acting in good faith.

steps.title: Two doctrines
steps.body:
- **Constructive notice**: anyone dealing with a company is presumed to know the contents of its public documents (MoA, AoA) filed with the Registrar
- **Indoor management** (Royal British Bank v Turquand, 1856): outsiders may assume internal procedures have been properly followed; they need not check the company's internal acts

Exceptions to indoor management: the outsider **knew** of the irregularity; **forgery**; **negligence** (no inquiry despite suspicious circumstances); acts that could not be within anyone's authority.

steps.title: Solved: Turquand-type case
steps.body:
AoA allow directors to borrow if authorised by an ordinary resolution. Directors borrow without one.

- Lender knew of the AoA rule (constructive notice) but could assume the resolution was passed (indoor management)
- **Company is bound**, provided the lender acted in good faith

steps.title: Solved: exception
steps.body:
A share certificate bearing a forged signature of the company secretary is relied upon by a buyer.

- Forgery is a nullity — indoor management **does not** protect the buyer against the company (Ruben v Great Fingall Consolidated, 1906)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking constructive notice protects outsiders (it protects the company; indoor management protects outsiders).
- Applying indoor management where the outsider was an insider who knew.
- Ignoring the forgery exception.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

statements.s: Outsiders are presumed to know the company's MoA and AoA.
Indoor management protects an outsider who knew the required resolution was not passed.
Royal British Bank v Turquand established indoor management.
A forged document can bind the company under indoor management.

quiz.q: Doctrine protecting outsiders:
quiz.why: The doctrine of indoor management protects outsiders dealing in good faith from internal irregularities (Turquand's rule).

quiz.q: Constructive notice relates to:
quiz.why: Constructive notice means outsiders are deemed to know the contents of public documents, such as the MoA and AoA.

quiz.q: Which is an exception to indoor management?
quiz.why: Forgery is an exception to indoor management, because a forged document is a nullity.

quiz.q: An outsider is put on inquiry when:
quiz.why: An outsider is put on inquiry when the circumstances are suspicious. Then he can't rely on indoor management.

quiz.q: Turquand's case year:
quiz.why: Royal British Bank v Turquand was decided in 1856.

scenes.text: A popular food-delivery company files for an IPO; the newspapers discuss its 'red herring prospectus' and price band.
Company law sets out what the prospectus must contain and who is liable for misstatements.

steps.title: Prospectus
steps.body:
- A **prospectus** invites the public to subscribe for securities; includes shelf prospectus and red herring prospectus (without final price/quantity)
- Misstatements: **civil liability** (Section 35) to compensate investors and **criminal liability** (Section 34) for untrue or misleading statements
- Public issues are also regulated by SEBI regulations

steps.title: Share capital
steps.body:
- Authorised (nominal) → issued → subscribed → called-up → paid-up
- **Equity shares** (voting, residual claim) and **preference shares** (priority for dividend and capital repayment)
- **Securities premium** (Section 52): may be used only for specified purposes, e.g. issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses or issue expenses, buy-back
- Shares generally **cannot be issued at a discount** (Section 53), except sweat equity shares (Section 54)
- **Rights issue** (Section 62), **bonus issue** (Section 63)
- **Buy-back** (Section 68): generally up to 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves; board approval up to 10%; post-buy-back debt–equity ratio not above 2 : 1

steps.title: Solved: capital structure
steps.body:
Authorised 10,00,000 shares of ₹10; issued 6,00,000; subscribed 5,50,000; ₹8 called; all calls paid except ₹2 on 10,000 shares.

- Authorised capital ₹1,00,00,000
- Subscribed ₹55,00,000
- Called-up ₹44,00,000; calls in arrears ₹20,000
- Paid-up **₹43,80,000**

steps.title: Solved: buy-back limit
steps.body:
Paid-up capital ₹40 crore + free reserves ₹60 crore = ₹100 crore.

- Maximum buy-back with a special resolution = 25% = **₹25 crore** (equity buy-back is also capped at 25% of paid-up equity capital in a year)
- Board alone can approve up to 10% = ₹10 crore

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using securities premium to pay dividends (not permitted).
- Saying shares may freely be issued at a discount.
- Confusing subscribed with paid-up capital.
- Forgetting SEBI rules apply in addition to the Act for listed companies.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Permitted use of securities premium?

quiz.q: Shares can be issued at a discount only as:
quiz.why: Shares can be issued at a discount only as sweat equity shares, which is a statutory exception.

quiz.q: Civil liability for misstatement in a prospectus is under Section:
quiz.why: Civil liability for a misstatement in a prospectus is under Section 35 of the Companies Act, 2013.

quiz.q: Bonus issue section:
quiz.why: Bonus issues are under Section 63 of the Companies Act, 2013.

quiz.q: Debt–equity ratio after buy-back must not exceed:
quiz.why: After a buy-back, the debt–equity ratio must not exceed 2 : 1 (the general limit).

quiz.q: A red herring prospectus lacks:
quiz.why: A red herring prospectus lacks the final price and quantity of shares. It is used in book-building.

questions.q: A company is a:
questions.why: A company is an artificial legal person: created by law, with its own legal identity.

questions.q: Minimum members in a private company:
questions.why: A private company needs a minimum of 2 members.

questions.q: The charter of a company:
questions.why: The Memorandum of Association (MoA) is the charter of a company.

questions.q: OPC member must be:
questions.why: The member of a One Person Company (OPC) must be a natural person, an individual.

questions.q: Indoor management protects:
questions.why: Indoor management protects outsiders who deal with the company in good faith.

questions.q: Securities premium can be used for:
questions.why: Securities premium may be used for issuing fully paid bonus shares, among other permitted uses (Section 52). It can't be used for salaries or dividends.

questions.q: Assertion: An ultra vires contract cannot be ratified by shareholders. Reason: It is void ab initio, being beyond the company's capacity.
questions.why: An ultra vires contract is beyond the company's capacity, so it is void from the start. Even all shareholders can't ratify it. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: A company with 51% of paid-up capital held jointly by Central and a State government is:
questions.why: A government company is one where at least 51% of paid-up capital is held by the Central Government, State Governments, or both.

questions.q: Which may lead courts to lift the corporate veil?
questions.why: Courts may lift the veil when a company is used to evade tax, as this is an abuse of the corporate form.

questions.q: Case: Directors needed a members' resolution to borrow above ₹1 crore (AoA). They borrowed ₹2 crore without it. The lender did not know. Is the company bound?
questions.why: The lender didn't know about the missing members' resolution, which is an internal irregularity. Under the indoor management rule, the company is bound.

questions.q: Paid-up capital ₹50 crore; free reserves ₹30 crore. Maximum buy-back by board resolution alone:
questions.why: A buy-back by board resolution alone is limited to 10% of the paid-up capital plus free reserves. Here that is 10% × (50 + 30) = ₹8 crore.

questions.q: Subscribed 1,00,000 shares of ₹10, ₹7 called, calls in arrears ₹15,000. Paid-up capital:
questions.why: Paid-up capital = amount called and paid. 1,00,000 × ₹7 = 7,00,000 called, less 15,000 in arrears = ₹6,85,000.

questions.q: A buyer relies on a share certificate with the secretary's forged signature. Under company law:
options: the company is bound by indoor management
the company is not bound (forgery is a nullity)
questions.why: A forged share certificate is a nullity, so indoor management doesn't protect the buyer. The company is not bound (Ruben v Great Fingall).

questions.q: Which statement about MoA alteration is correct?
options: Board alone can change the objects
Shifting registered office between states needs Central Government approval
questions.why: Shifting the registered office from one state to another needs Central Government approval. The board alone can't change the objects.

questions.q: Members of a private company exceeding 200 (excluding employee-members) means it:
options: can no longer qualify as a private company
questions.why: A private company can have at most 200 members (excluding employees and certain others). Beyond that it no longer meets the definition of a private company.
