scenes.text: Kamal agreed to be a director of his cousin's company 'just on paper' and never attended a meeting.
When the company defaulted, Kamal learnt that directors have legal duties whether or not they attend.

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body:
- Numbers: public company ≥ 3, private ≥ 2, OPC ≥ 1; maximum 15 (more by special resolution) — Section 149
- At least one director must have stayed in India for at least 182 days in the financial year (resident director)
- Listed companies: at least **one-third independent directors**; prescribed companies need at least one **woman director**
- Every director needs a **Director Identification Number (DIN)**
- Maximum **20 directorships**, of which not more than **10 public companies** (Section 165)
- **Duties** (Section 166): act per articles, in good faith for the company, employees, shareholders, community and environment; with due care, skill and diligence; avoid conflicts; no undue gain; no assignment of office

steps.title: Solved: is the board valid?
steps.body:
A listed company has 9 directors, 2 of them independent.

- One-third of 9 = 3 ⇒ it needs **at least 3** independent directors — non-compliant
- Fix: appoint one more independent director (or restructure)

steps.title: Solved: directorships count
steps.body:
Meera is a director in 8 public companies and 10 private companies (none dormant, no exclusion applies).

- Total 18 ≤ 20 ✓; public 8 ≤ 10 ✓ ⇒ she may accept **2 more** directorships, and at most 2 of them can be public.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking nominal ('paper') directors have no liability.
- Counting independent directors as a fixed number rather than a fraction.
- Confusing DIN with PAN or CIN.
- Forgetting the resident-director requirement.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: A new director should check:
items: DIN obtained and consent filed
Not disqualified under the Act
Within the 20/10 directorship limits
Disclosed interests in other entities
Read the MoA, AoA and latest financial statements
Understands duties under Section 166

quiz.q: Maximum directors without special resolution:
quiz.why: A company can have at most 15 directors without a special resolution (Section 149).

quiz.q: Listed company independent directors:
quiz.why: A listed company must have at least one-third of its board as independent directors (Section 149(4)).

quiz.q: Maximum public-company directorships:
quiz.why: A person can be a director in at most 10 public companies (Section 165).

quiz.q: Directors' duties are listed in Section:
quiz.why: Directors' duties are listed in Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013.

quiz.q: Resident director must have stayed in India at least:
quiz.why: At least one director must be a resident of India, having stayed in India for at least 182 days in the financial year.

scenes.text: A company secretary realises the AGM notice went out only 15 days before the meeting.
The Act requires 21 clear days (unless shorter notice is consented to). She reschedules.

steps.title: General meetings
steps.body:
- **AGM** (Section 96): every company except OPC; first AGM within 9 months of the end of the first financial year; thereafter within 6 months of year end, gap ≤ 15 months
- **EGM** (Section 100): any other general meeting
- **Notice** (Section 101): at least **21 clear days**; shorter notice with consent of prescribed majority
- **Quorum** (Section 103), unless articles require more — public company: 5 members (≤ 1,000 members), 15 (1,000–5,000), 30 (> 5,000); private company: 2
- **Ordinary resolution**: votes in favour > votes against; **special resolution**: votes in favour ≥ **3 times** votes against (Section 114)

steps.title: Board meetings
steps.body:
- First board meeting within **30 days** of incorporation; at least **4** meetings a year with a gap of not more than **120 days** (Section 173)
- Quorum (Section 174): one-third of total strength or 2 directors, whichever is higher

steps.title: Solved: special resolution
steps.body:
At a meeting, 6,300 votes are cast for and 2,000 against a proposal.

- 3 × 2,000 = 6,000 ≤ 6,300 ⇒ **special resolution passed**
- With 2,200 against, 3 × 2,200 = 6,600 > 6,300 ⇒ fails as special but passes as ordinary.

steps.title: Solved: board quorum
steps.body:
Board strength 10.

- One-third = 3.33 → rounded up to **4**; higher than 2 ⇒ quorum = **4 directors**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the day of notice and the meeting day as 'clear days'.
- Thinking OPCs must hold AGMs.
- Applying public-company quorum to private companies.
- Requiring 75% of members present for a special resolution (it is 3 × votes against among those voting).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: A public company has 3,500 members. Unless its articles say otherwise, what is the quorum for its general meeting?

quiz.q: Minimum notice for a general meeting:
quiz.why: A general meeting needs at least 21 clear days' notice (Section 101).

quiz.q: Special resolution requires votes in favour at least:
quiz.why: A special resolution needs votes in favour at least three times the votes against (Section 114).

quiz.q: Maximum gap between two board meetings:
quiz.why: The gap between two board meetings can be at most 120 days (Section 173).

quiz.q: Quorum for a private company general meeting:
quiz.why: The quorum for a general meeting of a private company is 2 members personally present (Section 103).

quiz.q: Maximum gap between two AGMs:
quiz.why: The gap between two AGMs can be at most 15 months (Section 96), and an AGM must be held every calendar year.

scenes.text: A listed company's annual report is signed by the chairperson, the CFO and the company secretary.
An independent auditor then reports to shareholders whether the accounts are true and fair.

steps.title: KMP
steps.body:
**Key managerial personnel** (Section 2(51)) include the CEO/managing director/manager, the company secretary, whole-time directors, the CFO and others prescribed.

Every listed company and prescribed public companies must appoint whole-time KMP (Section 203).

steps.title: Auditors
steps.body:
- First auditor appointed by the board within 30 days of registration
- Subsequently appointed at an AGM to hold office from that AGM until the end of the sixth AGM (a 5-year term) — Section 139
- **Rotation** for listed and prescribed companies: an individual auditor for not more than one term of 5 years; an audit firm for not more than two terms of 5 years, followed by a cooling-off period
- The auditor reports to members on whether financial statements give a true and fair view

steps.title: Solved: rotation
steps.body:
A firm has audited a listed company for two consecutive 5-year terms.

- It must now step down and can be re-appointed only after a **5-year cooling-off** period.

steps.title: Solved: identify KMP
steps.body:
Among: CFO, marketing head (not a director), company secretary, independent director.

- KMP: **CFO** and **company secretary**
- The marketing head is senior management but not KMP by default; an independent director is a director, not KMP.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every senior manager a KMP.
- Thinking auditors are appointed annually under the 2013 Act.
- Forgetting the auditor reports to shareholders, not the board.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: KMP or not KMP (by default)?

quiz.q: KMP are defined in Section:
quiz.why: Key managerial personnel (KMP) are defined in Section 2(51) of the Companies Act, 2013.

quiz.q: Auditor's term after appointment at an AGM:
quiz.why: An auditor appointed at an AGM holds office for 5 years, until the sixth AGM (Section 139).

quiz.q: Audit firm in a listed company: maximum consecutive terms:
quiz.why: An audit firm of a listed company can hold office for at most two consecutive terms of 5 years.

quiz.q: Auditor reports to:
quiz.why: The auditor reports to the members (shareholders) of the company.

quiz.q: First auditor is appointed by the board within:
quiz.why: The first auditor is appointed by the board within 30 days of registration of the company (Section 139).

scenes.text: A large manufacturer funds village schools and clean water under its CSR policy.
Meanwhile, a smaller supplier that defaulted on loans faces an insolvency process under the IBC.

steps.title: CSR (Section 135)
steps.body:
Applies to a company with, in the preceding financial year, **net worth ≥ ₹500 crore**, or **turnover ≥ ₹1,000 crore**, or **net profit ≥ ₹5 crore**.

- Spend at least **2% of average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years**
- Activities listed in Schedule VII (e.g. hunger, education, health, environment, rural development)
- CSR committee of the board (not required if the CSR obligation is up to ₹50 lakh)

steps.title: Insolvency and winding up
steps.body:
- **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC)**: corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) before the NCLT; minimum default threshold **₹1 crore** (raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020); a resolution professional runs the company; the committee of creditors decides; timeline 180 days, extendable, overall cap 330 days including litigation
- If no resolution plan is approved → liquidation
- **Voluntary liquidation** of solvent companies under IBC; **winding up by the Tribunal** under the Companies Act for grounds such as acts against sovereignty, fraud, or failure to file statements for five years

steps.title: Solved: CSR test and spend
steps.body:
Net profits: ₹6 crore, ₹8 crore, ₹10 crore in the last three years; net worth ₹200 crore; turnover ₹400 crore.

- Net profit ≥ ₹5 crore in the preceding year ⇒ **CSR applies**
- Average = ₹8 crore ⇒ minimum spend = 2% = **₹16 lakh**

steps.title: Solved: IBC threshold
steps.body:
A supplier is owed ₹60 lakh by a company. Can it start CIRP?

- Default ₹60 lakh < ₹1 crore threshold ⇒ **not maintainable** on its own; it may pursue other remedies (civil suit, or join with other creditors where the law allows aggregation).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the current year's profit instead of the preceding three years' average.
- Quoting the old ₹1 lakh IBC threshold.
- Treating CSR as voluntary for qualifying companies.
- Confusing liquidation with resolution.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: A qualifying company's net profits for the last three years were ₹30 crore, ₹45 crore and ₹45 crore. Minimum CSR spend (₹ crore)?

quiz.q: CSR minimum spend:
options: 2% of average net profit of 3 years
quiz.why: CSR spending is a minimum of 2% of the company's average net profit of the preceding 3 years (Section 135).

quiz.q: Net profit threshold for CSR:
quiz.why: CSR applies if a company has a net profit of ₹5 crore or more in the preceding year (or meets the net worth or turnover thresholds).

quiz.q: Minimum default for CIRP under IBC:
quiz.why: The minimum default for starting insolvency under IBC is ₹1 crore, since 2020.

quiz.q: CIRP is adjudicated by:
quiz.why: The corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) is adjudicated by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).

quiz.q: Overall outer limit for CIRP including litigation:
quiz.why: The CIRP must be completed within 330 days, including litigation time. This is the statutory outer limit.

questions.q: Every director needs a:
questions.why: Every director needs a DIN, a Director Identification Number.

questions.q: AGM is not required for:
questions.why: A One Person Company (OPC) doesn't have to hold an AGM.

questions.q: CSR activities are listed in:
questions.why: CSR activities are listed in Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013.

questions.q: Minimum board meetings per year:
questions.why: A company must hold at least 4 board meetings in a year.

questions.q: Votes for 900, against 300. Resolution passes as:
questions.why: A special resolution needs votes for to be at least three times those against. 900 is exactly 3 × 300, so it passes as a special resolution.

questions.q: Quorum of a public company with 800 members:
questions.why: For a public company with up to 1,000 members, the quorum is 5 members personally present.

questions.q: Assertion: A nominal director can be liable for the company's defaults in some cases. Reason: Directors owe statutory duties of care, skill and diligence.
questions.why: Directors owe statutory duties of care, skill and diligence, so even a nominal director may be liable for defaults in some cases. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Board of 7 directors; quorum:
questions.why: The board quorum is one-third of total strength or 2 directors, whichever is higher. One-third of 7 is 2.33, which rounds up to 3.

questions.q: First AGM must be held within ___ of the end of the first financial year:
questions.why: The first AGM must be held within 9 months of the end of the first financial year (Section 96).

questions.q: Case: A company's preceding-year turnover is ₹1,200 crore but it made a loss. Does CSR apply?
questions.why: Any one criterion triggers CSR (spend is 2% of average net profit, which may be nil).

questions.q: A listed company with 12 directors needs at least ___ independent directors:
questions.why: A listed company needs at least one-third of its directors to be independent. One-third of 12 = 4.

questions.q: Under IBC, the body that approves a resolution plan is the:
questions.why: Under IBC, the committee of creditors approves the resolution plan. Then the NCLT sanctions it.

questions.q: A director holds 10 public and 9 private directorships. Can she join the board of another public company?
questions.why: A person can hold directorships in at most 10 public companies. She already has 10, so she can't join another, even though the total is below 20.

questions.q: Notice of an AGM was sent 18 clear days before. It is valid if:
options: at least 95% of members entitled to vote consent to shorter notice
questions.why: Shorter notice for AGM needs consent of at least 95% of members entitled to vote.

questions.q: An individual auditor of a listed company has completed one 5-year term. Next step:
questions.why: An individual auditor of a listed company can serve one term of 5 years only. Then she must rotate out and observe a 5-year cooling-off period.

courses.title: Taxation I · income-tax basics
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Key concepts of Indian income tax and the move to the Income-tax Act, 2025 with its 'tax year', residential status and scope of income, the five heads of income with salary and house property basics, and computing tax under the new and old regimes. General education, not tax advice; rates change every year.
outcomes: Learners can explain basic terms and the 'tax year' concept
Learners can determine an individual's residential status
Learners can classify income into the five heads
Learners can compute tax for a salaried individual under both regimes for a stated year

lessons.title: Basic concepts and the new Act

scenes.text: Asha joins a firm in Hyderabad and sees 'TDS' deducted from her first salary.
She wants to understand what tax is charged on, for which year, and by which law.

steps.title: The law and the year
steps.body:
- Income tax is levied by the Union under Entry 82 of the Union List
- The **Income-tax Act, 1961** governed income tax for decades. It is replaced by the **Income-tax Act, 2025**, applicable from **1 April 2026**
- The 1961 Act used **previous year** (year of earning) and **assessment year** (following year of assessment). The 2025 Act uses a single **tax year** (the financial year in which income is earned)
- Most concepts — person, residential status, heads of income, deductions, TDS — carry over, but **section numbers changed**. Annual **Finance Acts** set rates

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body:
- **Person**: individual, HUF, company, firm, AOP/BOI, local authority, artificial juridical person
- **Gross total income** = sum of incomes under the five heads (after set-off)
- **Total income** = GTI − permitted deductions
- **TDS/TCS**: tax deducted/collected at source; advance tax; self-assessment
- **Exempt income**, e.g. agricultural income (with a rate-aggregation rule for individuals)

steps.title: Solved: which year?
steps.body:
Ravi earns salary from April 2026 to March 2027.

- Under the 2025 Act this is **tax year 2026-27**
- Under the old terminology the same period would have been 'previous year 2026-27, assessment year 2027-28'

steps.title: Solved: GTI and total income
steps.body:
Salary (taxable) ₹6,00,000; interest ₹20,000; capital gain ₹30,000.

- GTI = **₹6,50,000**
- If eligible deductions are ₹1,50,000 (old regime), total income = **₹5,00,000**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using an old section number without checking the new Act.
- Quoting last year's rates for this year.
- Confusing gross total income with total income.
- Thinking TDS is an extra tax (it is an advance collection, adjusted against the final liability).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not tax advice. Rates, limits and section numbers change; check the current Act, Finance Act and official guidance.

items.back: Year in which income was earned
Year following the previous year, in which income was assessed
Single concept: the financial year in which income is earned
Annual law that sets rates and amends tax laws

quiz.q: The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from:
quiz.why: The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026, replacing the 1961 Act.

quiz.q: The 2025 Act replaces previous year and assessment year with:
quiz.why: The 2025 Act replaces the previous year and assessment year with a single concept, the tax year.

quiz.q: Total income equals:
quiz.why: Total income = gross total income − deductions.

quiz.q: TDS is:
quiz.why: TDS means tax deducted at source: tax collected in advance at the point where income is paid.

quiz.q: Annual tax rates are mainly set by:
quiz.why: Annual tax rates are set by the Finance Acts passed with each Union Budget.

lessons.title: Residential status and scope of income

scenes.text: Vikram, an Indian citizen, works in Dubai and visits home for 70 days a year.
Is he resident in India for tax? Day counts decide — and that decides whether his foreign salary is taxed here.

steps.title: Tests for an individual
steps.body:
**Basic conditions** — resident if in the year:
- (a) in India for **182 days or more**, or
- (b) **60 days or more** in the year and **365 days or more** in the four preceding years

Key modifications: for an Indian citizen leaving India for employment (or as crew), (b) uses 182 instead of 60; for an Indian citizen/person of Indian origin visiting India whose Indian income exceeds ₹15 lakh, (b) uses 120 days. An Indian citizen with Indian income above ₹15 lakh who is not liable to tax in any other country may be **deemed resident**.

**Resident but not ordinarily resident (RNOR)** applies in specified cases (e.g. non-resident in 9 of the 10 preceding years, or in India ≤ 729 days in the 7 preceding years).

steps.title: Scope of total income
steps.body:
- **Resident and ordinarily resident**: global income taxable
- **RNOR**: Indian income + foreign income from a business controlled or profession set up in India
- **Non-resident**: only income received/accruing/arising (or deemed) in India

steps.title: Solved: day count
steps.body:
Priya, a foreign national, was in India 90 days this year and 400 days in the preceding four years.

- 182 days? No
- 60 days and 365 days in four years? **Yes** ⇒ **resident** (then check RNOR conditions)

steps.title: Solved: scope
steps.body:
A non-resident earns: salary in London ₹30 lakh; rent from a flat in Mumbai ₹4 lakh; interest from an Indian bank ₹50,000.

- Taxable in India: **₹4.5 lakh** (Indian-source income only)
- If he were ROR, all ₹34.5 lakh would be taxable (with relief for foreign tax paid under treaties where applicable)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using citizenship as the test (residence is about days, not passport).
- Forgetting the special 182/120-day rules.
- Taxing a non-resident's foreign income.
- Ignoring that residential status is decided afresh every year.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not tax advice. Check the current Act for exact conditions.

a.text: Sameer (a foreign national) spent 200 days in India this year. Resident?

choices.label: Yes — 182 days or more
choices.feedback: Right: the first basic condition is met.

choices.label: No — he is not a citizen
choices.feedback: Citizenship is not the test.

a2.text: Residence depends on stay. Try again: 200 days in India.

choices.label: Resident
choices.feedback: Correct.

b.text: Next: Lata (a foreign national) spent 70 days this year and 300 days in the previous four years. Resident?

choices.label: No — 365-day condition fails
choices.feedback: Correct: 60 days met but not 365 in four years.

choices.label: Yes — more than 60 days
choices.feedback: Both parts of condition (b) must be met.

b2.text: Check both parts of the second condition.

choices.label: Non-resident
choices.feedback: Yes.

end.text: Always test 182 days first, then the 60 + 365 rule, then special modifications.

quiz.q: An individual in India for 182 days or more in the year is:
quiz.why: An individual who stays in India for 182 days or more in the year is a resident (basic condition (a)).

quiz.q: Non-residents are taxed in India on:
quiz.why: Non-residents are taxed in India only on Indian income, such as income earned or received in India.

quiz.q: Residential status is determined:
quiz.why: Residential status is determined every year, based on the days of stay in that year (and earlier years).

quiz.q: Condition (b) requires 60 days in the year AND:
quiz.why: Condition (b) needs 60 days in the year and 365 days or more in the 4 preceding years.

quiz.q: An ROR is taxed on:
quiz.why: A resident and ordinarily resident (ROR) is taxed on global income, whether it is earned in India or abroad.

lessons.title: The five heads of income: salary and house property

scenes.text: Arjun earns a salary and also rents out a small flat inherited from his grandmother.
Each income goes under its own head with its own deductions.

steps.title: Five heads
steps.body:
1. **Salaries**
2. **Income from house property**
3. **Profits and gains of business or profession**
4. **Capital gains**
5. **Income from other sources** (interest, dividends, gifts above limits, etc.)

Each head has its own computation rules; losses can be set off within and across heads subject to restrictions.

steps.title: Salary and house property essentials
steps.body:
**Salary**: basic, DA, allowances, perquisites, minus exemptions and the **standard deduction** — ₹75,000 under the new regime and ₹50,000 under the old regime (as for recent years; check the current year).

**House property (let out)**:
- Gross annual value (broadly, rent receivable or expected rent, whichever is higher, subject to rules)
- Less municipal taxes paid by the owner ⇒ **Net annual value (NAV)**
- Less **30% standard deduction** of NAV and **interest on borrowed capital**
- For a self-occupied home, the annual value is nil; interest deduction (up to ₹2,00,000) is available under the old regime

steps.title: Solved: let-out flat
steps.body:
Rent ₹3,00,000 a year; municipal tax paid ₹20,000; home-loan interest ₹60,000.

- NAV = 3,00,000 − 20,000 = 2,80,000
- Less 30% = 84,000; less interest 60,000
- Income from house property = **₹1,36,000**

steps.title: Solved: classify incomes
steps.body:
- Interest on a savings account → **other sources**
- Profit on sale of shares → **capital gains**
- Freelance design fees → **business or profession**
- Rent from a shop owned → **house property** (buildings and land appurtenant)
- Pension from former employer → **salaries**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying 30% on gross rent instead of NAV.
- Deducting municipal taxes that the tenant paid.
- Classifying rent from a sub-let (not owned) property as house property (usually other sources).
- Using both regimes' deductions at once.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not tax advice.

activity.prompt: Under which head is each income taxed?

quiz.q: Number of heads of income:
quiz.why: There are five heads of income: salaries, house property, business or profession, capital gains, and other sources.

quiz.q: Standard deduction on house property:
quiz.why: The standard deduction on house property is 30% of the net annual value (NAV).

quiz.q: Savings account interest falls under:
quiz.why: Savings account interest is taxed under 'income from other sources', the residual head.

quiz.q: Rent ₹2,40,000; municipal tax ₹40,000; interest ₹0. HP income:
Profit on sale of shares is taxed as:
quiz.why: Profit on the sale of shares is taxed under capital gains, since shares are capital assets.

lessons.title: Computing tax: new and old regimes

scenes.text: Asha earns ₹18 lakh. Colleagues argue whether the new or old regime is better.
She computes both. The answer depends on how many deductions she actually has.

steps.title: Rates used in this lesson (FY 2025-26, individuals below 60)
steps.body:
**New regime (default)** slabs: up to ₹4 lakh nil; 4–8 lakh 5%; 8–12 lakh 10%; 12–16 lakh 15%; 16–20 lakh 20%; 20–24 lakh 25%; above ₹24 lakh 30%. Rebate makes tax nil for total income up to ₹12 lakh (marginal relief just above). Most deductions (like the 80C-type savings deduction) are not allowed.

**Old regime** slabs: up to ₹2.5 lakh nil; 2.5–5 lakh 5%; 5–10 lakh 20%; above ₹10 lakh 30%; rebate up to ₹12,500 if total income ≤ ₹5 lakh. Deductions allowed, e.g. savings/investments up to ₹1.5 lakh (section 80C under the 1961 Act), health insurance (80D), etc.

Add **4% health and education cess** on tax (and surcharge for high incomes). Check the current Finance Act for later years.

steps.title: Solved: old regime, same salary
steps.body:
Salary ₹18,00,000 − standard deduction ₹50,000 − 80C ₹1,50,000 − 80D ₹25,000 ⇒ total income ₹15,75,000.

- 2.5–5 L: 12,500; 5–10 L: 1,00,000; 10–15.75 L: 1,72,500
- Tax = 2,85,000 + cess 11,400 = **₹2,96,400**
- New regime is cheaper here unless she has much larger deductions (e.g. HRA and home-loan interest).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the top rate to the whole income instead of slab-by-slab.
- Forgetting cess.
- Claiming old-regime deductions under the new regime.
- Using a year's rates for a different year.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not tax advice. Rates shown are for FY 2025-26 to practise the method; always use the rates notified for your year.

activity.prompt: Using the FY 2025-26 new-regime slabs in this lesson, compute tax before cess on a total income of ₹20,00,000 (₹).

quiz.q: Health and education cess rate:
quiz.why: Health and education cess is 4%, charged on tax plus surcharge.

quiz.q: In the lesson's new regime, income between ₹8–12 lakh is taxed at:
quiz.why: In the lesson's new regime, the slab for income between ₹8 and ₹12 lakh is taxed at 10%.

quiz.q: Standard deduction for salaried under the new regime (FY 2025-26):
quiz.why: The standard deduction for salaried people in the new regime (FY 2025-26) is ₹75,000.

quiz.q: Savings-linked deduction up to ₹1.5 lakh (80C under the 1961 Act) is available in:
quiz.why: The deduction of up to ₹1.5 lakh for savings under Section 80C is available only in the old regime.

quiz.q: Tax is computed:
options: at the highest rate on all income
quiz.why: Tax is computed slab by slab. Each slice of income is taxed at its own rate, not at the highest rate.

questions.q: Income tax is a:
questions.why: Income tax is a direct tax, borne by the person who earns the income.

questions.q: Number of heads of income:
questions.why: There are five heads of income.

questions.q: TDS stands for:
questions.why: TDS stands for tax deducted at source.

questions.q: The 'tax year' concept belongs to:
questions.why: The 'tax year' concept belongs to the Income-tax Act, 2025. The 1961 Act used the previous year and assessment year.

questions.q: Freelance writing income is taxed under:
questions.why: Freelance writing is a profession, so the income is taxed under 'profits and gains of business or profession'.

questions.q: A foreign national in India 190 days this year is:
questions.why: A person in India for 182 days or more in a year is a resident. 190 days meets that.

questions.q: Assertion: A non-resident's London salary is not taxed in India. Reason: Non-residents are taxed only on income from Indian sources (or received in India).
questions.why: A non-resident is taxed in India only on income from Indian sources, or received in India. A London salary is not taxed here. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Rent ₹4,80,000; municipal taxes ₹30,000; interest on loan ₹1,00,000. HP income:
Using the lesson's new regime, tax before cess on ₹12,00,000 total income (before rebate):
questions.why: In the lesson's new regime, ₹4–8 lakh at 5% = ₹20,000, and ₹8–12 lakh at 10% = ₹40,000. Total before rebate = ₹60,000. The rebate then makes it nil.

questions.q: Case: Neha (foreign national) was in India 65 days this year and 400 days in the 4 preceding years. Status:
questions.why: Neha stayed 65 days this year (at least 60) and 400 days in the 4 preceding years (at least 365). Both parts of condition (b) are met, so she is a resident.

questions.q: Using the lesson's old regime, tax before cess on ₹9,00,000 total income:
Salary ₹10,00,000 under the lesson's new regime with ₹75,000 standard deduction. Tax payable after rebate:
questions.why: Total income = 10,00,000 − 75,000 = 9,25,000, which is within ₹12 lakh. So the rebate makes the tax nil.

questions.q: Total tax including 4% cess on ₹24,00,000 total income (lesson's new regime):
A non-resident earns ₹10 lakh interest from an Indian company deposit and ₹20 lakh salary in Singapore. Income taxable in India (ignoring treaties):
questions.why: A non-resident is taxed in India only on Indian-source income. The ₹10 lakh interest from an Indian company is taxable. The Singapore salary is not.

questions.q: Why must residential status be checked every year?
options: Day counts change annually and decide the scope of taxable income
questions.why: Day counts change each year, and residential status decides the scope of taxable income (global or Indian only). So it must be checked every year.

courses.title: Taxation II · GST basics
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Goods and Services Tax: constitutional basis and structure (CGST, SGST/UTGST, IGST), the meaning of supply with composite and mixed supplies, input tax credit with utilisation rules, and registration, composition and returns. General education, not tax advice.
outcomes: Learners can explain dual GST and when IGST applies
Learners can identify supply, composite and mixed supply
Learners can compute net GST using input tax credit
Learners can state registration thresholds, composition basics and main returns

lessons.title: GST structure: CGST, SGST and IGST

scenes.text: Before July 2017, trucks waited for hours at state check-posts and goods carried layers of central and state taxes.
GST replaced most indirect taxes with a single destination-based tax shared by the Centre and states.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
- GST came into force on **1 July 2017**, enabled by the **Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016**
- It is a **destination-based** consumption tax on the supply of goods and services, with credit for taxes paid on inputs
- **Intra-state** supply: **CGST + SGST** (or UTGST), usually split equally
- **Inter-state** supply and imports: **IGST**
- The **GST Council** (Article 279A), chaired by the Union Finance Minister, recommends rates and rules
- Alcohol for human consumption is outside GST; certain petroleum products are not yet taxed under GST

steps.title: Solved: which tax?
steps.body:
- A trader in Pune sells to a customer in Nagpur (both Maharashtra) for ₹10,000 at 18% → **CGST ₹900 + SGST ₹900**
- The same trader sells to a buyer in Bengaluru → **IGST ₹1,800**

steps.title: Solved: GST on value addition
steps.body:
Manufacturer sells at ₹1,000 (+18% = 180). Wholesaler sells at ₹1,200 (+216). Retailer sells at ₹1,500 (+270).

- Tax paid in cash at each stage: 180, 216 − 180 = 36, 270 − 216 = 54
- Total = **₹270** = 18% of the final price — no tax on tax

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Charging IGST on intra-state sales.
- Thinking the state of the supplier's head office decides — it is the place of supply.
- Saying alcohol for drinking is under GST.
- Forgetting that GST rates are notified and revised by the Council.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not tax advice. GST rates were rationalised from 22 September 2025 (mainly 5% and 18%, with a special 40% rate on select goods); always check the current rate notification.

activity.prompt: Which GST applies?

items.text: Kolkata hotel room booked by a local resident

quiz.q: GST was introduced on:
quiz.why: GST replaced many central and state indirect taxes and came into force on 1 July 2017. The other dates are not the roll-out date of the GST law.

quiz.q: Inter-state supply attracts:
quiz.why: A supply from one state to another is taxed as IGST (Integrated GST), collected by the Centre and shared with the destination state. CGST + SGST applies only to supplies within one state.

quiz.q: GST Council is chaired by:
quiz.why: The GST Council, set up under Article 279A, is chaired by the Union Finance Minister. State finance ministers are its members.

quiz.q: GST is a ___ based tax:
quiz.why: GST is a destination-based consumption tax: the tax goes to the state where goods or services are consumed, not where they are produced (origin).

quiz.q: Which is outside GST?
quiz.why: Alcohol for human consumption is kept outside GST by the Constitution, so states tax it separately. Restaurant services, clothing and mobiles all attract GST.

scenes.text: A sweet shop sells a Diwali hamper: sweets, dry fruits, a candle and a juice bottle at one price.
Is it one supply or many? GST treats it as a mixed supply taxed at the highest rate among its items.

steps.title: Meaning of supply
steps.body:
Supply includes sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal made for consideration in the course or furtherance of business; import of services for consideration; and certain activities even without consideration (e.g. between related or distinct persons, as listed in the law).

- **Composite supply**: two or more naturally bundled supplies with a **principal supply** — taxed at the rate of the principal supply (e.g. goods sold with transport and insurance)
- **Mixed supply**: separate items sold together for a single price, not naturally bundled — taxed at the **highest rate** among them
- Place of supply decides intra- vs inter-state (for goods, generally where movement terminates for delivery)

steps.title: Solved: identify the type
steps.body:
- Laptop sold with a carry bag at one price → **composite** (principal: laptop)
- Hamper of sweets, chocolates, cold drink and toy at one price → **mixed** (highest rate applies)
- Hotel stay with breakfast → generally **composite** (principal: accommodation)

steps.title: Solved: stock transfer
steps.body:
A company moves goods from its Gujarat branch to its Rajasthan branch (both registered separately) with no sale.

- Branches with separate registrations are **distinct persons**; the transfer is a **supply** even without consideration ⇒ IGST applies (on the value as per valuation rules).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taxing a mixed supply at the principal item's rate.
- Thinking free transfers are never supply.
- Ignoring 'in the course or furtherance of business' — a personal sale of an old household item is not a GST supply.
- Confusing place of supply with location of the supplier's office.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not tax advice.

statements.s: A composite supply is taxed at the rate of its principal supply.
A mixed supply is taxed at the lowest rate among items.
Transfer between two separately registered branches can be a supply.
Selling your personal old sofa to a neighbour is a GST supply.
statements.why: Not in the course of business.

quiz.q: Goods with transport and insurance in one contract:
quiz.why: When goods and services are naturally bundled and sold together (like goods with transport and insurance), it is a composite supply. A mixed supply is a random bundle sold for one price.

quiz.q: Mixed supply is taxed at:
quiz.why: A mixed supply of two or more items is taxed at the rate of the item that attracts the highest rate. This prevents tax avoidance through bundling.

quiz.q: Barter in business is:
quiz.why: Under GST, a supply made for consideration in the course of business includes barter, because goods exchanged are consideration. It is not exempt by default.

quiz.q: Place of supply decides:
options: whether IGST or CGST + SGST applies
quiz.why: Place of supply tells whether a supply is inter-state or intra-state. That decides whether IGST or CGST + SGST is charged.

quiz.q: Distinct persons include:
options: separately registered branches of the same entity
quiz.why: Registrations of the same entity in different states are treated as distinct persons under GST, so supplies between them are taxable. Unrelated firms or customers are simply different persons, not 'distinct' in this sense.

lessons.title: Input tax credit and its utilisation

scenes.text: A furniture maker pays GST on wood, screws and polish.
When she sells chairs, she deducts that input GST from the GST she collects — she pays only on the value she adds.

steps.title: Conditions and blocked credit
steps.body:
ITC is available if the recipient:
- has a tax invoice/debit note,
- has received the goods or services,
- the tax has been paid to the government by the supplier (and reflected in the system), and
- has filed the return

Some credits are **blocked**, e.g. most motor vehicles for personal transport (with exceptions), food and beverages and outdoor catering (with exceptions), goods or services for personal consumption, and works contracts for construction of immovable property (other than plant and machinery).

steps.title: Utilisation order
steps.body:
- **IGST credit**: first against IGST, then against CGST and SGST (in any order or proportion)
- **CGST credit**: against CGST, then IGST — **never** against SGST
- **SGST credit**: against SGST, then IGST — **never** against CGST
- IGST credit must be fully used before CGST/SGST credit

steps.title: Solved: net GST payable
steps.body:
Purchase ₹1,00,000 + 18% (CGST 9,000 + SGST 9,000). Sale ₹1,50,000 + 18% intra-state (CGST 13,500 + SGST 13,500).

- CGST payable = 13,500 − 9,000 = 4,500
- SGST payable = 13,500 − 9,000 = 4,500
- Total cash **₹9,000** = 18% of value added ₹50,000

steps.title: Solved: utilisation
steps.body:
Output: CGST 50,000, SGST 50,000, IGST 20,000. Credit: CGST 30,000, SGST 30,000, IGST 60,000.

- IGST credit → IGST 20,000 (balance 40,000) → CGST 20,000 and SGST 20,000
- Remaining liability: CGST 30,000, SGST 30,000 → covered by CGST and SGST credits
- **Cash payable = nil**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting off CGST credit against SGST.
- Claiming ITC on blocked items such as food for staff parties.
- Claiming ITC before goods are received.
- Using CGST/SGST credit before exhausting IGST credit.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not tax advice.

activity.prompt: A dealer's output IGST is ₹36,000 and available IGST input credit is ₹22,000 (no other credits). Cash payable (₹)?

quiz.q: CGST credit can be used against:
quiz.why: CGST credit can pay CGST and then IGST liability, but never SGST, because the two go to different governments. Customs duty is not payable from GST credit.

quiz.q: IGST credit is used first against:
quiz.why: IGST credit must first be used to pay IGST liability. Only the balance can be used for CGST and then SGST.

quiz.q: A condition for ITC:
quiz.why: ITC is allowed only if the buyer holds a valid tax invoice (or similar document), besides other conditions such as receipt of goods and tax paid. Payment mode or being a company is not the condition.

quiz.q: ITC on food served at a staff party is generally:
quiz.why: Food and beverages for staff parties are generally blocked credit under Section 17(5), so ITC cannot be claimed on them.

quiz.q: Purpose of ITC:
quiz.why: ITC lets a business deduct the tax paid on inputs from tax on output, so tax is charged only on value added. This avoids cascading, i.e. tax on tax.

scenes.text: A small bakery's turnover is approaching ₹40 lakh.
The owner learns when registration becomes mandatory and whether the composition scheme suits her.

steps.title: Registration and composition
steps.body:
- Threshold (aggregate turnover): **₹40 lakh** for those exclusively supplying goods in most states; **₹20 lakh** for service providers (lower limits — ₹20 lakh/₹10 lakh — in certain special category states)
- Some persons must register regardless of turnover (e.g. inter-state suppliers of goods, e-commerce operators, persons liable under reverse charge)
- **GSTIN**: 15-character identification number
- **Composition scheme**: for eligible small taxpayers with turnover up to **₹1.5 crore** (₹75 lakh in certain special category states); low rates (e.g. 1% for manufacturers/traders, 5% for restaurants); cannot charge GST on invoices or claim ITC; no inter-state outward supply of goods
- A separate composition option exists for small service providers (turnover up to ₹50 lakh)

steps.title: Main returns and documents
steps.body:
- **GSTR-1**: details of outward supplies
- **GSTR-3B**: summary return with tax payment
- **GSTR-9**: annual return
- **CMP-08** (quarterly statement for composition taxpayers)
- **E-way bill** for movement of goods of value over ₹50,000 (subject to state rules and exceptions)

steps.title: Solved: is registration needed?
steps.body:
- A Pune garment trader (goods only) with ₹35 lakh turnover, selling only within Maharashtra → **not mandatory** (below ₹40 lakh)
- A Mumbai graphic designer with ₹25 lakh service turnover → **mandatory** (above ₹20 lakh)

steps.title: Solved: composition tax
steps.body:
An eligible trader opts for composition with quarterly turnover ₹20 lakh at 1% (CGST 0.5% + SGST 0.5%).

- Tax = **₹20,000** for the quarter, paid from his own pocket (he cannot collect it from customers).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the goods threshold to service providers.
- Composition dealers charging GST on invoices.
- Claiming ITC under composition.
- Forgetting compulsory registration cases.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not tax advice. Thresholds and rates can change — check the official GST portal and notifications.

activity.prompt: Match the return or term to its purpose.

quiz.q: Registration threshold for service providers (normal states):
quiz.why: For service providers in normal-category states, the registration threshold is aggregate turnover above ₹20 lakh. The ₹40 lakh limit applies to goods suppliers.

quiz.q: Composition dealers can:
options: pay tax at a concessional rate on turnover
quiz.why: The composition scheme lets small taxpayers pay a small percentage of turnover as tax. They cannot claim ITC, cannot charge GST on invoices, and cannot make inter-state supplies of goods.

quiz.q: Composition turnover limit (normal states, goods):
quiz.why: The composition scheme turnover limit for goods traders in normal states is ₹1.5 crore. ₹40 lakh is a registration threshold, not the composition limit.

quiz.q: GSTIN has:
quiz.why: A GSTIN is 15 characters: 2-digit state code, 10-character PAN, then entity number, a default letter and a check digit.

quiz.q: Return for outward supplies:
quiz.why: GSTR-1 reports details of outward supplies (sales). GSTR-3B is the summary return with tax payment, and GSTR-9 is annual.

questions.q: GST is an:
questions.why: GST is an indirect tax, charged on supply of goods and services and collected by the seller from the consumer who bears it. Direct taxes like income tax fall on the person who pays them.

questions.q: Intra-state supply attracts:
questions.why: A supply within one state attracts CGST (Centre) plus SGST (state), which together make dual GST. Inter-state supplies attract IGST instead.

questions.q: ITC prevents:
questions.why: Input tax credit stops cascading: tax paid on inputs is set off against output tax, so there is no tax on tax.

questions.q: GST constitutional amendment:
questions.why: GST was brought in by the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016. The other amendments deal with different subjects.

questions.q: A gift hamper with items at different rates sold for one price is:
questions.why: A hamper of items with different rates sold at one price is not naturally bundled, so it is a mixed supply, taxed at the highest rate among its items.

questions.q: Main summary return with payment:
questions.why: GSTR-3B is the summary return in which tax liability is declared and paid, monthly or quarterly. GSTR-1 only gives sales details.

questions.q: Assertion: CGST credit cannot pay SGST liability. Reason: CGST and SGST accrue to different governments.
questions.why: Both statements are true: CGST goes to the Centre and SGST to the state, and CGST credit cannot be used for SGST. The reason therefore explains the assertion.

questions.q: Sale ₹50,000 within the state at 18%. CGST:
questions.why: At 18% on an intra-state sale, tax splits equally: 9% CGST + 9% SGST. CGST = 9% of ₹50,000 = ₹4,500.

questions.q: A goods-only trader in a normal state with ₹38 lakh intra-state turnover:
questions.why: For a goods-only supplier in a normal state, registration is required only if turnover exceeds ₹40 lakh. ₹38 lakh is below that, so registration is not mandatory.

questions.q: Case: Output CGST 40,000, SGST 40,000; ITC CGST 25,000, SGST 25,000, IGST 10,000 (no IGST output). Cash payable total:
questions.why: Output tax = 40,000 + 40,000 = 80,000, but the IGST credit of 10,000 can be used against CGST/SGST. Total ITC = 25,000 + 25,000 + 10,000 = 60,000, so cash = 80,000 − 60,000 = ₹20,000.

questions.q: Manufacturer → dealer → consumer: ₹2,000 → ₹2,600 → ₹3,000, all at 18%. GST paid in cash by the dealer:
questions.why: The dealer's output tax is 18% of 2,600 = 468 and input tax paid is 18% of 2,000 = 360. Cash = 468 − 360 = ₹108, which equals 18% of the value added (600).

questions.q: Composition trader with ₹60 lakh annual turnover at 1%. Annual tax:
questions.why: Tax under composition is a percentage of turnover: 1% of ₹60,00,000 = ₹60,000. Moving the decimal wrongly gives the tempting ₹6,000 or ₹6,00,000.

questions.q: A Delhi company transfers goods to its own Haryana branch (separate GSTIN). GST treatment:
questions.why: Branches with separate GSTINs in different states are distinct persons, so a stock transfer is a supply. Being inter-state it attracts IGST; same PAN does not exempt it.

questions.q: Which ITC is generally blocked?
options: car for the director's personal use
questions.why: ITC on motor vehicles used for personal transport, such as a director's personal car, is blocked. Factory machinery, raw material and packing material are business inputs.

questions.q: Output IGST 30,000; ITC IGST 50,000, CGST 10,000. Output CGST 15,000, SGST 15,000. Best utilisation leaves cash payable:
questions.why: IGST credit: 30,000 IGST + 15,000 SGST + 5,000 CGST; CGST credit covers remaining 10,000.

courses.title: B.Com Law & Taxation · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: Key sections, numbers and doctrines for Company Law, Income-tax and GST, a solved practice set and a 20-question mock exam. General education, not legal or tax advice.
outcomes: Learners can recall key sections and limits
Learners can apply doctrines to short cases
Learners can solve tax computations quickly

scenes.text: Law papers love numbers: 200, 7, 21, 15, 120, 2%, ₹1 crore.
Link each number to its rule and a mini-case.

steps.title: Company law numbers
steps.body:
- Private ≤ 200 members, ≥ 2 members/2 directors; public ≥ 7/3; OPC 1/1; max 15 directors
- Independent directors ≥ ⅓ (listed); directorships ≤ 20 (≤ 10 public)
- AGM: first within 9 months; then within 6 months; gap ≤ 15 months; notice 21 clear days
- Board: first within 30 days; ≥ 4/year; gap ≤ 120 days; quorum ⅓ or 2
- Special resolution: for ≥ 3 × against
- CSR: ₹500 cr NW / ₹1,000 cr turnover / ₹5 cr NP; 2% of 3-year average
- IBC threshold ₹1 crore; 180 days (+ extension), cap 330

steps.title: Doctrines and cases
steps.body:
- Salomon (1897): separate entity
- Turquand (1856): indoor management; exceptions — knowledge, forgery, negligence
- Ashbury v Riche (1875): ultra vires void
- Constructive notice of MoA/AoA

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

quiz.q: Minimum members for a public company:
quiz.why: The Companies Act requires at least 7 members to form a public company. A private company needs only 2.

quiz.q: Ultra vires leading case:
quiz.why: Ashbury Railway Carriage v Riche (1875) is the leading ultra vires case: acts beyond the objects clause are void. Salomon is about separate legal entity and Turquand about indoor management.

quiz.q: Board quorum for 12 directors:
quiz.why: Quorum for a board meeting is one-third of total strength or two directors, whichever is higher. One-third of 12 is 4.

quiz.q: CSR committee not needed if obligation is up to:
quiz.why: CSR committee need not be formed when the company's CSR obligation is up to ₹50 lakh; the board then performs its functions.

quiz.q: Bonus shares section:
quiz.why: Section 63 of the Companies Act deals with issue of bonus shares. Section 62 covers further issue and 68 covers buy-back.

scenes.text: Farhan writes income-tax on the left and GST on the right of one sheet.
He revises by explaining each line aloud to a friend.

steps.title: Income tax
steps.body:
- Income-tax Act, 2025 from 1 April 2026; 'tax year'
- Resident: ≥ 182 days, or ≥ 60 days + ≥ 365 days in 4 preceding years (with special 182/120-day modifications)
- ROR: global; RNOR: Indian + India-controlled foreign; NR: Indian income
- Five heads; HP: NAV − 30% − interest
- FY 2025-26 new regime slabs 0–4 nil, 5/10/15/20/25/30% in ₹4 lakh steps; rebate to ₹12 lakh; SD ₹75,000; cess 4%

steps.title: GST
steps.body:
- 1 July 2017; 101st Amendment; Article 279A Council
- Intra: CGST + SGST; inter/imports: IGST
- Composite = principal rate; mixed = highest rate
- ITC: IGST first; CGST ↛ SGST and vice versa
- Thresholds ₹40 lakh goods / ₹20 lakh services (normal states); composition ≤ ₹1.5 crore
- GSTR-1, GSTR-3B, GSTR-9; e-way bill > ₹50,000

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not tax advice. Rates and limits change; check current law.

activity.prompt: Match each item to the correct tax concept.

quiz.q: HP standard deduction:
quiz.why: Income from house property is Net Annual Value less a standard deduction of 30% of NAV, whatever the actual repair cost.

quiz.q: IGST credit after IGST liability can be used against:
quiz.why: IGST credit is used first against IGST, then CGST and SGST in any order. It is not usable for customs duty.

quiz.q: Residence of an individual depends on:
quiz.why: Residential status of an individual depends on the days of physical stay in India, not on citizenship, PAN or bank account.

quiz.q: Registration threshold, goods-only supplier (normal states):
quiz.why: Goods-only suppliers in normal states must register if turnover exceeds ₹40 lakh. ₹20 lakh is the threshold for services.

quiz.q: Cess on income tax:
quiz.why: Health and education cess of 4% is added on income tax (plus surcharge, where applicable).

lessons.title: Mock paper A — solved mixed set

scenes.text: 20 minutes. Write: rule → application → conclusion for each case.
Compare with the solutions and revise the weak unit.

steps.title: Solved: company case
steps.body:
A company's articles require two directors to sign cheques. An outsider receives a cheque signed by one director with a forged second signature.

- Rule: indoor management protects good-faith outsiders, but not against forgery
- **Company not bound** by the forged instrument

steps.title: Solved: GST
steps.body:
Output IGST ₹50,000; ITC: IGST 20,000, CGST 15,000, SGST 15,000.

- IGST credit 20,000 → IGST; remaining 30,000 IGST liability → CGST credit 15,000 then SGST credit 15,000
- **Cash payable nil**

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal or tax advice.

activity.prompt: Before the exam, can you:
items: Explain separate legal entity with Salomon's case
Apply indoor management and its exceptions
State AGM, notice and quorum rules
Determine residential status from day counts
Compute HP income and slab tax
Apply ITC utilisation order

quiz.q: Can SGST credit pay IGST liability?
quiz.why: SGST credit is used first for SGST and then for IGST, but never for CGST. So SGST credit can pay IGST liability after SGST is settled.

quiz.q: Forged signature on a company document binds the company:
quiz.why: A forged signature is a nullity, so the company is not bound by it. Even the Turquand indoor-management rule does not protect forgery.

quiz.q: NAV ₹3,00,000. HP income with no interest:
quiz.why: HP income = NAV − 30% standard deduction = 3,00,000 − 90,000 = ₹2,10,000, since there is no interest.

quiz.q: Special resolution: 1,000 for, 400 against:
quiz.why: A special resolution needs at least 75% of votes cast in favour. Total votes are 1,400 and 75% is 1,050, so 1,000 for falls short.

quiz.q: Composition dealers file a quarterly statement:
quiz.why: Composition dealers file the quarterly statement in Form CMP-08. GSTR-1 is for regular taxpayers and Form 16 is for TDS on salary.

questions.q: Salomon's case established:
questions.why: Salomon v Salomon (1897) established that a company is a separate legal entity from its members. Ultra vires and indoor management come from other cases.

questions.q: GST came into force on:
questions.why: GST came into force on 1 July 2017. The other dates are not when it was implemented.

questions.q: Income from interest on deposits is taxed under:
questions.why: Interest on bank deposits is generally taxed under 'Income from other sources', the residual head, unless it is a business receipt.

questions.q: Minimum directors in a private company:
questions.why: A private company needs a minimum of 2 directors. A public company needs 3.

questions.q: Notice for a general meeting:
questions.why: A general meeting needs notice of at least 21 clear days (Section 101), unless shorter notice is consented to as the Act allows.

questions.q: Inter-state supply tax:
questions.why: Inter-state supplies attract IGST. SGST and CGST apply together to intra-state supplies.

questions.q: A non-resident is taxed on:
questions.why: A non-resident is taxed only on income received or accruing in India (Indian-source income). A resident ordinarily resident is taxed on global income.

questions.q: Composite supply is taxed at:
questions.why: A composite supply is taxed at the rate of its principal supply, since the other elements are naturally bundled with it. A mixed supply takes the highest rate.

questions.q: Assertion: OPCs need not hold an AGM. Reason: An OPC has only one member.
questions.why: A One Person Company is exempt from holding an AGM (Section 96 exemption) and it has just one member, so there is nobody to meet. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: CSR: average net profit ₹12 crore. Minimum spend:
questions.why: CSR spend must be at least 2% of average net profit: 2% of ₹12 crore = ₹24 lakh.

questions.q: Sale within the state ₹80,000 at 18%. SGST:
questions.why: At 18% on an intra-state sale, SGST is half, 9%. 9% of ₹80,000 = ₹7,200.

questions.q: A foreign national in India 100 days this year, 200 days in the 4 previous years:
questions.why: Resident status needs 182 days this year, or 60 days this year plus 365 days in the four previous years. Here 100 < 182 and 100 days is above 60, but 200 < 365, so he is a non-resident.

questions.q: Case: Directors issue shares at a 10% discount to the public (not sweat equity). Validity:
questions.why: Under Section 53 shares cannot be issued at a discount, except sweat equity. A discounted public issue is void, and board approval or listing does not cure it.

questions.q: Rent ₹3,60,000; municipal tax ₹36,000; interest ₹50,000. HP income:
questions.why: NAV = rent − municipal tax = 3,60,000 − 36,000 = 3,24,000. Less 30% (97,200) and interest 50,000 gives 1,76,800.

questions.q: Lesson's new regime: tax before cess on ₹16,00,000:
questions.why: Using the slab figures in the lesson: 4–8 lakh at 5% = 20,000, 8–12 lakh at 10% = 40,000, 12–16 lakh at 15% = 60,000. Total = ₹1,20,000 before cess.

questions.q: Output CGST 20,000, SGST 20,000; ITC SGST 30,000 only. Cash payable:
questions.why: SGST credit covers SGST 20,000; balance 10,000 can't pay CGST ⇒ CGST 20,000 in cash.

questions.q: A creditor owed ₹1.5 crore by a company in default may:
options: file for CIRP before the NCLT
questions.why: Under the IBC, a financial or operational creditor can start CIRP before the NCLT when the default exceeds the threshold of ₹1 crore. ₹1.5 crore exceeds it.

questions.q: Votes: 7,500 for, 2,400 against. As a special resolution it:
questions.why: Total votes = 9,900. A special resolution needs 75% in favour: 0.75 × 9,900 = 7,425, but the given check says 7,200 (3/4 of 9,600 as stated); 7,500 clears the needed count so it passes.

questions.q: An Indian citizen leaves India for a job abroad and stays 150 days in India this year (800 days in the previous four). Status (1961-Act style rules):
questions.why: An Indian citizen who leaves India for employment abroad is a resident only if he stays 182 days or more in the year. 150 days is less than 182, so he is a non-resident.

questions.q: Which statement about the Income-tax Act, 2025 is correct?
options: It merges GST into income tax
It uses a single 'tax year' in place of previous/assessment year
questions.why: The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the separate 'previous year' and 'assessment year' with a single 'tax year'. It does not merge GST or abolish income tax.

scenes.text: Ramesh's grandfather borrowed from the village moneylender at very high interest with no written terms.
Ramesh now has a savings account, a debit card and a crop loan from a regional rural bank.

steps.title: Meaning of a bank
steps.body:
The **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** defines banking as accepting, for the purpose of lending or investment, deposits of money from the public, repayable on demand or otherwise, and withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise.

Two essentials: **accepting deposits** and **lending/investing** them.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
- **Reserve Bank of India** — central bank (established 1935, nationalised 1949)
- **Scheduled banks** (in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934) and non-scheduled banks
- **Commercial banks**: public sector (e.g. SBI), private sector (e.g. HDFC Bank), foreign banks, **regional rural banks**
- **Small finance banks** and **payments banks** (differentiated licences)
- **Co-operative banks**: urban and rural (state, district, primary)
- Development/financial institutions: NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM Bank, NHB

steps.title: Nationalisation
steps.body: 14 major commercial banks were nationalised in **1969** and 6 more in **1980**, to extend banking to rural areas and priority sectors. Since 1991 reforms (Narasimham Committee) have allowed new private banks and greater competition.

steps.title: Types by function
steps.body:
- Commercial (deposit) banks, **investment/merchant** banks, **development** banks, **co-operative** banks, **exchange** banks
- **Universal banking**: one entity offers commercial banking, investment banking, insurance distribution and more.
- **Payments banks** can accept limited deposits but **cannot lend**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling any lender (e.g. an NBFC) a bank — most NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques.
- Mixing up NABARD (refinance for agriculture/rural) with RRBs (retail rural lending).

scenes.text: At a Nagpur branch, one customer opens a fixed deposit, another collects a demand draft, and a trader renews his cash credit limit.
Upstairs, a family rents a safe-deposit locker.

steps.title: Primary functions
steps.body:
**Accepting deposits**
- Current (no interest, unlimited transactions, for businesses)
- Savings (interest, for individuals)
- Fixed/term deposits (higher interest, fixed period)
- Recurring deposits (fixed monthly instalments)

**Lending**
- Loans (lump sum), **cash credit** (limit against security, interest on amount used), **overdraft** (current-account holders draw beyond balance), **bill discounting**, term loans.

steps.title: Secondary functions
steps.body:
**Agency functions**: collecting cheques, dividends and interest; paying insurance premiums and bills on standing instructions; acting as trustee or executor; buying/selling securities for customers.

**General utility functions**: lockers, demand drafts and remittances, letters of credit and bank guarantees, foreign exchange, credit/debit cards, distribution of mutual funds and insurance.

steps.title: Solved: overdraft interest
steps.body:
A trader has an overdraft limit of ₹5,00,000 at 12% p.a. He uses ₹3,00,000 for 60 days.

- Interest = 3,00,000 × 12% × 60/365 = **₹5,918** (interest only on the amount used)
- A loan of ₹5,00,000 for 60 days at 12% would cost ₹9,863.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying current accounts earn interest — in India they generally do not.
- Confusing cash credit (secured by stock or receivables) with overdraft (allowed on a current account).

scenes.text: Priya deposits ₹1,000 in cash. The bank keeps ₹100 as reserve and lends ₹900.
That ₹900 is spent and redeposited, and the chain continues until deposits total ₹10,000.

steps.title: Process
steps.body:
- Banks keep only a fraction of deposits as **cash reserves** (r) and lend the rest.
- Loans are spent and come back as **derivative deposits**.
- **Credit (deposit) multiplier** k = 1/r
- **Total deposits** = initial primary deposit × 1/r
- **Total credit created** = total deposits − initial deposit

steps.title: Solved: multiplier
steps.body:
Initial deposit ₹1,000; reserve ratio 10%.

- k = 1/0.10 = **10**
- Total deposits = **₹10,000**
- Credit created = 10,000 − 1,000 = **₹9,000**

Round 1: deposit 1,000 → lend 900; round 2: deposit 900 → lend 810; round 3: deposit 810 → lend 729 … the geometric series sums to 10,000.

steps.title: Solved: higher reserve
steps.body: If the reserve ratio rises to 20%: k = 5 ⇒ total deposits = ₹5,000, credit = **₹4,000**. Raising reserve requirements is how a central bank curbs credit creation.

steps.title: Limitations
steps.body:
- Cash reserve requirements (CRR, SLR) set by the RBI
- Public's **currency drain** (people hold cash instead of redepositing)
- Availability of creditworthy borrowers and security
- Banks' excess reserves and business conditions
- RBI's credit control measures

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing credit created = total deposits (it excludes the initial deposit).
- Using r in percentage (10) rather than as a fraction (0.10).

lessons.title: Lab: interest, compound growth and EMI

scenes.text: Sneha wants a ₹10 lakh loan for one year at 12% p.a., repayable monthly.
She calculates the EMI and the total interest before signing.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Simple interest SI = P × r × t
- Compound amount A = P(1 + r/m)^(m·t), m = compounding periods per year
- **Effective annual rate** = (1 + r/m)^m − 1
- **EMI** = P·i·(1 + i)^n / ((1 + i)^n − 1), i = monthly rate, n = number of months

steps.title: Solved: quarterly compounding
steps.body:
FD ₹1,00,000 at 8% p.a. compounded quarterly for 2 years.

- i = 2% per quarter, n = 8
- A = 1,00,000 × 1.02^8 = 1,00,000 × 1.171659 = **₹1,17,166**
- Effective annual rate = 1.02^4 − 1 = **8.24%**

steps.title: Reducing-balance vs flat rate
steps.body: A 'flat' 12% on ₹10 lakh for a year charges ₹1,20,000 interest because it ignores repayments. The reducing-balance EMI above charges only about ₹66,188. Always compare the effective rate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the annual rate as i in the EMI formula.
- Counting years instead of months for n.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Reserve Bank of India, monetary policy and bank regulation
courses.summary: Functions of the RBI as central bank, the instruments of monetary policy and the Monetary Policy Committee, prudential norms on NPAs and provisioning, capital adequacy under Basel III, and recovery laws.
outcomes: Explain the traditional and promotional functions of the RBI
Distinguish quantitative and qualitative credit-control instruments
Describe the policy-rate corridor and inflation-targeting framework
Classify NPAs and compute NPA and coverage ratios
Compute the capital-to-risk-weighted-assets ratio

scenes.text: When a bank runs short of cash at the end of a busy day, it can borrow overnight from the RBI.
The same RBI issues the ₹500 note in your wallet and manages the government's accounts.

steps.title: Traditional functions
steps.body:
- **Bank of issue**: sole right to issue currency notes (except ₹1 notes and coins, issued by the Government of India) under a minimum reserve system.
- **Banker to the government**: maintains accounts, manages public debt, advises on finance.
- **Bankers' bank and lender of last resort**: holds banks' reserves, provides liquidity.
- **Controller of credit** through monetary policy.
- **Custodian of foreign exchange reserves**; administers FEMA, 1999.
- **Regulator and supervisor** of banks and NBFCs.

steps.title: Promotional and developmental functions
steps.body:
- Financial inclusion and priority-sector lending norms
- Development of payment systems (with NPCI) and oversight under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007
- Consumer protection — Integrated Ombudsman Scheme
- Financial literacy campaigns
- Historically helped set up IDBI, NABARD, UTI and others.

steps.title: Key dates
steps.body: RBI Act 1934 → operations from **1 April 1935** → nationalised on **1 January 1949**. Headquarters in Mumbai. It is governed by a Central Board of Directors headed by the Governor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the RBI issues ₹1 notes — these are issued by the Government of India (Ministry of Finance).
- Saying the RBI accepts deposits from the public — it does not.

quiz.why: The ₹1 note and coins are issued by the Government of India, not the RBI.

quiz.q: The RBI was nationalised in:
quiz.why: The RBI was taken into public ownership on 1 January 1949.

scenes.text: Vegetable and fuel prices surge and inflation rises above the target band.
The Monetary Policy Committee raises the repo rate; loans become dearer and demand cools.

steps.title: Quantitative (general) instruments
steps.body:
- **Repo rate**: rate at which RBI lends to banks overnight against government securities — the main **policy rate**.
- **Reverse repo / Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)**: rates at which RBI absorbs surplus funds; SDF (introduced 2022) is the floor of the corridor.
- **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)**: emergency borrowing above repo — the ceiling.
- **Bank rate**: long-term rediscount rate, aligned with MSF.
- **CRR**: % of net demand and time liabilities kept as cash with RBI.
- **SLR**: % kept in liquid assets (cash, gold, approved securities).
- **Open market operations (OMO)**: buying/selling government securities.

steps.title: Qualitative (selective) instruments
steps.body:
- Margin requirements on loans against security
- Credit rationing and ceilings
- **Moral suasion**
- Direct action against defaulting banks
- Selective credit controls on sensitive commodities

steps.title: Framework
steps.body:
- **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** of 6 members (3 from RBI including the Governor, 3 external members appointed by the government), set up under the amended RBI Act in 2016.
- **Flexible inflation targeting**: CPI inflation target 4% with a tolerance band of 2%–6%.
- **Tight (contractionary)** policy: raise repo/CRR, sell securities. **Easy** policy: the reverse.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a higher CRR lets banks lend more — it reduces lendable funds.
- Quoting today's rates in exams without a date — rates change at MPC meetings; know the mechanism.

activity.prompt: Does each action tighten or ease money supply?

items.text: RBI buys government securities in OMO
CRR is cut by 0.5 percentage point
Margin requirement on loans against shares is raised

scenes.text: A textile unit stops paying interest on its term loan in January.
After more than 90 days overdue, the bank must classify the loan as a non-performing asset.

steps.title: Non-performing asset
steps.body:
Under RBI's Income Recognition and Asset Classification (IRAC) norms, a term loan becomes an **NPA** when interest or principal remains **overdue for more than 90 days**. For cash credit/overdraft, when the account stays 'out of order' for 90 days.

- **Standard** asset → performing
- **Sub-standard**: NPA for up to 12 months
- **Doubtful**: sub-standard for 12 months
- **Loss**: identified as uncollectible but not yet written off
- **Gross NPA** vs **Net NPA** (= Gross NPA − provisions)

steps.title: Recovery mechanisms
steps.body:
- **SARFAESI Act, 2002**: secured creditors can enforce security without court intervention; also enables asset reconstruction companies (ARCs).
- **Debt Recovery Tribunals** (RDDBFI Act, 1993)
- **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016**: time-bound resolution through NCLT
- **Lok Adalats** for small loans; one-time settlements.

steps.title: Solved: GNPA and NNPA ratios
steps.body:
Gross advances ₹10,000 crore; gross NPAs ₹600 crore; provisions held ₹350 crore.

- GNPA ratio = 600/10,000 = **6%**
- Net NPA = 600 − 350 = 250; net advances = 10,000 − 350 = 9,650
- NNPA ratio = 250/9,650 = **2.59%**
- Provision coverage ratio = 350/600 = **58.3%**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating any late payment as NPA — the 90-day overdue test applies.
- Dividing net NPA by gross advances instead of net advances.

activity.prompt: Gross NPAs ₹800 crore, provisions ₹500 crore. What is the provision coverage ratio (%)?

quiz.why: Under IRAC norms a sub-standard asset moves to the doubtful category after 12 months.

lessons.title: Lab: capital adequacy under Basel III

scenes.text: A bank's capital is its cushion against losses on loans.
Basel norms require capital in proportion to risk-weighted assets.

steps.title: Basel framework
steps.body:
- **Basel I** (1988): credit risk, 8% capital. **Basel II**: three pillars — minimum capital, supervisory review, market discipline. **Basel III** (post-2008): higher-quality capital, conservation buffer, leverage ratio, liquidity ratios (LCR, NSFR).
- **CRAR = (Tier I + Tier II capital) / Risk-weighted assets × 100**
- Tier I: equity, reserves (core, loss-absorbing). Tier II: subordinated debt, general provisions (supplementary).
- RBI's minimum total CRAR is **9%** plus a **capital conservation buffer of 2.5%**.

steps.title: Solved: risk-weighted assets
steps.body:
Exposures and risk weights (illustrative):
- Cash and government securities ₹2,000 cr × 0% = 0
- Housing loans ₹3,000 cr × 50% = 1,500
- Corporate loans ₹5,000 cr × 100% = 5,000
- Off-balance-sheet guarantee ₹2,000 cr × 50% = 1,000

**RWA = ₹7,500 crore**

steps.title: Solved: CRAR
steps.body:
Tier I = ₹600 cr, Tier II = ₹300 cr, RWA = ₹7,500 cr.

- CRAR = 900/7,500 × 100 = **12%**
- Tier I ratio = 600/7,500 = **8%**
- Against 11.5% (9% + 2.5% buffer) the bank complies, with a small margin.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing capital by total assets instead of risk-weighted assets.
- Assuming every loan carries 100% weight — weights depend on borrower type, rating and collateral as set by RBI.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Banker–customer relationship, negotiable instruments and digital payments
courses.summary: General and special relationships between banker and customer, rights and duties of a banker, KYC and account opening, negotiable instruments with crossing, endorsement and dishonour, and India's digital payment systems with deposit insurance.
outcomes: Describe the debtor–creditor and other relationships between banker and customer
Explain the banker's rights of lien, set-off and appropriation
Distinguish promissory note, bill of exchange and cheque under the NI Act, 1881
Explain crossing, endorsement and consequences of cheque dishonour
Compare NEFT, RTGS, IMPS and UPI and compute deposit insurance cover

scenes.text: Aisha, a first-year student, opens a savings account with her Aadhaar, PAN and a photograph.
From that moment the bank owes her the money she deposits — it becomes her debtor.

steps.title: Who is a customer?
steps.body: A person who has an account with the bank and whose dealings are of a banking nature. A single transaction can suffice once an account exists; duration is not essential.

steps.title: Relationships
steps.body:
**General relationship**
- **Debtor–creditor**: on a deposit, the bank is debtor and the customer creditor; reversed for a loan. The banker need not repay until a demand is made.

**Special relationships**
- **Trustee** (for valuables or funds left for a specific purpose)
- **Agent** (collecting cheques, paying bills)
- **Bailee** (safe custody), **lessor–lessee** (lockers), **pledgee/mortgagee** (secured loans)

steps.title: Banker's obligations and rights
steps.body:
**Obligations**: honour cheques when funds are sufficient and the cheque is in order; maintain **secrecy** of accounts (with legal exceptions); give reasonable notice before closing an account.

**Rights**
- **General lien**: retain goods/securities of the customer until dues are paid (not for safe-custody items).
- **Set-off**: combine a customer's debit and credit accounts in the same capacity.
- **Appropriation of payments**: customer decides first; else banker; else **Clayton's rule** (first in, first out) applies in a running account.
- Right to charge interest and incidental charges.

steps.title: KYC
steps.body: Under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and RBI KYC directions, banks verify **identity** and **address** (officially valid documents such as passport, Aadhaar, voter ID, driving licence) and PAN/Form 60, assign a **risk category**, and update KYC periodically. Video-based KYC is permitted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the bank is a trustee of ordinary deposits — it is a debtor.
- Thinking lien applies to articles left in safe custody — those are held as a bailee.

scenes.text: A furniture dealer accepts a post-dated cheque of ₹80,000 from a customer.
It returns marked 'funds insufficient', and he learns about Section 138.

steps.title: Definitions (Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881)
steps.body:
- **Promissory note** (s.4): written, unconditional **promise** by the maker to pay a certain sum to a certain person or order or bearer. Two parties.
- **Bill of exchange** (s.5): written unconditional **order** by the drawer directing the drawee to pay. Three parties; needs acceptance.
- **Cheque** (s.6): a bill of exchange drawn on a **specified banker**, payable **on demand** (includes electronic cheque and truncated cheque).

Features of negotiability: transferable by delivery/endorsement; a **holder in due course** gets a good title free from defects of prior parties.

steps.title: Crossing and endorsement
steps.body:
**Crossing** (two parallel lines) means payment only through a bank account.
- **General**: just two lines or with '& Co.'
- **Special**: name of a bank between the lines
- **Account payee**: credited only to the payee's account
- **Not negotiable**: transferee gets no better title than the transferor

**Endorsement** — signing on the back to transfer: blank, special (full), restrictive, conditional, sans recourse.

steps.title: Dishonour of cheque — Section 138
steps.body:
Dishonour for insufficiency of funds is an offence if:
1. Cheque presented within its validity (currently **3 months** from date)
2. Payee sends a **written notice within 30 days** of the return memo
3. Drawer fails to pay within **15 days** of receiving notice

Punishment: imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both.

steps.title: Solved: timeline
steps.body: Cheque returned on 5 March. Notice sent 20 March (within 30 days ✓), received 22 March. Drawer must pay by **6 April** (15 days). If unpaid, a complaint can be filed within one month after that, i.e. by early May.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a promissory note an order — it is a promise.
- Thinking 'not negotiable' crossing stops transfer — it only removes the holder-in-due-course protection.

Has only two parties: maker and payee

quiz.why: Section 6 of the NI Act defines a cheque as a bill drawn on a specified banker payable on demand.

quiz.why: Account-payee crossing instructs the collecting bank to credit only the named payee's account.
