scenes.text: A student scans a QR code and pays ₹15 for tea in two seconds.
The same day his father's company pays a supplier ₹40 lakh through RTGS.

steps.title: Major systems
steps.body:
- **NEFT**: deferred net settlement in half-hourly batches, available 24×7; no minimum amount.
- **RTGS**: real-time gross settlement for high-value transfers; minimum **₹2 lakh**; available 24×7.
- **IMPS** (NPCI): instant 24×7 interbank transfer via mobile/net banking.
- **UPI** (NPCI, 2016): instant payments using a virtual payment address and QR codes; supports collect requests and AutoPay mandates.
- **NACH**: bulk credits (salaries, dividends) and debits (EMIs, SIPs).
- **Cards**: debit, credit, prepaid; RuPay is India's domestic card network.
- **CTS**: cheque truncation — images instead of physical movement.

steps.title: Safety and protection
steps.body:
- **Deposit insurance** by DICGC: up to **₹5 lakh per depositor per bank** (principal + interest, same right and capacity), since February 2020.
- Customer liability rules: report unauthorised electronic transactions promptly (zero liability if bank is at fault or if reported within 3 working days for third-party breach).
- Never share OTP/UPI PIN; a PIN is needed only to **pay**, never to **receive**.

steps.title: Solved: deposit insurance
steps.body:
Ravi has, in one bank, savings ₹2,50,000, FD ₹3,00,000 (both in his own name), and a joint account with his wife ₹4,00,000.

- Individual capacity: 5,50,000 ⇒ insured **₹5,00,000**, uninsured ₹50,000
- Joint account is a different capacity ⇒ insured up to ₹5,00,000 separately ⇒ **₹4,00,000** covered

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking RTGS works for ₹50,000 — use NEFT/IMPS/UPI.
- Believing DICGC cover is per account — it is per depositor per bank in the same capacity.

activity.prompt: A depositor holds ₹3,20,000 in savings and ₹4,10,000 in an FD in her own name at one bank, which fails. How much (₹) is uninsured under DICGC?

quiz.q: Minimum amount for RTGS is:
quiz.why: RTGS is meant for high-value transfers with a minimum of ₹2 lakh.

scenes.text: Each morning the manager gets tricky cases: a stale cheque, a lien dispute, a customer's death.
Apply the rules to decide.

steps.title: Case 1: stale cheque
steps.body: A cheque dated 2 January is presented on 10 April. **Decision**: return it as **stale** — cheques are valid for 3 months from their date; the drawer can issue a fresh one or revalidate it.

steps.title: Case 2: death of a customer
steps.body: The bank learns that an account holder has died. **Decision**: stop payment of all cheques; settle the balance to the **nominee** (or legal heirs) after verifying the death certificate and following the bank's claim procedure.

steps.title: Case 3: garnishee order
steps.body: A court attaches a customer's account balance. **Decision**: freeze the attached amount and remit as directed by the court; inform the customer. Credits received after the order are not attached unless the order says so.

steps.title: Case 4: Clayton's rule
steps.body: A partner retires on 1 July when the firm's overdraft is ₹1,00,000. Later credits of ₹1,20,000 and debits of ₹80,000 pass through the same account. **Decision**: by first-in-first-out, the credits extinguish the old ₹1,00,000 debt — the retired partner's liability is discharged. Banks therefore **stop the account** and open a new one on retirement.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paying a cheque after notice of the drawer's death — authority ends on notice.
- Continuing the same account after a partner retires, which releases the old partner's liability under Clayton's rule.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Principles of insurance and life insurance
courses.summary: Risk and its management, the nature and fundamental principles of insurance, life insurance products, premium and bonus computation, and human life value with claim settlement.
outcomes: Distinguish types of risk and the methods of handling risk
Explain the seven fundamental principles of insurance with examples
Compare term, endowment, whole-life, money-back and unit-linked plans
Compute pure premium, bonus additions and maturity value
Estimate insurance need by the human life value method

lessons.title: Risk and the nature of insurance

scenes.text: Out of 1,000 shops in a market, perhaps two catch fire each year — but no one knows which.
If each shopkeeper pays a small premium into a pool, the two unlucky ones can be fully compensated.

steps.title: Risk
steps.body:
- **Risk**: uncertainty about a future loss.
- **Pure risk** (loss or no loss: fire, death) vs **speculative risk** (loss or gain: share trading). Only pure risks are normally insurable.
- **Static vs dynamic**, **fundamental** (affects many: war, inflation) vs **particular** (individual: theft).
- **Risk management**: avoid, reduce (prevention), retain (self-insure), **transfer** (insurance), share.

steps.title: Insurance
steps.body:
Insurance is a **contract** in which the insurer, for a consideration called **premium**, agrees to compensate the insured for a specified loss or pay a sum on the happening of a specified event. It works on **pooling** and the **law of large numbers**: the larger the group, the more predictable the total loss.

**Insurable risk**: large number of similar units, accidental and unintentional loss, measurable loss, not catastrophic for the pool, economically feasible premium.

steps.title: Functions
steps.body:
- **Primary**: provide certainty, protection, risk sharing.
- **Secondary**: loss prevention, capital formation (long-term funds invested in infrastructure), credit support (insured assets are better collateral).
- Life insurance is a contract of **assurance** (death certain, timing uncertain); general insurance is a contract of **indemnity**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling share-market loss insurable — it is a speculative risk.
- Treating insurance as gambling — gambling creates risk; insurance transfers an existing risk.

activity.prompt: Is the risk pure (normally insurable) or speculative?

quiz.q: The law of large numbers helps insurers because:
options: total losses of a big group are predictable
quiz.why: Individual losses are uncertain, but the average loss in a large pool is stable and can be priced.

quiz.q: Transferring risk to an insurer is a method of:
quiz.why: Buying insurance shifts the financial consequence of the loss to the insurer.

quiz.q: War and inflation are examples of:
quiz.why: They affect large sections of society at once, so they are fundamental risks.

scenes.text: Vikram buys a health policy without disclosing his diabetes.
When he claims for a related hospitalisation, the insurer may repudiate the claim for breach of utmost good faith.

steps.title: The seven principles
steps.body:
1. **Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei)**: both parties must disclose all material facts.
2. **Insurable interest**: the insured must suffer financial loss from the event (owner of property; self, spouse for life).
3. **Indemnity**: compensation only up to the actual loss — no profit (not for life insurance).
4. **Contribution**: with multiple policies on the same risk, insurers share the loss rateably.
5. **Subrogation**: after paying, the insurer steps into the insured's rights against third parties.
6. **Proximate cause** (causa proxima): the dominant, effective cause must be an insured peril.
7. **Loss minimisation**: the insured must act as if uninsured to limit loss.

steps.title: When insurable interest must exist
steps.body:
- **Life**: at the time of contract.
- **Marine**: at the time of loss.
- **Fire/other property**: both at the time of contract and of loss.

steps.title: Solved: contribution
steps.body:
A building worth ₹20 lakh is insured with A for ₹12 lakh and B for ₹8 lakh. Loss ₹5 lakh.

- A pays 12/20 × 5 = **₹3 lakh**; B pays 8/20 × 5 = **₹2 lakh**
- Total ₹5 lakh = actual loss (indemnity respected).

steps.title: Solved: subrogation
steps.body: A truck negligently damages an insured shop; the insurer pays ₹2 lakh. The insurer can now recover ₹2 lakh from the truck owner. If the shopkeeper had also collected from the truck owner, he would have to pass that sum to the insurer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying indemnity to life insurance — a life cannot be valued, so the sum assured is paid.
- Confusing contribution (between insurers) with subrogation (insurer vs third party).

activity.prompt: Which principle applies?

Payout limited to the actual repair cost of a car

Insured cannot profit from an inflated claim

quiz.why: Marine cargo changes hands during transit, so interest is needed when the loss occurs.

quiz.q: Contribution applies when:
options: several policies cover the same risk
the insurer sues a third party
quiz.why: Insurers on the same subject matter share a loss rateably so the insured is not over-compensated.

quiz.q: Which principle does NOT apply to life insurance?
quiz.why: Human life cannot be valued in money, so life policies pay the agreed sum rather than indemnify a loss.

scenes.text: Arjun, 30, earns ₹12 lakh a year and has a young daughter.
An agent pushes an endowment plan; a friend advises a large term plan. Which fits his need?

steps.title: Types of policies
steps.body:
- **Term insurance**: pure risk cover for a fixed term; pays only on death; lowest premium.
- **Whole life**: cover for the entire life; pays on death.
- **Endowment**: pays on death within term or on survival to maturity; saving + protection; higher premium.
- **Money-back**: periodic survival benefits plus death cover.
- **ULIP**: premium split between cover and market-linked funds; 5-year lock-in.
- **Pension/annuity** plans; **joint life** and **children's** plans.
- **With-profit** (participating) policies share in bonuses; without-profit do not.

steps.title: Industry and regulation
steps.body:
- Life insurance was nationalised in **1956** with the formation of **LIC**.
- The **IRDA Act, 1999** opened the sector to private insurers and created the regulator, now **IRDAI**.
- Key policyholder protections: free-look period, grievance redressal (Bima Bharosa, Insurance Ombudsman), and claim-settlement timelines set by IRDAI regulations.
- **Nomination** and **assignment** are governed by sections 39 and 38 of the Insurance Act, 1938.

steps.title: Solved: reversionary bonus
steps.body:
Endowment sum assured ₹5,00,000 for 20 years; simple reversionary bonus ₹50 per ₹1,000 SA per year (assumed constant).

- Annual bonus = 50 × 500 = ₹25,000
- 20 years ⇒ ₹5,00,000
- **Maturity value = 5,00,000 + 5,00,000 = ₹10,00,000** (plus any final additional bonus)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating bonuses as guaranteed — they are declared annually based on the insurer's surplus.
- Comparing an endowment's return with a term plan's — a term plan buys protection, not savings.

activity.prompt: Sum assured ₹2,00,000, bonus ₹45 per ₹1,000 per year for 15 years. What is the total bonus (₹)?

quiz.q: The cheapest pure protection policy is:
quiz.why: Term insurance pays only on death and has no savings element, so its premium is lowest.

quiz.q: LIC was formed in:
quiz.why: Life insurance business was nationalised and LIC set up in 1956.

quiz.q: Nomination under a life policy is governed by section:
quiz.why: Section 39 of the Insurance Act, 1938 deals with nomination by the policyholder.

lessons.title: Lab: premium, human life value and claims

scenes.text: Arjun's adviser estimates what his family would lose if he died tomorrow.
The answer is the present value of his future contribution to the family.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Pure (risk) premium** = probability of death × sum assured (from mortality tables).
- **Office (gross) premium** = pure premium + loading for expenses, commission and profit.
- **Human life value (HLV)** = PV of future net income contributed to the family = annual contribution × PV annuity factor.
- PV annuity factor = (1 − (1 + r)^(−n))/r.

steps.title: Solved: pure premium
steps.body:
Probability of death at age 30 within a year = 0.002 (illustrative). Sum assured ₹50 lakh.

- Pure premium = 0.002 × 50,00,000 = **₹10,000**
- With 25% loading, office premium ≈ **₹12,500**

steps.title: Solved: human life value
steps.body:
Arjun earns ₹10 lakh a year; spends ₹3 lakh on himself. Working years left 20; discount rate 7%.

- Annual contribution = ₹7 lakh
- 1.07^20 = 3.8697 ⇒ factor = (1 − 0.25842)/0.07 = **10.594**
- HLV = 7 × 10.594 = **₹74.16 lakh** ⇒ roughly ₹75 lakh of cover.

steps.title: Claim settlement steps
steps.body:
1. Intimation to the insurer with policy number
2. Claim form, death certificate, ID of nominee, bank details
3. Additional documents for early/unnatural death (FIR, post-mortem)
4. Insurer's assessment and settlement within IRDAI timelines
5. Grievance → Ombudsman if unresolved

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using gross income instead of net contribution in HLV.
- Ignoring discounting — ₹7 lakh × 20 = ₹1.4 crore overstates the need.

quiz.why: HLV measures the economic value the family would lose, i.e. the PV of future contributions.

questions.why: It is Latin for utmost good faith.

questions.why: The creditor stands to lose the amount owed, so interest is limited to the debt.

questions.q: Indemnity means:

questions.why: Indemnity compensates the actual loss, no more and no less.

questions.why: Pure premium = ₹10,000; with 20% loading = ₹12,000.

courses.summary: Fire, marine, motor and health insurance with the average clause, deductibles, co-payment and no-claim bonus; claim computations; and a whole-subject revision sheet with a full exam.
outcomes: Explain the kinds of fire and marine policies and marine losses
Describe motor third-party and own-damage cover and health insurance features

scenes.text: A Ludhiana trader insured his godown stock for ₹6 lakh though it was worth ₹8 lakh.
A fire caused a ₹2 lakh loss, and he was surprised to receive only ₹1.5 lakh.

steps.title: Fire insurance
steps.body:
Covers loss by fire and allied perils (lightning, explosion, riot, storm, flood as per policy wording).

- **Specific policy**: fixed sum regardless of value.
- **Average policy**: contains the **average clause** — if under-insured, claim is reduced proportionately.
- **Floating policy**: one sum covering goods in several locations.
- **Reinstatement policy**: pays the cost of replacement rather than depreciated value.
- **Consequential loss (loss of profit)**: covers business interruption.

steps.title: Marine insurance
steps.body:
- **Hull** (ship), **cargo** (goods), **freight** (shipping income).
- Policies: **voyage**, **time**, **mixed**, **valued**, **open/floating**.
- Losses: **total loss** (actual or constructive), **partial loss**: **particular average** (borne by the owner of the damaged property) and **general average** (deliberate sacrifice for common safety, shared by all interests — e.g. jettisoning cargo in a storm).
- Marine Insurance Act, 1963 governs marine contracts in India.

steps.title: Solved: average clause
steps.body:
Claim = Loss × (Sum insured / Value of property at time of loss)

- Sum insured ₹6,00,000; value ₹8,00,000; loss ₹2,00,000
- Claim = 2,00,000 × 6/8 = **₹1,50,000**
- The trader bears ₹50,000 as his own insurer for the uninsured portion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the average clause when the property is fully insured — claim then equals the loss.
- Confusing general average (shared sacrifice) with particular average (accidental, owner bears).

activity.prompt: Stock worth ₹10,00,000 insured for ₹7,00,000 with an average clause. Fire loss ₹3,00,000. Claim admissible (₹)?

quiz.why: A voluntary sacrifice for the common safety of the voyage is general average, shared by all interests.

quiz.q: A policy that pays the cost of replacing damaged property is a:
quiz.why: A reinstatement policy pays to rebuild or replace rather than the depreciated value.

quiz.q: Marine insurance in India is governed by the:
quiz.why: The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 codifies marine insurance law in India.

scenes.text: Meera hasn't made a claim in three years, so her own-damage premium has a no-claim bonus.
Her father's health policy has a 20% co-payment because he is a senior citizen.

steps.title: Motor insurance
steps.body:
- **Third-party liability** cover is **compulsory** under the **Motor Vehicles Act, 1988** — death, injury and property damage to others.
- **Comprehensive** = third party + **own damage** (accident, theft, fire, natural calamities).
- **IDV** (insured declared value) = manufacturer's price less depreciation — the maximum payable on total loss/theft.
- **No-claim bonus (NCB)**: discount on own-damage premium for claim-free years; belongs to the owner and can be transferred to a new vehicle.
- Add-ons: zero depreciation, engine protect, roadside assistance.

steps.title: Health insurance
steps.body:
- **Indemnity** (hospitalisation) plans and **benefit** (fixed sum on diagnosis, e.g. critical illness) plans.
- **Individual** vs **family floater**.
- Features: cashless treatment at network hospitals via TPA, pre- and post-hospitalisation cover, waiting periods for pre-existing diseases, **co-payment** (insured bears a % of each claim), **deductible**, sub-limits on room rent.
- Premium is deductible under section 80D of the Income-tax Act (subject to limits and the tax regime chosen).

steps.title: Solved: co-payment and deductible
steps.body:
Hospital bill ₹2,00,000; sum insured ₹5,00,000; co-payment 20%.

- Insurer pays 80% = **₹1,60,000**; insured pays ₹40,000.

With a ₹50,000 deductible (no co-pay): insurer pays 2,00,000 − 50,000 = **₹1,50,000**.

steps.title: Solved: NCB
steps.body:
Own-damage premium before discount ₹10,000; NCB 20%.

- OD premium = 10,000 × 0.8 = **₹8,000**
- Third-party premium (fixed by IRDAI) is added without NCB.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying NCB to the third-party premium.
- Assuming cashless means free — co-pays, deductibles and non-payable items still apply.

activity.prompt: Health claim ₹3,50,000, sum insured ₹10,00,000, co-payment 10%. Amount paid by insurer (₹)?

quiz.why: The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 makes third-party cover mandatory for vehicles on public roads.

quiz.why: The no-claim bonus is a discount on the own-damage component only.

quiz.why: In a floater, the whole family draws from a single shared sum insured.

steps.title: Banking
steps.body:
- Credit multiplier = 1/r; total deposits = initial × 1/r; credit = total − initial
- EMI = P·i(1+i)^n/((1+i)^n − 1); effective rate = (1 + r/m)^m − 1

steps.title: Insurance
steps.body:

- Pure premium = q × SA; office premium = pure + loading

The law asks: was there a definite offer, an absolute acceptance, and an intention to create legal relations?

steps.title: Contract = agreement + enforceability
steps.body: Section 2(h): a contract is an agreement enforceable by law. Section 2(e): every promise and every set of promises forming consideration for each other is an agreement. So: offer (proposal, s.2(a)) + acceptance (s.2(b)) = promise; promise + consideration = agreement; agreement + enforceability = contract. All contracts are agreements, but not all agreements are contracts (social and domestic agreements usually are not — Balfour v Balfour).

steps.title: Essentials (Section 10)
steps.body: An agreement is a contract if made by (1) free consent (2) of parties competent to contract (3) for a lawful consideration and (4) a lawful object, and (5) not expressly declared void. Add the case-law essentials: offer and acceptance, intention to create legal relations, certainty of meaning and possibility of performance.

steps.title: Rules of a valid offer
steps.body: An offer must be definite, communicated to the offeree, and made with intent to obtain assent. It may be specific (to one person) or general (to the world — Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.). An invitation to offer is not an offer: price lists, catalogues, goods displayed in a shop (Pharmaceutical Society v Boots), tenders and auction calls. A mere statement of price is not an offer (Harvey v Facey). Cross offers do not make a contract.

steps.title: Rules of acceptance
steps.body: Acceptance must be absolute and unqualified (a counter-offer kills the original offer — Hyde v Wrench), communicated in the prescribed or a usual manner, by the offeree, while the offer is alive. Silence is not acceptance (Felthouse v Bindley). Knowledge of the offer is needed before acting on it (Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt).

steps.title: Worked example: communication by post (s.4)
steps.body:
A posts an offer on 1 March; B receives it 3 March and posts acceptance 4 March; A receives it 6 March.
Step 1: Communication of the offer is complete when it reaches B — 3 March.
Step 2: Acceptance is complete against A (the proposer) when the letter is posted — 4 March.
Step 3: Acceptance is complete against B (the acceptor) when it reaches A — 6 March.
Step 4: So B may revoke the acceptance before 6 March (s.5), and A may revoke the offer only before 4 March.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling a shop display an offer; treating a conditional 'yes, but…' as acceptance; forgetting that revocation of an offer is effective only when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree; assuming silence can be imposed as acceptance.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Ravi's 'I will sell for ₹30,000' with a clear 'Done!' and intention to be bound is a valid offer and acceptance. Decide: would it change if the friend said 'Done, if you fix the brakes'?

activity.prompt: Sort each statement into offer or invitation to offer.

items.text: Reward advertised for finding a lost dog
Company prospectus inviting applications for shares
'I will sell you my laptop for ₹40,000' said to a friend
Goods displayed with price tags in a supermarket

quiz.q: Which section defines 'contract'?
quiz.why: Section 2(h) defines a contract as an agreement enforceable by law.

quiz.q: A counter-offer has the effect of
quiz.why: A counter-offer is a rejection of the original offer and a new offer in its place, as held in Hyde v Wrench.

quiz.q: Acceptance by post is complete against the proposer when
quiz.why: Under Section 4 acceptance is complete against the proposer once it is put in course of transmission beyond the acceptor's power.

quiz.q: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. is the leading case on
quiz.why: The case held that an advertisement promising a reward to anyone fulfilling its conditions is a general offer accepted by performance.

scenes.text: Seventeen-year-old Mohori mortgages a house to a moneylender for a loan.
Later the lender sues to recover the money. The Privy Council (Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose, 1903) said the minor's agreement was void from the start.

steps.title: Consideration — Section 2(d)
steps.body: When at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains, or promises to do or abstain from doing something, such act, abstinence or promise is consideration. Rules: it must move at the desire of the promisor; it may move from the promisee or any other person (Chinnaya v Ramayya); it may be past, present or future; it need not be adequate but must be real and lawful.

steps.title: No consideration, no contract — and the exceptions (s.25)
steps.body: An agreement without consideration is void, except: (1) a written and registered agreement made on account of natural love and affection between near relatives; (2) a promise to compensate someone who has voluntarily done something for the promisor; (3) a written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt. Gifts actually made are also valid (s.25 explanation 1).

steps.title: Capacity — Sections 11 and 12
steps.body: Competent: a person of the age of majority (18 under the Indian Majority Act), of sound mind, and not disqualified by law (e.g. alien enemy, insolvent for some acts). A minor's agreement is void ab initio; no ratification on attaining majority; no estoppel against a minor; but a minor can be a promisee or beneficiary, and necessaries supplied to a minor can be recovered from the minor's property (s.68).

steps.title: Worked example: necessaries
steps.body:
A tailor supplies school uniforms worth ₹6,000 to a 16-year-old whose parents are absent; the minor has inherited property.
Step 1: Uniforms are necessaries suited to his condition in life.
Step 2: Under s.68 the supplier is entitled to be reimbursed from the minor's property.
Step 3: The minor is not personally liable; recovery is limited to his estate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking consideration must be adequate (inadequacy matters only as evidence of free consent); saying a minor's contract is voidable — it is void; forgetting that a stranger to consideration may sue in India although a stranger to the contract generally cannot.

a.text: A mother promises in a registered writing to give ₹2 lakh to her son out of love. No consideration. Is it enforceable?

choices.label: Yes — s.25(1) exception
choices.feedback: Correct: written, registered, near relation, natural love and affection.

choices.label: No — no consideration
choices.feedback: Look again at the exceptions in Section 25.

b.text: A 17-year-old borrows ₹50,000 and, at 18, signs a fresh promise to repay. Is the old loan now enforceable?

choices.label: No — a minor's agreement cannot be ratified
choices.feedback: Right: a void agreement cannot be ratified.

choices.label: Yes — ratified at majority
choices.feedback: Ratification needs a valid act to ratify.

c.text: Well done — you applied s.25 and the minor's agreement rule.

quiz.q: Consideration must move at the desire of
quiz.why: Section 2(d) requires the act or abstinence to be done at the desire of the promisor.

quiz.q: An agreement with a minor is
quiz.why: Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose held that a minor's agreement is void from the beginning.

quiz.q: A promise to pay a time-barred debt is enforceable if
quiz.why: Section 25(3) requires the promise to be in writing and signed by the debtor or his agent.

scenes.text: A seller knowingly says a lame horse is sound. The buyer pays.
The buyer discovers the truth. Can he cancel? The law says the contract is voidable at his option because of fraud.

steps.title: Consent and free consent (ss.13–14)
steps.body: Consent is agreeing upon the same thing in the same sense (consensus ad idem). Consent is free when not caused by coercion (s.15), undue influence (s.16), fraud (s.17), misrepresentation (s.18) or mistake (ss.20–22). Absence of the first four makes the contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was not free (ss.19, 19A).

steps.title: The five vitiating factors
steps.body: Coercion: committing or threatening an act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code (now read with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023) or unlawfully detaining property. Undue influence: a person in a position to dominate the will uses it to obtain an unfair advantage (fiduciary, real or apparent authority, mental distress). Fraud: deliberate false statement, active concealment or promise without intention to perform, to deceive. Misrepresentation: innocent false statement believed true. Mistake: bilateral mistake of fact makes the agreement void (s.20); mistake of Indian law is no excuse (s.21).

steps.title: Expressly void agreements
steps.body: Agreements in restraint of marriage (s.26), restraint of trade (s.27, except sale of goodwill), restraint of legal proceedings (s.28, subject to arbitration), uncertain agreements (s.29), wagers (s.30), agreements to do impossible acts (s.56), and agreements without consideration (s.25).

steps.title: Worked example: classify the defect
steps.body: Case: a doctor induces an old patient to sell land at half its value. Step 1: relationship — fiduciary, the doctor can dominate. Step 2: transaction is unconscionable. Step 3: burden shifts to the doctor (s.16(3)) to prove no undue influence. Result: voidable at the patient's option.

steps.title: Memory hook
steps.body: Void = no contract at all; voidable = valid until the aggrieved party avoids it; illegal = void plus tainting collateral transactions; unenforceable = valid but cannot be sued on for a technical defect (e.g. unstamped).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating silence as fraud (it is not, unless there is a duty to speak or silence is itself equivalent to speech); confusing unilateral mistake (contract usually valid) with bilateral mistake of essential fact (void).

activity.prompt: Classify the effect on the agreement.

items.text: Both parties mistakenly believe the cargo exists; it had sunk
Consent obtained by threatening to burn the house
A bet on a cricket match
Seller innocently misstates the year of manufacture
Agreement not to marry anyone ever
Guru obtains a gift from a devotee by spiritual pressure

quiz.q: A contract induced by fraud is
options: voidable at the option of the deceived party
quiz.why: Section 19 makes an agreement caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.

quiz.q: Which agreement is expressly void?
options: Sale of goodwill with a reasonable restraint
quiz.why: Section 30 declares agreements by way of wager void.

quiz.q: Bilateral mistake of an essential fact makes the agreement
quiz.why: Section 20 provides that where both parties are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void.

scenes.text: A supplier fails to deliver 100 quintals of wheat at ₹2,400 per quintal on the agreed date.
The market price that day is ₹2,700. What can the buyer claim?

steps.title: Modes of discharge
steps.body: By performance (actual or attempted — tender), by mutual agreement (novation, rescission, alteration, remission, waiver — s.62–63), by impossibility (s.56 — frustration), by lapse of time (Limitation Act), by operation of law (death in personal contracts, insolvency, merger), and by breach (actual or anticipatory).

steps.title: Damages — Section 73 (Hadley v Baxendale)
steps.body: The injured party gets compensation for loss which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew when contracting would be likely to result. Remote and indirect loss is not recoverable. The injured party must mitigate. Other remedies: rescission, quantum meruit, specific performance and injunction (Specific Relief Act 1963). Section 74 deals with a stipulated penalty or liquidated damages — the court awards reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount named.

steps.title: Worked example: market-price damages
steps.body:
Contract price 100 × ₹2,400 = ₹2,40,000. Market price on due date 100 × ₹2,700 = ₹2,70,000.
Step 1: Ordinary damages = market price − contract price = ₹30,000.
Step 2: Buyer's special loss (a lost export order) is recoverable only if the seller knew of it at the time of contract.
Step 3: If the buyer could have bought at ₹2,650 elsewhere immediately, mitigation limits damages to ₹25,000.

steps.title: Worked example: frustration
steps.body: A hall is booked for a wedding; before the date it is destroyed by fire without fault. Step 1: Performance has become impossible after the contract. Step 2: Under s.56 the contract becomes void. Step 3: Under s.65 any advance paid must be restored.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Awarding the whole contract price instead of the difference; ignoring the duty to mitigate; treating commercial hardship or price rise as frustration — it is not.

activity.prompt: Contract: 50 tonnes of steel at ₹52,000 per tonne. Seller defaults; market price on the due date ₹55,500 per tonne. Ordinary damages (₹).

quiz.q: Hadley v Baxendale concerns
quiz.why: It laid down the two-limb test that damages cover natural loss and loss within the parties' contemplation.

quiz.q: Substituting a new contract for the old one is
quiz.why: Novation under Section 62 replaces the original contract with a new one, discharging the old.

quiz.q: Supervening impossibility makes the contract
quiz.why: Section 56 provides that a contract to do an act which afterwards becomes impossible becomes void.

questions.q: Under Section 10, which is NOT an essential of a valid contract?
questions.why: Writing is required only where a particular law demands it; oral contracts are valid in general.

questions.q: An advertisement of goods for sale is generally
questions.why: Advertisements of goods invite customers to make offers, so they are invitations to offer.

questions.q: Revocation of an offer by post is complete against the person who makes it when
questions.why: Section 4 makes revocation complete against the revoker when put in course of transmission.

questions.q: Chinnaya v Ramayya establishes that consideration
options: may move from a third person
questions.why: The case held that consideration may move from the promisee or any other person.

questions.q: Age of majority for contracting in India is generally
questions.why: The Indian Majority Act 1875 fixes majority at 18 years.

questions.q: Suppliers of necessaries to a minor recover
questions.why: Section 68 allows reimbursement from the property of the incapable person.

questions.q: Threat of committing a crime to obtain consent is
questions.why: Section 15 defines coercion as committing or threatening an act forbidden by penal law.

questions.q: A promise made without any intention of performing it amounts to
questions.why: Section 17(3) includes such a promise in the definition of fraud.

questions.q: Restraint of trade is permitted where
options: an employee agrees never to work again
the seller of goodwill agrees not to compete within reasonable limits
questions.why: The exception to Section 27 allows a reasonable restraint on the seller of goodwill.

questions.q: Contract price ₹1,20,000; market price at breach ₹1,32,000. Ordinary damages to buyer:
questions.why: Damages equal the difference between market and contract price, ₹12,000.

questions.q: Liquidated damages and penalties are governed by
questions.why: Section 74 lets the court award reasonable compensation up to the stipulated amount.

questions.q: Felthouse v Bindley held that
questions.why: An offeror cannot impose silence of the offeree as acceptance.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Special Contracts & Sale of Goods Act 1930
courses.summary: Indemnity and guarantee, bailment and pledge, agency, and the Sale of Goods Act: conditions and warranties, caveat emptor, transfer of property and the rights of an unpaid seller.
outcomes: Distinguish indemnity from guarantee and state the surety's rights
Explain duties of bailor and bailee and the pawnee's rights
Describe creation and termination of agency
Distinguish sale from agreement to sell and condition from warranty
Apply caveat emptor and its exceptions; list unpaid seller's rights

scenes.text: Anil takes a ₹5 lakh bank loan; his friend Kiran signs as guarantor.
Anil defaults. The bank comes to Kiran first. Can it?

steps.title: Indemnity (ss.124–125)
steps.body: A contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor or any other person. Two parties: indemnifier and indemnity-holder. The indemnity-holder may recover damages, costs of suits and sums paid under compromise (s.125). Insurance (other than life) is the commonest example.

steps.title: Guarantee (s.126)
steps.body: A contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. Three parties: creditor, principal debtor, surety; three contracts among them. It may be oral or written. Liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor (s.128) and arises immediately on default — the creditor need not sue the debtor first.

steps.title: Rights and discharge of the surety
steps.body: Rights: subrogation (s.140), indemnity from the principal debtor (s.145), benefit of creditor's securities (s.141), contribution from co-sureties (s.146). Discharge: revocation by notice for future transactions in a continuing guarantee (s.130), death (s.131), variance in terms without consent (s.133), release or discharge of the principal debtor (s.134), creditor's compounding with or giving time to the debtor (s.135), loss of security by the creditor (s.141).

steps.title: Worked example: co-sureties
steps.body: Three co-sureties of a ₹3,00,000 debt, no agreement on shares. Debtor defaults fully. Step 1: Under s.146 they are liable equally. Step 2: Each pays ₹1,00,000. Step 3: If one pays all ₹3,00,000, he recovers ₹1,00,000 from each of the others.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying the creditor must first exhaust remedies against the debtor; forgetting that a guarantee obtained by misrepresentation by the creditor is invalid (s.142).

activity.prompt: Indemnity or guarantee?

items.text: Two parties, primary liability of promisor
Father promises the bank to repay if his son defaults

quiz.q: Surety's liability is
options: only after the debtor is sued
quiz.why: Section 128 makes the surety liable to the same extent as the principal debtor unless the contract says otherwise.

quiz.q: A variance in contract terms without the surety's consent
options: discharges the surety as to later transactions
quiz.why: Section 133 discharges the surety for transactions after the variance.

quiz.q: Contract of indemnity has
quiz.why: An indemnity involves only the indemnifier and the indemnity-holder.

scenes.text: Meena pledges a gold chain for a ₹40,000 loan.
She defaults. The pawnbroker gives reasonable notice and sells the chain for ₹46,000. Who gets the surplus?

steps.title: Bailment (s.148)
steps.body: Delivery of goods by one person (bailor) to another (bailee) for some purpose, on a contract that they be returned or disposed of as directed when the purpose is accomplished. Bailee must take as much care as a man of ordinary prudence would of his own goods (s.151), must not make unauthorised use, must not mix goods, must return them with accretions. The bailee has a particular lien for charges on services rendered (s.170).

steps.title: Pledge (s.172)
steps.body: Bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. The pawnee may retain goods for debt, interest and expenses (s.173), and on default may sue, or sell after reasonable notice (s.176). If sale proceeds fall short the pawnor still owes the balance; any surplus goes to the pawnor.

steps.title: Agency (ss.182–238)
steps.body: An agent acts for the principal in dealings with third persons. Creation: express, implied, by necessity, by estoppel, by ratification (s.196 — principal must be in existence and competent at the time of the act, and ratify the whole). Termination: revocation, renunciation, completion, death or insanity, insolvency of principal, destruction of subject-matter. An agency coupled with interest cannot be revoked to the agent's prejudice (s.202).

steps.title: Worked example: pledge sale
steps.body: Debt ₹40,000 + interest ₹3,000 + sale expenses ₹1,000 = ₹44,000. Sale proceeds ₹46,000. Step: surplus ₹46,000 − ₹44,000 = ₹2,000 is paid to Meena. If proceeds had been ₹42,000, she would still owe ₹2,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling a deposit of money in a bank a bailment (money is not goods returned in specie); allowing ratification of an act void from the start.

activity.prompt: Pledged goods sold for ₹78,000. Debt ₹70,000, interest ₹5,500, expenses of sale ₹1,200. Surplus payable to the pawnor (₹).

quiz.q: Bailee's standard of care is that of
quiz.why: Section 151 requires the care a man of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods of the same kind.

quiz.q: An agency coupled with interest
options: ends on the principal's death automatically
cannot be revoked to the agent's prejudice
quiz.why: Section 202 protects an agent who has an interest in the property forming the subject of the agency.

quiz.q: The pawnee may sell pledged goods after
quiz.why: Section 176 allows sale on reasonable notice of the sale to the pawnor.

lessons.title: Sale of Goods: conditions, warranties, caveat emptor

scenes.text: A buyer asks the chemist for a hair dye safe for sensitive skin and relies on his choice.
The dye causes a skin reaction. Can 'buyer beware' save the chemist?

steps.title: Sale vs agreement to sell (s.4)
steps.body: In a sale, property in goods passes to the buyer at once; it is an executed contract. In an agreement to sell, property passes at a future time or on fulfilment of a condition; it is executory. Risk prima facie passes with property (s.26). Essentials: two parties, goods (movable property, s.2(7)), price in money, transfer of property.

steps.title: Condition vs warranty (s.12)
steps.body: A condition is essential to the main purpose; breach gives the right to repudiate. A warranty is collateral; breach gives only damages. A buyer may treat breach of condition as breach of warranty (s.13). Implied conditions: title (s.14), sale by description (s.15), quality or fitness when the buyer relies on seller's skill (s.16(1)), merchantability (s.16(2)), sale by sample (s.17). Implied warranties: quiet possession, freedom from encumbrance.

steps.title: Caveat emptor and exceptions
steps.body: Section 16: no implied condition as to quality or fitness, except (1) buyer makes known the purpose and relies on seller's skill; (2) goods bought by description from a dealer — merchantable quality; (3) usage of trade; (4) fraud by the seller; (5) sale by sample or by sample and description.

steps.title: Worked example: apply the rule
steps.body: The hair-dye buyer disclosed the purpose and relied on the chemist. Step 1: Exception s.16(1) applies. Step 2: Implied condition of fitness breached. Step 3: Buyer may reject and claim damages; caveat emptor gives no defence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing a warranty in insurance language with the Sale of Goods meaning; forgetting that if the buyer examined goods, no condition of merchantability applies for defects examination ought to have revealed.

activity.prompt: Condition or warranty?

items.text: Seller has the right to sell
Goods are free from any undisclosed charge

quiz.q: In an agreement to sell, property passes
options: at a future time or on a condition
quiz.why: Section 4(3) treats a future or conditional transfer as an agreement to sell.

quiz.q: Breach of warranty entitles the buyer to
quiz.why: Section 12(3) gives a claim for damages but not a right to reject on breach of warranty.

quiz.q: Caveat emptor does NOT apply when
options: buyer relies on seller's skill for a disclosed purpose
quiz.why: Section 16(1) implies a condition of fitness when the buyer relies on the seller's skill.

lessons.title: Lab: Transfer of property and the unpaid seller

scenes.text: Goods are in transit when the seller learns the buyer has become insolvent.
The seller calls the carrier: 'Stop! Do not deliver.'

steps.title: When does property pass? (ss.18–24)
steps.body: Specific goods in a deliverable state: when the contract is made (s.20). Specific goods needing something to be done: when done and buyer has notice (s.21). Unascertained goods: when appropriated to the contract (s.23). Goods on approval or sale or return: when the buyer signifies approval, retains beyond the time, or does an act adopting the transaction (s.24). Nemo dat quod non habet — no one can give a better title than he has (s.27), with exceptions (mercantile agent, joint owner, voidable title not rescinded, seller or buyer in possession).

steps.title: Unpaid seller (s.45) and rights
steps.body: A seller is unpaid when the whole price is not paid or tendered, or a negotiable instrument given is dishonoured. Rights against goods: lien while in possession (s.47), stoppage in transit on buyer's insolvency (s.50), resale (s.54). Rights against the buyer: suit for price (s.55), damages for non-acceptance (s.56), interest.

steps.title: Worked example: resale loss
steps.body: Price ₹2,00,000; buyer refuses; seller gives notice and resells for ₹1,82,000 with resale expenses ₹3,000. Step: recoverable from buyer = 2,00,000 − 1,82,000 + 3,000 = ₹21,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Exercising stoppage in transit when the buyer is merely late (needs insolvency); confusing lien (needs possession) with stoppage (goods with carrier).

a.text: Seller still holds the goods; buyer has paid nothing and credit period has expired. Best right?

choices.feedback: Correct under s.47.

choices.label: Stoppage in transit
choices.feedback: Goods are not in transit.

b.text: Now goods are with the carrier and the buyer is declared insolvent.

choices.label: Stoppage in transit
choices.feedback: Right under s.50.

choices.label: Lien
choices.feedback: Lien is lost once goods leave the seller's possession.

c.text: Good — you matched each unpaid seller's right to its trigger.

options: no one gives what he does not have
quiz.why: Section 27 states that a seller who is not the owner cannot pass a better title than he has, subject to exceptions.

quiz.why: Section 50 allows stoppage in transit only when the buyer becomes insolvent.

questions.why: Section 130 allows the surety to revoke a continuing guarantee for future transactions by notice.

questions.why: Section 140 gives the paying surety all the rights the creditor had against the debtor.

questions.why: Section 170 gives a particular lien for services involving skill or labour on the goods.

questions.q: Ratification is NOT possible when
questions.why: A void act cannot be validated by later ratification.

options: buyer retains beyond the fixed time

questions.why: Section 12(2) defines a condition as essential to the main purpose of the contract.

questions.why: Section 16(2) applies to goods bought by description from a seller who deals in such goods.

questions.why: Loss is 90,000 − 81,000 plus 1,500 resale expenses, which equals ₹10,500.

questions.why: There are contracts between creditor and debtor, creditor and surety, and surety and debtor.
