courses.title: Unit 3 · Partnership, LLP & Negotiable Instruments
courses.summary: The Indian Partnership Act 1932, the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008 and the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 including holder in due course, crossing and dishonour of cheques under Section 138.
outcomes: State the essentials of partnership and test for its existence
Explain registration and effects of non-registration (s.69)
Compare partnership firm, LLP and company
Distinguish promissory note, bill of exchange and cheque
Walk through the Section 138 dishonour procedure

scenes.text: Three cousins run a sweet shop, share profits equally and each signs bills for supplies.
They never registered the firm. A customer owes them ₹80,000. Can the firm sue?

steps.title: Definition and essentials (s.4)
steps.body: Partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. Essentials: agreement (not status, s.5), business, sharing of profits, mutual agency (the real test — s.6). Maximum number of partners: 50 under the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules 2014 read with s.464 of the Companies Act 2013.

steps.title: Rights and duties (ss.9–17)
steps.body: Unless agreed otherwise: every partner may take part in business, no remuneration, profits and losses shared equally, interest on capital not payable (if agreed, only out of profits), interest at 6% p.a. on advances beyond capital (s.13(d)), access to books. Duties: utmost good faith, indemnify for fraud, account for secret profits, not compete.

steps.title: Registration and s.69
steps.body: Registration is optional but an unregistered firm and its partners cannot sue third parties or each other to enforce rights arising from a contract; it cannot claim set-off above ₹100. It can still be sued, and a partner may sue for dissolution and accounts. Dissolution: by agreement, compulsory (insolvency, illegality), on contingencies, by notice in partnership at will, by court (s.44).

steps.title: Worked example: interest on advance
steps.body: A partner advanced ₹2,00,000 to the firm for 9 months beyond capital, with no agreement on interest. Step 1: s.13(d) — 6% p.a. Step 2: 2,00,000 × 6% × 9/12 = ₹9,000 interest due to him.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming profit-sharing alone proves partnership (mutual agency is decisive — Cox v Hickman); assuming registration is compulsory.

activity.prompt: No partnership deed. Partner lends the firm ₹1,50,000 for 8 months beyond his capital. Interest due (₹).

quiz.q: The true test of partnership is
quiz.why: Section 6 and Cox v Hickman make mutual agency the decisive test.

quiz.q: An unregistered firm
options: cannot sue third parties on contracts
quiz.why: Section 69(2) bars an unregistered firm from suing third parties to enforce contractual rights.

quiz.q: Default sharing of profits among partners is
quiz.why: Section 13(b) provides equal sharing of profits and losses in the absence of agreement.

scenes.text: Two architects want partnership flexibility but fear unlimited personal liability.
Their CA suggests an LLP.

steps.title: Features
steps.body: An LLP is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a legal entity separate from its partners. Liability of a partner is limited to the agreed contribution, except for his own wrongful acts. Minimum two partners, no maximum; at least two designated partners who are individuals, at least one resident in India. Governed by the LLP agreement, otherwise by the First Schedule.

steps.title: LLP vs firm vs company
steps.body: Firm: no separate entity, unlimited liability, registration optional, max 50 partners. LLP: separate entity, limited liability, registration compulsory with the Registrar, flexible internal management, annual statement of accounts and annual return filings. Company: separate entity, limited liability, heavier compliance (board, AGM, audit as per the Companies Act).

steps.title: Worked example: liability
steps.body: An LLP owes ₹50 lakh to creditors and has assets of ₹30 lakh. Partner contributions agreed: A ₹5 lakh paid; B ₹5 lakh of which ₹2 lakh unpaid. Step 1: Creditors recover from LLP assets ₹30 lakh. Step 2: B must pay the unpaid ₹2 lakh contribution. Step 3: Partners' personal assets are otherwise protected unless fraud is proved.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying an LLP has no partner liability at all (contribution and personal wrongs remain); forgetting the resident designated partner requirement.

activity.prompt: Which form fits each feature?

quiz.q: Minimum number of partners in an LLP
quiz.why: The LLP Act requires at least two partners, failing which liability consequences follow.

quiz.q: An LLP is
quiz.why: Section 3 of the LLP Act declares an LLP a body corporate with perpetual succession.

quiz.q: LLP partners are personally liable for
quiz.why: Liability is limited to contribution except for the partner's own wrongful act or omission.

scenes.text: A trader receives a bill of exchange from a buyer, payable 90 days after sight.
He endorses it to his supplier. Who can be made liable if it is dishonoured?

steps.title: Three instruments
steps.body: Promissory note (s.4): written unconditional undertaking signed by the maker to pay a certain sum to, or to the order of, a certain person or bearer — two parties. Bill of exchange (s.5): written unconditional order by the drawer directing the drawee to pay — three parties; needs acceptance. Cheque (s.6): a bill drawn on a specified banker payable on demand; includes electronic image of a truncated cheque and a cheque in electronic form.

steps.title: Holder and holder in due course (ss.8–9)
steps.body: A holder in due course takes the instrument for consideration, before maturity, in good faith without notice of defect in title. He gets a better title than the transferor; prior parties remain liable to him until the instrument is satisfied (s.36); and certain defences are not available against him.

steps.title: Crossing and endorsement
steps.body: General crossing: two parallel lines (with or without '& Co.') — pay only through a bank. Special crossing: name of a bank — pay only to that bank. 'Account payee' — collecting bank credits only the payee's account. Endorsements: blank, special (full), restrictive, conditional, sans recourse.

steps.title: Worked example: maturity date
steps.body: Bill dated 10 January, payable 60 days after date. Step 1: Exclude the date of the bill; count 60 days: 21 remaining in Jan, 28 in Feb (non-leap), 11 in March gives 11 March. Step 2: Under s.22, add 3 days of grace for bills payable otherwise than on demand: 14 March. Step 3: If that is a public holiday, it is due on the preceding business day (s.25).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Giving days of grace on a cheque (payable on demand — no grace); treating a conditional note as negotiable.

activity.prompt: Which instrument?

items.text: Contains a promise by the maker
Always drawn on a banker, payable on demand
Requires acceptance by drawee if payable after sight

quiz.q: Days of grace allowed on a time bill
quiz.why: Section 22 adds three days of grace to instruments not payable on demand.

quiz.q: 'Account payee' crossing means
quiz.why: It is an instruction to the collecting banker to credit the proceeds only to the payee's account.

quiz.q: A holder in due course must take the instrument
options: for consideration and in good faith
quiz.why: Section 9 requires consideration, possession before maturity and good faith.

lessons.title: Lab: Section 138 — dishonour of a cheque

scenes.text: A ₹2,50,000 cheque given for supplies returns with the memo 'funds insufficient'.
The supplier's lawyer starts the clock.

steps.title: Ingredients of the offence
steps.body: (1) Cheque drawn for discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability; (2) presented within its validity (three months from date, per RBI); (3) returned unpaid for insufficient funds or exceeding arrangement; (4) payee sends written demand notice within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour; (5) drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving notice. Complaint must be filed within one month after the cause of action arises (s.142). Punishment: imprisonment up to two years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both.

steps.title: Worked example: timeline
steps.body: Bank memo received 2 June. Step 1: Notice must be sent by 2 July; sent 20 June, served 23 June. Step 2: 15 days for payment end 8 July. Step 3: Cause of action arises 9 July; complaint by 8 August. Step 4: Maximum fine 2 × 2,50,000 = ₹5,00,000.

steps.title: Presumption
steps.body: Section 139 presumes the cheque was received for discharge of a debt; the drawer may rebut it on a preponderance of probabilities. Section 143A allows interim compensation up to 20% of the cheque amount.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Counting 30 days from the cheque date instead of the date of information of dishonour; filing the complaint before the 15-day period expires.

activity.prompt: Cheque of ₹3,40,000 dishonoured. Maximum fine the court may impose under s.138 (₹).

quiz.q: Demand notice must be sent within
quiz.why: Section 138(b) requires notice within thirty days of receiving information of dishonour.

quiz.q: Drawer gets how many days to pay after notice?
quiz.why: Section 138(c) gives fifteen days from receipt of notice.

quiz.q: Maximum imprisonment under s.138
quiz.why: The section provides imprisonment up to two years, or fine up to twice the amount, or both.

questions.q: Partnership arises from
questions.why: Section 5 says partnership arises from contract and not from status.

questions.q: Interest on partner's loan without agreement
questions.why: Section 13(d) allows 6 percent per annum on advances beyond capital.

questions.q: Max partners in a firm under current rules
questions.why: The Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules 2014 cap a partnership at 50 partners.

questions.q: Dissolution by court is under section
questions.why: Section 44 lists grounds such as insanity, misconduct and just and equitable grounds.

questions.q: Designated partners in an LLP: at least
questions.why: The LLP Act requires at least two individual designated partners with one resident in India.

questions.q: A cheque is a bill of exchange drawn on
questions.why: Section 6 defines a cheque as a bill on a specified banker payable on demand.

questions.q: Bill dated 1 March payable 30 days after date: due date including grace
questions.why: Thirty days after 1 March is 31 March and three days of grace make it 3 April.

questions.q: Promissory note has how many original parties?
questions.why: Only the maker and the payee are parties to a promissory note.

questions.q: Section 139 of the NI Act provides
questions.why: It presumes that the holder received the cheque for discharge of a debt or liability.

questions.q: Interim compensation in s.138 cases is up to
questions.why: Section 143A allows interim compensation not exceeding twenty percent of the cheque amount.

questions.q: An LLP partner's liability for LLP debts is limited to
questions.why: A partner is liable only up to contribution except for personal wrongful acts.

questions.q: Special crossing means the cheque is paid
questions.why: Section 124 requires payment only to the banker named in the special crossing.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Companies Act 2013 — Nature, Formation & Capital
courses.summary: Corporate personality and lifting the veil, kinds of companies, incorporation, Memorandum and Articles, doctrines of ultra vires, constructive notice and indoor management, prospectus and share capital.
outcomes: Explain separate legal entity and when the veil is lifted
Classify private, public, one person, small, holding and subsidiary companies
Describe incorporation and the clauses of MoA and AoA
Apply ultra vires, constructive notice and indoor management
Explain prospectus liability, allotment and buy-back limits

lessons.title: Corporate personality and kinds of companies

scenes.text: Salomon sold his business to a company he controlled and took secured debentures.
When it failed, creditors said company and Salomon were one. The House of Lords (1897) disagreed: the company is a separate person.

steps.title: Meaning and features
steps.body: Section 2(20): company means a company incorporated under this Act or a previous company law. Features: separate legal entity, limited liability, perpetual succession, common seal (optional since 2015), separate property, capacity to sue and be sued, transferability of shares (restricted in private companies).

steps.title: Lifting the corporate veil
steps.body: Courts ignore separate personality where it is used for fraud or improper conduct, to evade tax, where the company is a sham or agent, to determine enemy character (Daimler v Continental Tyre), or in public interest. Statutory instances include misstatement in prospectus (s.34–35), fraudulent conduct of business (s.339), and failure to refund application money.

steps.title: Kinds of companies
steps.body: Private (s.2(68)): restricts transfer, members up to 200 (excluding employees), prohibits public invitation; minimum 2 members, 2 directors. Public (s.2(71)): minimum 7 members, 3 directors. One Person Company (s.2(62)): single natural person member, a resident Indian. Small company (s.2(85)): private company within prescribed paid-up capital and turnover limits. Holding and subsidiary (s.2(46), 2(87)): control of composition of board or more than one-half of total voting power. Section 8 company: charitable objects, profits applied to objects, no dividend. Government company (s.2(45)): at least 51% paid-up capital held by governments.

steps.title: Worked example: subsidiary test
steps.body: H Ltd holds 4,80,000 of 9,00,000 equity shares (all voting) of S Ltd. Step 1: 4,80,000 ÷ 9,00,000 = 53.3%. Step 2: more than one-half of total voting power. Step 3: S Ltd is a subsidiary of H Ltd.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying a private company can have unlimited members (cap 200); counting employee-members in the 200 limit; thinking limited liability means directors are never liable.

activity.prompt: Private or public company feature?

items.text: May invite the public to subscribe

quiz.q: Salomon v Salomon & Co. established
quiz.why: The House of Lords held that a duly incorporated company is a person distinct from its members.

quiz.q: Minimum members of a public company
quiz.why: Section 3 requires at least seven persons to form a public company.

quiz.q: A government company needs government holding of at least
quiz.why: Section 2(45) defines a government company as one with not less than 51 percent paid-up share capital held by governments.

scenes.text: Two founders file SPICe+ online with the Registrar of Companies.
They draft the Memorandum and Articles and wait for the Certificate of Incorporation with a CIN.

steps.title: Incorporation (s.7)
steps.body: Name reservation, filing of MoA, AoA, declarations by professionals and subscribers, particulars of first directors (DIN), registered office. The Registrar issues a Certificate of Incorporation with a Corporate Identity Number — conclusive evidence of incorporation. Promoters' pre-incorporation contracts are not binding on the company unless adopted, as permitted by the Specific Relief Act.

steps.title: Memorandum of Association (s.4)
steps.body: The charter defining the company's relationship with the outside world. Clauses: name, registered office (state), objects, liability, capital, and association/subscription. Alteration (s.13) generally by special resolution; change of registered office between states needs Central Government (Regional Director) approval.

steps.title: Articles of Association (s.5)
steps.body: Rules for internal management — subordinate to the MoA and the Act. Tables F (shares), G–J in Schedule I are model articles. Alteration by special resolution (s.14). Entrenchment provisions require stricter conditions. MoA and AoA bind the company and members as if signed by each (s.10).

steps.title: Three doctrines
steps.body: Ultra vires: acts beyond the objects are void and cannot be ratified even unanimously (Ashbury Railway Carriage v Riche). Constructive notice: outsiders are deemed to know the public documents (MoA, AoA). Indoor management (Royal British Bank v Turquand): outsiders acting in good faith may assume internal procedures were complied with — not available if the outsider knew of the irregularity, was negligent, or the document was forged.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Articles allow directors to borrow above ₹1 crore only with an ordinary resolution. Directors borrow ₹1.5 crore from a bank without it. Step 1: Borrowing is within the objects (not ultra vires). Step 2: The resolution is an internal matter. Step 3: The bank, in good faith, is protected by indoor management; the loan binds the company.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying ultra vires acts can be ratified by shareholders; letting the AoA override the MoA.

a.text: A company formed to make carriages finances a railway line abroad. Shareholders unanimously ratify. Valid?

choices.label: No — ultra vires the MoA, void
choices.feedback: Correct, as in Ashbury v Riche.

choices.label: Yes — unanimous ratification cures it
choices.feedback: Ultra vires acts cannot be ratified.

b.text: A lender knew the required general meeting approval had not been obtained. Can it rely on indoor management?

choices.label: No — it had knowledge of the irregularity
choices.feedback: Right: knowledge is an exception.

choices.label: Yes — always protected
choices.feedback: Protection needs good faith without notice.

c.text: Good — you applied the three doctrines.

quiz.q: Conclusive evidence of incorporation is
quiz.why: Section 7(7) and case law treat the certificate as conclusive of due incorporation.

quiz.q: Turquand's rule is also called
quiz.why: Royal British Bank v Turquand protects outsiders regarding internal irregularities.

quiz.q: Articles are altered by
quiz.why: Section 14 requires a special resolution to alter articles.

scenes.text: A prospectus claims a factory is 'fully operational'. It is not.
Investors lose money. Who is liable?

steps.title: Prospectus (s.2(70))
steps.body: Any document described or issued as a prospectus inviting offers from the public to subscribe for securities. Kinds: red herring (without price/quantity, s.32), shelf (s.31), abridged (s.33 — must accompany application forms), deemed (s.25 — offer for sale through issue house). Public issues must comply with SEBI (ICDR) Regulations. Private placement (s.42) is limited to identified persons.

steps.title: Liability for misstatement
steps.body: Criminal liability (s.34) for every person authorising the issue, punishable under s.447 (fraud). Civil liability (s.35) to persons who subscribed relying on the misstatement — directors, promoters, experts, persons named as directors. Defences: withdrawal of consent before issue; issue without knowledge and public notice on becoming aware; reasonable belief in truth.

steps.title: Minimum subscription and allotment
steps.body: Under s.39, no allotment unless the minimum subscription stated in the prospectus is received; SEBI requires at least 90% of the issue size for public issues, else refund within the prescribed time. Return of allotment filed with the Registrar. Securities premium (s.52) can be used only for specified purposes such as issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, issue expenses, premium on redemption, and buy-back.

steps.title: Worked example: minimum subscription
steps.body: Issue size 50,00,000 shares; applications received 44,00,000. Step 1: 90% of 50,00,000 = 45,00,000. Step 2: 44,00,000 is below 45,00,000. Step 3: No allotment; full application money must be refunded.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating an advertisement of an issue as outside prospectus rules; using securities premium to pay dividends (not permitted).

activity.prompt: Issue of 80,00,000 shares; SEBI 90% minimum subscription. Minimum number of shares to be subscribed before allotment.

quiz.q: Red herring prospectus is governed by
quiz.why: Section 32 permits a red herring prospectus that omits price and quantity details.

quiz.q: Securities premium can be used for
quiz.why: Section 52(2) lists bonus issue among the permitted uses of securities premium.

quiz.q: Civil liability for misstatement is under
quiz.why: Section 35 provides compensation to persons who subscribed relying on misleading statements.

lessons.title: Lab: Share capital, buy-back and debentures

scenes.text: A company with large free reserves wants to return cash to shareholders.
The board considers a buy-back — but how much is allowed?

steps.title: Kinds of share capital
steps.body: Authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up, paid-up. Equity shares (with voting rights, or with differential rights) and preference shares (preferential dividend and repayment). Preference shares must be redeemable within 20 years (longer for infrastructure projects as prescribed). Sweat equity (s.54), rights issue (s.62(1)(a)), bonus issue (s.63) and ESOPs.

steps.title: Buy-back (s.68)
steps.body: Sources: free reserves, securities premium, or proceeds of a different issue. Limits: board resolution up to 10% of total paid-up equity capital and free reserves; special resolution up to 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves; equity shares bought back in a year not to exceed 25% of paid-up equity capital; post-buy-back debt–equity ratio not more than 2:1. Shares must be fully paid; bought-back shares are extinguished within seven days of completion.

steps.title: Worked example: buy-back limit
steps.body: Paid-up equity ₹10 crore, free reserves ₹30 crore. Step 1: Board limit = 10% × (10 + 30) = ₹4 crore. Step 2: Special resolution limit = 25% × 40 = ₹10 crore. Step 3: Also check the debt-equity test: if debt is ₹60 crore, post-buy-back equity of ₹30 crore after ₹10 crore buy-back gives 60:30 = 2:1 — just within the limit.

steps.title: Debentures (s.71)
steps.body: Instrument of debt; holders are creditors with no voting rights. May be secured or unsecured, convertible or non-convertible, redeemable. Debenture redemption reserve and a debenture trustee are required in the prescribed cases. Charges on company assets must be registered with the Registrar within 30 days (s.77).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using paid-up capital alone as the base for buy-back (base is paid-up capital plus free reserves); forgetting the 2:1 debt-equity cap.

activity.prompt: Paid-up equity ₹8 crore, free reserves ₹16 crore. Maximum buy-back with a special resolution (₹ crore).

quiz.q: Maximum buy-back by board resolution alone
quiz.why: The proviso to Section 68(2)(b) allows the board to approve up to ten percent.

quiz.q: Post buy-back debt-equity ratio must not exceed
quiz.why: Section 68(2)(d) caps secured and unsecured debt at twice paid-up capital and free reserves.

quiz.q: Debenture holders are
quiz.why: A debenture acknowledges a debt, so holders are creditors of the company.

questions.q: Which is NOT a feature of a company?
questions.why: Most companies are limited, and limited liability is a standard feature.

questions.q: Daimler v Continental Tyre is about lifting the veil to determine
questions.why: The court looked behind the company to find its controllers were enemy aliens.

questions.q: An OPC may have
questions.why: Section 2(62) defines an OPC as a company with only one person as member.

questions.q: Holding of more than one-half of voting power makes a company a
questions.why: Section 2(87) treats control of more than half the voting power as creating a subsidiary.

questions.q: Clause showing the state of the registered office is in the
questions.why: The registered office clause is a compulsory clause of the memorandum.

questions.q: Ashbury Railway Carriage v Riche held an ultra vires contract
questions.why: The House of Lords held that an act beyond the objects is void and cannot be ratified.

questions.q: Indoor management does NOT protect an outsider who
questions.why: Forgery is a nullity and is an established exception to Turquand's rule.

questions.q: Abridged prospectus must accompany
questions.why: Section 33 requires every application form to be accompanied by an abridged prospectus.

questions.q: Securities premium may NOT be used to
questions.why: Dividends are not among the purposes listed in Section 52(2).

questions.q: Paid-up ₹5 crore, free reserves ₹15 crore. Board-approved buy-back limit:
questions.why: Ten percent of ₹20 crore is ₹2 crore.

questions.q: Charges must be registered with the ROC within
questions.why: Section 77 requires registration within thirty days of creation, extendable with fees as prescribed.

questions.q: Preference shares must generally be redeemed within
questions.why: Section 55 limits the term of redeemable preference shares to twenty years except as prescribed for infrastructure.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Directors, Meetings & Winding Up
courses.summary: Board composition, appointment, duties and disqualification of directors; key managerial personnel; general and board meetings, resolutions and quorum; oppression and mismanagement; winding up under the Companies Act 2013 and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016.
outcomes: State board size, directorship limits and independent and woman director rules
Explain duties of directors under s.166 and disqualifications under s.164
Apply rules on AGM, EGM, notice, quorum and resolutions
Distinguish ordinary from special resolutions numerically
Outline winding up by tribunal and voluntary liquidation under the IBC

scenes.text: Ms Rao already sits on 19 company boards, 10 of them public. A new public company invites her.
Can she accept? The Act caps directorships.

steps.title: Board composition
steps.body: Minimum directors: public 3, private 2, OPC 1; maximum 15 (more by special resolution) (s.149). At least one director resident in India (182 days in the financial year). Listed companies and prescribed public companies need at least one woman director. Listed public companies: at least one-third independent directors. Every director needs a Director Identification Number (DIN).

steps.title: Duties (s.166)
steps.body: Act in accordance with the articles; act in good faith to promote the objects for the benefit of members, employees, shareholders, community and environment; exercise due and reasonable care, skill, diligence and independent judgement; avoid conflicts of interest; not achieve undue gain (must pay any gain to the company); not assign office. Contravention: fine as prescribed.

steps.title: Disqualification (s.164) and limits (s.165)
steps.body: Disqualified if of unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, convicted with imprisonment of six months or more (seven years or more bars for life), order of disqualification, unpaid calls for six months, or, under s.164(2), director of a company that has not filed financial statements or annual returns for three continuous years or has defaulted on deposits/debentures for one year. Directorship cap: 20 companies, of which not more than 10 public companies.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Ms Rao: 19 directorships, 10 public. Step 1: Total cap 20 — one more allowed in total. Step 2: Public cap 10 — already reached. Step 3: She cannot join the new public company unless she resigns one public directorship; she could join a private company that is not a subsidiary of a public company.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing directorship limit (20/10) with the board size limit (15); assuming independent directors are mandatory in every private company.

activity.prompt: Before accepting a directorship, check:
items: DIN obtained and consent (Form DIR-2) given
Not disqualified under s.164
Within 20 / 10 directorship limits
Disclosure of interest in other entities (s.184)
Read MoA, AoA and latest financial statements
Understands s.166 duties

quiz.q: Max directorships including alternate
quiz.why: Section 165 limits a person to twenty companies, of which at most ten may be public.

quiz.q: Listed company independent directors: at least
quiz.why: Section 149(4) requires at least one-third of the total directors to be independent in a listed public company.

quiz.q: Duties of directors are listed in
quiz.why: Section 166 codifies directors' duties for the first time in Indian company law.

scenes.text: Financial year ends 31 March 2026. The company secretary plans the AGM.
How late can it be held, how much notice, and who must attend?

steps.title: Annual General Meeting (s.96)
steps.body: First AGM within nine months of the close of the first financial year; thereafter within six months of the close of the financial year, and not more than fifteen months between two AGMs. The Registrar may extend by up to three months (not for the first AGM). OPCs need not hold an AGM. Ordinary business: financial statements, dividend, appointment of directors in place of those retiring, appointment and remuneration of auditors.

steps.title: Notice and quorum
steps.body: At least 21 clear days' notice in writing or electronically (s.101); shorter notice with consent of 95% of members entitled to vote (AGM: majority in number holding 95%). Quorum of public company (s.103): 5 members present in person if members ≤ 1,000; 15 if 1,001–5,000; 30 if > 5,000. Private company: 2 members. EGM may be called by the board or on requisition of members holding at least one-tenth of voting paid-up capital (s.100).

steps.title: Resolutions (s.114)
steps.body: Ordinary: votes cast in favour exceed votes against. Special: intention specified in notice, and votes in favour are not less than three times the votes against. Board meetings (s.173): first within 30 days of incorporation; at least four a year with not more than 120 days between two consecutive meetings; quorum one-third of total strength or two directors, whichever is higher (s.174).

steps.title: Worked example: is it special?
steps.body: Votes for 7,400; against 2,500; abstain 900. Step 1: Abstentions are ignored. Step 2: Three times against = 7,500. Step 3: 7,400 < 7,500, so the special resolution FAILS — although it passes as an ordinary resolution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using 75% of members present instead of three times votes cast against; counting the day of sending notice and the meeting day in 21 clear days.

activity.prompt: Votes against a proposed special resolution: 3,260. Minimum votes in favour needed to pass it.

quiz.q: Quorum of a public company with 6,200 members
quiz.why: Section 103 requires thirty members personally present where members exceed five thousand.

quiz.q: Maximum gap between two AGMs
quiz.why: Section 96 says not more than fifteen months shall elapse between two AGMs.

quiz.q: Minimum board meetings per year
quiz.why: Section 173 requires at least four board meetings each year.

scenes.text: Majority shareholders divert contracts to their own firm and refuse dividends for years.
Minority holders approach the NCLT.

steps.title: Key managerial personnel (s.2(51), s.203)
steps.body: CEO / Managing Director / Manager, Company Secretary, Whole-time Director, CFO. Listed companies and prescribed public companies must appoint whole-time KMP. Managerial remuneration of a public company is capped at 11% of net profits computed under s.198, unless approved otherwise as per Schedule V.

steps.title: Oppression and mismanagement (ss.241–242)
steps.body: Members may apply to the National Company Law Tribunal when affairs are conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or oppressive to any member. Eligibility (s.244): in a company with share capital, at least 100 members or one-tenth of members, whichever is less, or members holding one-tenth of issued share capital (tribunal may waive). Class action (s.245) is also available.

steps.title: Worked example: eligibility
steps.body: Company has 800 members and issued capital ₹5 crore. Step 1: One-tenth of members = 80; 100 members — the lesser is 80. Step 2: Alternatively holders of ₹50 lakh of capital. Step 3: A group of 85 members qualifies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying to the civil court instead of the NCLT; assuming every grievance is oppression (it must be burdensome, harsh and wrongful conduct).

activity.prompt: Company with 1,600 members. Minimum number of members (by number test) to apply under s.244.

quiz.q: Oppression petitions are heard by
quiz.why: Sections 241–242 vest jurisdiction in the National Company Law Tribunal.

quiz.q: Which is a KMP?
quiz.why: Section 2(51) lists the Company Secretary among key managerial personnel.

quiz.q: Overall managerial remuneration cap for a public company
quiz.why: Section 197 caps total managerial remuneration at eleven percent of net profits, subject to Schedule V approvals.

lessons.title: Lab: Winding up and insolvency resolution

scenes.text: A manufacturer defaults on ₹4 crore of bank loans.
The bank files under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. What happens next?

steps.title: Two routes
steps.body: Insolvency: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 (IBC) — Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated by financial creditor (s.7), operational creditor (s.9) or the corporate debtor (s.10) before the NCLT; minimum default ₹1 crore (notified 2020). Interim resolution professional is appointed; moratorium (s.14); committee of creditors approves a resolution plan by 66% vote; else liquidation (s.33). Voluntary liquidation of a solvent company: s.59 IBC. uni-bcom-business-economics.title: B.Com — Business Economics, unit by unit
uni-bcom-business-economics.description: Microeconomics for commerce students: demand and supply, elasticity, consumer behaviour, production and costs, market structures and factor pricing, with solved numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Nature of business economics, demand and supply
courses.summary: Scope of business economics, the basic economic problem, the law of demand and its exceptions, determinants of demand and supply, and market equilibrium with solved numericals.
outcomes: Explain the nature and scope of business economics and the central problems of an economy
State the law of demand, its assumptions and exceptions

lessons.title: Nature and scope of business economics

scenes.text: Anita owns a bakery in Pune with limited flour, ovens and staff. Every morning she must decide what to bake, how much, and for whom.
These are the same questions every economy faces: what, how and for whom to produce, given scarce resources.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Economics** studies how society allocates **scarce resources** among **unlimited wants** with alternative uses (Robbins' scarcity definition).
- **Business (managerial) economics** applies economic theory and tools to business decision-making: demand forecasting, pricing, cost control, capital budgeting and profit planning.
- **Microeconomics** studies individual units (a consumer, a firm, an industry). **Macroeconomics** studies aggregates (national income, inflation, unemployment).

steps.title: Central problems and opportunity cost
steps.body:
- **What** to produce and in what quantities
- **How** to produce (labour-intensive or capital-intensive technique)
- **For whom** to produce (distribution)
- Problems of **full utilisation** and **growth** of resources

**Opportunity cost** = value of the next best alternative forgone. The **production possibility curve (PPC)** shows maximum combinations of two goods; it is concave to the origin because opportunity cost increases as resources are shifted.

steps.title: Solved: opportunity cost on a PPC
steps.body:
An economy can make (wheat, cloth): (0,30), (10,27), (20,21), (30,12), (40,0).

- Moving from 10 to 20 units wheat costs 27 − 21 = **6 cloth**, i.e. 0.6 cloth per wheat.
- From 20 to 30 wheat costs 21 − 12 = **9 cloth** (0.9 per wheat).
- From 30 to 40 costs **12 cloth** (1.2 per wheat).

Rising opportunity cost ⇒ PPC is concave to the origin.

steps.title: Positive vs normative
steps.body: Positive statements describe what is and can be tested ("A 10% GST on cars reduced sales by 4%"). Normative statements say what ought to be ("GST on cars should be lowered"). Business economics uses both: positive analysis for prediction, normative judgement for policy and decisions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling opportunity cost the money spent — it is the best alternative given up.
- Drawing the PPC convex — with increasing opportunity cost it is concave.
- Saying a point inside the PPC is impossible — it is attainable but shows unemployment or inefficiency; points outside are unattainable.

activity.prompt: On the PPC above, what is the opportunity cost (in units of cloth) of increasing wheat from 30 to 40 units?

quiz.q: The scarcity definition of economics is associated with:
quiz.why: Lionel Robbins defined economics as the study of behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means with alternative uses.

quiz.q: A point inside the PPC indicates:
quiz.why: A point inside the PPC means the economy could produce more of both goods, so resources are idle or used inefficiently.

quiz.q: The PPC is concave to the origin because of:
quiz.why: Resources are not equally suited to all goods, so each extra unit of one good costs more units of the other, bending the PPC outward.

quiz.q: Which is a normative statement?
options: Inflation in India was about 5% last year
The RBI should cut the repo rate
quiz.why: A statement with 'should' is a value judgement that cannot be tested, so it is normative.

scenes.text: In April Alphonso mangoes sell at ₹1,200 a dozen and Rahul buys one dozen; in late May the price falls to ₹600 and he buys three.
His demand schedule slopes downward, just as the law of demand predicts.

steps.title: Demand and the law of demand
steps.body:
- **Demand** = quantity of a good a consumer is willing **and able** to buy at each price, per period of time.
- **Demand function**: Qd = f(P, Pr, Y, T, E, N) — own price, prices of related goods, income, tastes, expectations, number of buyers.
- **Law of demand**: other things remaining constant (*ceteris paribus*), quantity demanded varies **inversely** with price.
- **Reasons** for the downward slope: law of diminishing marginal utility, income effect, substitution effect, new buyers entering at lower prices, multiple uses of a good.

steps.title: Movement vs shift
steps.body:
- **Movement along** the demand curve (extension/contraction) is caused only by a change in the good's **own price**.
- **Shift** of the demand curve (increase/decrease) is caused by any other determinant.
- Rise in income → demand for a **normal good** shifts right; for an **inferior good** shifts left.
- Rise in price of a **substitute** (tea for coffee) → demand for coffee shifts right; rise in price of a **complement** (petrol for cars) → demand for cars shifts left.

steps.title: Exceptions to the law
steps.body:
- **Giffen goods**: very inferior staples for poor households where the income effect outweighs the substitution effect.
- **Veblen (prestige) goods**: diamonds, luxury watches bought for status.
- **Expectation of further price rise** (speculative buying of shares or gold).
- **Ignorance**: price taken as a sign of quality.
- **Necessities** in emergencies (medicines).

steps.title: Solved: demand function
steps.body:
Qd = 120 − 4P.

- At P = ₹10: Qd = 120 − 40 = **80 units**
- At P = ₹15: Qd = 120 − 60 = **60 units**
- Price at which Qd = 0: 120 = 4P ⇒ **P = ₹30** (the vertical intercept)

The slope ΔQ/ΔP = −4: every ₹1 rise cuts quantity by 4 units.

steps.title: Solved: market demand
steps.body:
Two buyers: A has Qa = 20 − P, B has Qb = 30 − 2P (both for P ≤ 15 here).

- Market demand is the **horizontal sum**: Q = 50 − 3P
- At P = 10: Qa = 10, Qb = 10, market Q = **20** (check: 50 − 30 = 20 ✓)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'demand rose' when only quantity demanded rose due to a price fall.
- Treating every inferior good as a Giffen good — Giffen is a rare special case.
- Adding demand curves vertically instead of horizontally.

activity.prompt: Does each event cause a movement along the demand curve for coffee, or a shift of the curve?

items.text: Price of coffee falls from ₹400 to ₹350 per kg

quiz.q: If income rises and demand for coarse grain falls, the grain is:
quiz.why: An inferior good is one whose demand falls as income rises, because consumers switch to better alternatives.

quiz.q: A fall in the price of petrol will, for cars:
options: cause a movement along the curve
quiz.why: Petrol and cars are complements, so cheaper petrol makes cars more attractive and shifts car demand to the right.

quiz.q: Veblen goods are an exception because:
options: they are bought partly for status, so a higher price can raise demand
quiz.why: For prestige goods the high price itself signals status, so some buyers demand more at a higher price.

quiz.q: For Qd = 120 − 4P, quantity demanded at P = ₹20 is:
quiz.why: Substituting P = 20 gives Qd = 120 − 80 = 40 units.

scenes.text: When tomato prices in the Azadpur mandi jump to ₹60 a kg, farmers near Delhi rush more crates to market.
When a hailstorm destroys crops, supply shifts left at every price.

steps.title: Supply and the law of supply
steps.body:
- **Supply** = quantity sellers are willing and able to offer at each price per period.
- **Law of supply**: ceteris paribus, quantity supplied varies **directly** with price, because higher prices cover rising marginal cost and raise profit.
- **Determinants**: own price, prices of inputs, technology, prices of other goods produced, taxes and subsidies, number of firms, expectations, natural factors.
- Stock is the total quantity available; supply is the part actually offered at a price.

steps.title: Movement vs shift of supply
steps.body:
- Own-price change → **extension/contraction** (movement along).
- Better technology, cheaper inputs, subsidies → supply **increases** (shifts right).
- Higher input costs, a per-unit tax, natural disasters → supply **decreases** (shifts left).
- Exceptions: labour supply may bend backward at high wages; perishable goods may be sold at any price at day's end.

steps.title: Solved: supply function
steps.body:
Qs = −20 + 5P.

- At P = ₹10: Qs = −20 + 50 = **30**
- At P = ₹14: Qs = −20 + 70 = **50**
- Minimum price for any supply: Qs = 0 ⇒ P = **₹4**

steps.title: Solved: effect of a per-unit tax
steps.body:
Supply Qs = −20 + 5P is hit by a tax of ₹2 per unit paid by sellers. Sellers now receive P − 2, so new supply is Qs = −20 + 5(P − 2) = **−30 + 5P**.

At P = ₹10, quantity supplied falls from 30 to **20** — the curve shifts left (up by ₹2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the tax-shifted curve as −20 + 5P − 2 (subtracting from quantity instead of price).
- Confusing stock with supply.
- Saying higher input prices cause a movement along the curve — they shift it.

activity.prompt: Supply is Qs = −20 + 5P. What quantity is supplied at P = ₹18?

quiz.q: A subsidy to producers will:
quiz.why: A subsidy lowers producers' effective cost, so they offer more at every price and supply shifts right.

quiz.q: A rise in the good's own price causes:
quiz.why: A change in own price moves the seller along the existing supply curve, which is called extension.

quiz.q: Which does NOT shift the supply curve of wheat?
quiz.why: The price of wheat itself only causes a movement along the supply curve of wheat.

scenes.text: At ₹30 per kg onions pile up unsold; at ₹10 the stalls run out by noon.
Somewhere in between, buyers want exactly what sellers bring — the equilibrium.

steps.title: Equilibrium
steps.body:
- **Equilibrium** where Qd = Qs; price has no tendency to change.
- Above equilibrium price → **surplus** (excess supply) → price falls.
- Below → **shortage** (excess demand) → price rises.
- Demand up → P and Q both rise. Supply up → P falls, Q rises. If both shift, one of P or Q is ambiguous.

steps.title: Solved: demand increases
steps.body:
Demand rises to Qd = 120 − 2P with the same Qs = 20 + 2P.

- 120 − 2P = 20 + 2P ⇒ 4P = 100 ⇒ **P* = ₹25**
- Q* = 120 − 50 = **70**

Both price and quantity rise, as theory predicts.

steps.title: Price ceilings and floors
steps.body: A **price ceiling** below equilibrium (e.g. rent control) creates shortages and black markets. A **price floor** above equilibrium (e.g. minimum support price for wheat) creates surpluses that the government must buy and store, which is one reason FCI holds large buffer stocks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to substitute P* back into **both** equations to check.
- Calling Qs − Qd a shortage — when Qs > Qd it is a surplus.
- Assuming both P and Q are known when demand and supply shift together.

activity.prompt: Qd = 200 − 5P and Qs = 50 + 10P. Find the equilibrium price (₹).

quiz.q: For Qd = 200 − 5P and Qs = 50 + 10P, equilibrium quantity is:
If price is set above equilibrium, the market has:
quiz.why: Above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, leaving a surplus that pushes price down.

quiz.q: Supply increases while demand is unchanged. Then:
quiz.why: A rightward supply shift moves down the demand curve, lowering price and raising quantity.

quiz.q: Minimum support price in agriculture is an example of:
quiz.why: An MSP guarantees a minimum price to farmers, which acts as a floor above which price must stay.

questions.q: Business economics mainly deals with:
options: application of economic theory to business decisions
questions.why: Business economics applies economic tools such as demand, cost and pricing analysis to managerial decisions.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is:
options: the value of the next best alternative forgone
questions.why: Opportunity cost measures what you give up by choosing one option over the best alternative.

questions.q: A point outside the PPC is:
questions.why: Points outside the PPC need more resources or better technology than the economy currently has.

questions.q: The law of demand assumes:
questions.why: The law holds only ceteris paribus, i.e. when all determinants other than own price are constant.

questions.q: Tea and coffee are:
questions.why: Tea and coffee satisfy the same want, so they are substitutes.

questions.q: A Giffen good's demand curve slopes upward because:
options: a strong negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect
the substitution effect is very large
questions.why: For a Giffen good, a price rise makes the poor household so much poorer that it buys more of the staple, outweighing substitution.

questions.q: Which causes an increase in demand for cars?
questions.why: Cheaper car loans reduce the effective cost of buying a car, shifting demand right.

questions.q: Market demand is obtained by:
questions.why: At each price we add the quantities demanded by all buyers, which is horizontal summation.

questions.q: Qd = 90 − 3P, Qs = 10 + 5P. Equilibrium price is:
questions.why: 90 − 3P = 10 + 5P gives 80 = 8P, so P = ₹10 and Q = 60.

questions.q: With Qd = 90 − 3P and Qs = 10 + 5P, at P = ₹12 there is:
questions.why: At P = 12, Qd = 54 and Qs = 70, so there is a surplus of 16 units.

questions.q: A per-unit tax on sellers shifts supply:
questions.why: Sellers need a price higher by the tax to supply the same quantity, so supply shifts up/left.

questions.q: Demand increases and supply increases by a larger amount. Then:
questions.why: Both shifts raise quantity; the larger supply shift dominates price, so price falls.

scenes.text: A multiplex in Indore cuts weekday tickets from ₹250 to ₹200 and sales jump from 400 to 600 tickets a day.
Revenue rises from ₹1,00,000 to ₹1,20,000: demand was elastic.

steps.title: Definition and degrees
steps.body:
**Price elasticity of demand** Ep = (% change in Qd) / (% change in P). It is negative by the law of demand; we usually quote the absolute value.

- |Ep| > 1 **elastic**; |Ep| < 1 **inelastic**; |Ep| = 1 **unitary**
- |Ep| = 0 perfectly inelastic (vertical curve); |Ep| = ∞ perfectly elastic (horizontal curve)

**Determinants**: availability of substitutes, necessity vs luxury, share of income, number of uses, time period, habits.

steps.title: Methods of measurement
steps.body:
- **Percentage (proportionate) method**: Ep = (ΔQ/Q) ÷ (ΔP/P), using initial values.
- **Arc (mid-point) method**: Ep = [ΔQ/((Q1+Q2)/2)] ÷ [ΔP/((P1+P2)/2)] — same answer for a rise or fall.
- **Point method** on a linear curve: Ep = lower segment ÷ upper segment; at the mid-point Ep = 1.
- **Total outlay method** (Marshall): if price falls and total expenditure rises → elastic; unchanged → unitary; falls → inelastic.

steps.title: Solved: percentage and arc methods
steps.body:
Price rises from ₹10 to ₹12 and quantity falls from 100 to 80.

**Percentage method**: %ΔQ = −20/100 = −20%; %ΔP = 2/10 = 20% ⇒ |Ep| = **1.0**

**Arc method**: ΔQ/avg Q = 20/90 = 0.2222; ΔP/avg P = 2/11 = 0.1818 ⇒ |Ep| = 0.2222/0.1818 ≈ **1.22**

The arc method avoids the base-value problem.

steps.title: Solved: total outlay
steps.body:
The multiplex: P 250 → 200, Q 400 → 600.

- TR before = ₹1,00,000; after = ₹1,20,000 → price fell and outlay rose ⇒ **elastic**.
- Percentage method check: %ΔQ = 50%, %ΔP = −20% ⇒ |Ep| = **2.5** ✓

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing slope with elasticity — a straight-line demand curve has constant slope but varying elasticity.
- Using final values as the base in the percentage method.
- Saying necessities are elastic; they are usually inelastic.

activity.prompt: Price falls from ₹50 to ₹40 and quantity demanded rises from 200 to 260. Using the percentage method on initial values, find |Ep|.

quiz.q: If a price cut leaves total expenditure unchanged, demand is:
quiz.why: Under the total outlay method, unchanged spending after a price change means |Ep| = 1.

quiz.q: At the mid-point of a straight-line demand curve, elasticity is:
quiz.why: By the point method, Ep = lower segment / upper segment, which are equal at the mid-point, giving 1.

quiz.q: Demand for salt is usually:
quiz.why: Salt is a necessity taking a tiny share of income with few substitutes, so its demand is inelastic.

quiz.q: A firm facing inelastic demand that raises price will see total revenue:
quiz.why: With inelastic demand quantity falls proportionately less than price rises, so revenue increases.

scenes.text: Kavya's salary rises 25% and her spending on restaurant meals rises 50%, while her purchase of instant noodles falls.
Income elasticity tells which goods are luxuries, necessities or inferior.

steps.title: Income elasticity
steps.body:
Ey = (% change in Qd) / (% change in income).

- Ey > 1 → **luxury** (normal, income-elastic)
- 0 < Ey < 1 → **necessity** (normal, income-inelastic)
- Ey < 0 → **inferior** good

Used by firms to forecast which products grow fastest as incomes rise.

steps.title: Cross elasticity
steps.body:
Exy = (% change in Qd of X) / (% change in price of Y).

- Exy > 0 → **substitutes** (tea and coffee)
- Exy < 0 → **complements** (printers and ink)
- Exy = 0 → unrelated goods

**Advertising (promotional) elasticity** = %ΔQd / %Δ advertising expenditure.

steps.title: Solved: income elasticity
steps.body:
Income rises from ₹20,000 to ₹25,000 per month; demand for milk rises from 10 to 12 litres per week.

- %ΔQ = 2/10 = 20%; %ΔY = 5,000/20,000 = 25%
- Ey = 20/25 = **0.8** ⇒ normal necessity

steps.title: Solved: cross elasticity
steps.body:
Price of tea rises from ₹100 to ₹120 per 250 g; demand for coffee rises from 50 to 55 packs.

- %ΔQcoffee = 5/50 = 10%; %ΔPtea = 20/100 = 20%
- Exy = 10/20 = **+0.5** ⇒ substitutes

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping the sign: for income and cross elasticity the sign carries the meaning.
- Calling every normal good a luxury — only Ey > 1 is a luxury.

activity.prompt: Classify each good by the elasticity given.

quiz.q: Cross elasticity between car prices and petrol demand is likely:
quiz.why: Cars and petrol are complements, so a higher car price lowers petrol demand, giving a negative cross elasticity.

quiz.q: Income rises 10% and demand for a good falls 5%. Ey =
quiz.why: Ey = −5%/10% = −0.5, which marks an inferior good.

quiz.q: An income elasticity of 1.5 indicates:
quiz.why: When demand rises proportionately more than income (Ey > 1), the good is a luxury.

scenes.text: At a wedding, the first gulab jamun is heavenly; by the fourth, Arjun barely enjoys it.
Marshall called this the law of diminishing marginal utility.

steps.title: Utility concepts
steps.body:
- **Total utility (TU)**: total satisfaction from consuming units of a good.
- **Marginal utility (MU)** = ΔTU/ΔQ, the addition from one more unit.
- **Law of diminishing MU**: as more units are consumed continuously, MU falls; TU is maximum when MU = 0 and falls when MU < 0.
- Assumptions: utility is measurable in utils (cardinal), constant marginal utility of money, homogeneous units, continuous consumption.

steps.title: Equilibrium conditions
steps.body:
- **One good**: buy until MU = P (in money terms).
- **Law of equi-marginal utility** (two or more goods): MUx/Px = MUy/Py = MU of money, with the whole budget spent.
- **Consumer surplus** (Marshall) = what the consumer is willing to pay − what is actually paid = Σ(MU in ₹) − P × Q; graphically the area under demand above price.

steps.title: Solved: TU and MU
steps.body:
TU for 1–6 units: 10, 18, 24, 28, 30, 30.

- MU: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, **0**
- TU is maximum (30) at the 5th–6th unit, where MU reaches 0.
- A 7th unit with TU = 28 gives MU = −2 (disutility).

steps.title: Solved: consumer surplus
steps.body:
Willingness to pay for successive cups of tea: ₹50, ₹40, ₹30, ₹20, ₹10. Market price ₹20.

- She buys 4 cups (stops where MU = price).
- Willing to pay 50 + 40 + 30 + 20 = 140; actually pays 4 × 20 = 80.
- **Consumer surplus = ₹60**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying TU falls when MU falls — TU falls only when MU becomes negative.
- Forgetting that cardinal analysis assumes constant MU of money.

activity.prompt: Willingness to pay: ₹80, ₹65, ₹50, ₹35, ₹20 for successive units. Price is ₹35. Calculate consumer surplus (₹).

quiz.why: TU stops rising when the extra unit adds nothing, so TU peaks where MU = 0.

scenes.text: With ₹100 a week, Sameer can buy movie passes at ₹5 each or e-books at ₹10 each.
He picks the combination where his highest indifference curve just touches his budget line.

steps.title: Ordinal approach
steps.body:
Hicks and Allen: consumers rank combinations rather than measure utility.

- An **indifference curve (IC)** joins combinations giving equal satisfaction.
- **Marginal rate of substitution** MRSxy = −ΔY/ΔX, units of Y given up for one more X; it **diminishes** along the IC.
- **Properties**: ICs slope downward, are convex to the origin (diminishing MRS), never intersect, and a higher IC means higher satisfaction.

steps.title: Budget line and equilibrium
steps.body:
- **Budget line**: Px·X + Py·Y = M; intercepts M/Px and M/Py; slope = −Px/Py.
- Rise in income → parallel outward shift; fall in Px → line pivots outward on the X-axis.
- **Equilibrium**: tangency of budget line with the highest attainable IC, where **MRSxy = Px/Py** and the IC is convex at that point.
- A price change splits into a **substitution effect** and an **income effect**.

steps.title: Solved: budget line
steps.body:
M = ₹100, Px = ₹5, Py = ₹10.

- Max X = 100/5 = **20**; max Y = 100/10 = **10**
- Slope = −5/10 = **−0.5**: one more X costs half a unit of Y.
- If Px falls to ₹4, max X becomes 25 while max Y stays 10.

steps.title: Solved: equilibrium
steps.body:
With the budget above, Sameer's MRSxy at (10 X, 5 Y) is 0.5.

- Px/Py = 0.5 = MRS ✓
- Cost check: 10×5 + 5×10 = 100 ✓

So (10, 5) is his equilibrium bundle.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the budget slope as −Py/Px.
- Drawing intersecting ICs — it would contradict transitivity.
- Forgetting the full-budget condition when checking equilibrium.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Production and cost analysis
courses.summary: Production function, law of variable proportions, returns to scale and isoquants; short-run and long-run cost curves; revenue concepts and break-even analysis with worked tables.
outcomes: Compute TP, AP and MP and identify the three stages of production
Distinguish law of variable proportions from returns to scale
Use isoquants, isocost lines and MRTS to find the least-cost combination
Derive AFC, AVC, ATC and MC from a cost schedule
Calculate break-even output and sales

lessons.title: Production function and the law of variable proportions

scenes.text: A Surat workshop has one power loom. Adding a second and third worker raises output sharply.
By the sixth worker, people get in each other's way and output actually falls.

steps.title: Production function
steps.body:
- A **production function** Q = f(L, K) shows the maximum output from given inputs with given technology.
- **Short run**: at least one factor (capital) is fixed. **Long run**: all factors are variable.
- **TP** = total product; **AP** = TP/L; **MP** = ΔTP/ΔL.

steps.title: Law of variable proportions — three stages
steps.body:
With one factor fixed and another increased:

- **Stage I (increasing returns)**: MP rises then falls but AP rises; ends where AP is maximum (AP = MP).
- **Stage II (diminishing returns)**: AP and MP fall, MP still positive; ends where **MP = 0** and TP is maximum. A rational firm operates here.
- **Stage III (negative returns)**: MP negative, TP falls.

Reasons: better use of the fixed factor at first (indivisibility, specialisation), then the fixed factor becomes scarce relative to the variable one.

steps.title: Solved: TP, AP, MP
steps.body:
Workers 1–7, TP: 10, 24, 36, 44, 48, 48, 45.

- MP: 10, 14, 12, 8, 4, **0**, −3
- AP: 10, 12, 12, 11, 9.6, 8, 6.43
- Stage I up to 3 workers (AP max 12, where AP = MP = 12); Stage II from 3 to 6 workers (MP = 0 at 6); Stage III beyond 6.

steps.title: Relations to remember
steps.body:
- When MP > AP, AP rises; when MP < AP, AP falls; MP cuts AP at AP's maximum.
- When MP = 0, TP is maximum; when MP < 0, TP falls.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking diminishing returns means TP falls — TP keeps rising, only more slowly.
- Mixing up the law of variable proportions (short run) with returns to scale (long run).

activity.prompt: TP with 4 workers is 60 and with 5 workers is 70. What is the marginal product of the 5th worker?

quiz.q: A rational producer operates in:
quiz.why: In Stage I adding labour still raises AP, and in Stage III MP is negative, so only Stage II is rational.

quiz.q: TP is maximum when:
quiz.why: TP stops rising when the next worker adds nothing, i.e. where MP = 0.

quiz.q: MP cuts AP at:
quiz.why: AP rises while MP is above it and falls when MP is below it, so MP crosses AP at AP's peak.

lessons.title: Returns to scale, isoquants and least-cost combination

scenes.text: A cement company doubles both its kilns and its workforce.
Output more than doubles at first, thanks to specialisation and bulk buying.

steps.title: Returns to scale
steps.body:
When **all** inputs change in the same proportion (long run):

- **Increasing returns**: output rises more than proportionately (economies of scale: technical, managerial, marketing, financial).
- **Constant returns**: proportionate change.
- **Decreasing returns**: less than proportionate (diseconomies: coordination problems).

For Cobb–Douglas Q = A·L^a·K^b: a + b > 1 increasing, = 1 constant, < 1 decreasing.

steps.title: Isoquants and isocosts
steps.body:
- An **isoquant** joins L–K combinations producing the same output; downward sloping, convex, non-intersecting.
- **MRTS(L,K)** = −ΔK/ΔL = MPL/MPK, diminishing along the isoquant.
- An **isocost line** wL + rK = C, slope −w/r.
- **Least-cost combination**: isoquant tangent to the lowest isocost ⇒ **MPL/w = MPK/r** (MRTS = w/r).

steps.title: Solved: returns to scale
steps.body:
Q = 10·L^0.6·K^0.5.

- a + b = 0.6 + 0.5 = **1.1 > 1** ⇒ increasing returns to scale.
- Doubling L and K multiplies Q by 2^1.1 ≈ **2.14**.

steps.title: Solved: least-cost check
steps.body:
w = ₹200, r = ₹500. At the current mix MPL = 20, MPK = 40.

- MPL/w = 20/200 = 0.10; MPK/r = 40/500 = 0.08
- A rupee on labour yields more ⇒ **use more labour, less capital** until the ratios are equal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing MPL with MPK instead of MP per rupee.
- Calling economies of scale 'increasing returns to a factor'.

activity.prompt: Classify each Cobb–Douglas function by returns to scale.

quiz.q: The slope of an isoquant is the:
quiz.why: Along an isoquant one input substitutes for the other, and that rate is the marginal rate of technical substitution.

quiz.why: Cost is minimised when the last rupee spent on each input adds the same output.

quiz.q: Bulk buying of raw materials at a discount is a:
quiz.why: Discounts on large purchases are a marketing economy of scale.

scenes.text: Anita's bakery pays ₹100 a day rent whatever it bakes, plus flour and wages that rise with output.
To price her cakes she must know her average and marginal costs.

steps.title: Cost concepts
steps.body:
- **TFC** does not change with output (rent, salaries, insurance). **TVC** varies with output (materials, wages).
- TC = TFC + TVC; AFC = TFC/Q; AVC = TVC/Q; ATC = TC/Q = AFC + AVC; MC = ΔTC/ΔQ = ΔTVC/ΔQ.
- Other concepts: explicit vs implicit, opportunity cost, sunk cost, accounting vs economic cost.

steps.title: Shapes of the curves
steps.body:
- AFC falls continuously (rectangular hyperbola).
- AVC, ATC and MC are **U-shaped** because of the law of variable proportions.
- MC cuts AVC and ATC at their **minimum points**; minimum ATC lies to the right of minimum AVC.
- The gap between ATC and AVC (= AFC) narrows as output rises.

steps.title: Solved: implicit cost
steps.body:
An owner runs a shop with explicit costs of ₹6,00,000 and revenue of ₹9,00,000. She gave up a salary of ₹4,00,000.

- Accounting profit = 9,00,000 − 6,00,000 = **₹3,00,000**
- Economic profit = 3,00,000 − 4,00,000 = **−₹1,00,000** (an economic loss)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including fixed cost in MC — MC depends only on variable cost.
- Drawing AFC as U-shaped.
- Ignoring implicit costs when judging economic profit.

activity.prompt: TFC = ₹500. At Q = 10, TVC = ₹1,500. What is ATC (₹)?

quiz.q: MC intersects ATC at:
quiz.why: ATC falls while MC is below it and rises once MC is above it, so they meet at minimum ATC.

quiz.q: Which cost falls continuously as output rises?
quiz.why: A fixed amount spread over more units keeps falling, so AFC declines throughout.

It needs to know how many bottles must sell before it stops losing money.

steps.title: Long-run average cost (LAC)
steps.body:
- LAC is the **envelope** of short-run ATC curves (planning curve).
- It is U-shaped (flatter) due to economies then diseconomies of scale; the lowest point is the **minimum efficient scale**.
- Modern theory finds many industries with an **L-shaped** LAC.

steps.title: Revenue concepts
steps.body:
- TR = P × Q; AR = TR/Q = P; MR = ΔTR/ΔQ.
- Perfect competition: P = AR = MR (horizontal).
- Monopoly/imperfect competition: AR slopes down and MR lies below it; for linear AR, MR has twice the slope.
- **MR = AR(1 − 1/|e|)**: MR is zero where |e| = 1.

steps.title: Solved: MR from elasticity
steps.body: P = ₹40 and |e| = 2. MR = 40(1 − 1/2) = **₹20**. If |e| = 1, MR = 0, so TR is at its maximum.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing fixed cost by price instead of contribution per unit.
- Assuming MR = P for a firm facing a downward-sloping demand curve.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Market structures and pricing
courses.summary: Equilibrium of firm and industry under perfect competition, monopoly and price discrimination, monopolistic competition with selling costs, and oligopoly with the kinked demand curve and game theory.
outcomes: State the features of each market form
Apply MR = MC with second-order condition to find profit-maximising output
Explain short-run shutdown and long-run normal profit under perfect competition
Solve monopoly and third-degree price discrimination numericals
Explain price rigidity under oligopoly and a prisoners' dilemma payoff matrix

scenes.text: Gurpreet is one of lakhs of wheat farmers. Whatever he does, the mandi price stays the same.
He can only decide how much to grow — he is a price taker.

steps.title: Features
steps.body:
- Very large number of buyers and sellers
- Homogeneous product
- Free entry and exit
- Perfect knowledge and perfect mobility of factors
- No transport costs; a single uniform price

The **industry** sets price by demand and supply; each **firm** is a price taker with a horizontal demand curve P = AR = MR.

steps.title: Equilibrium conditions
steps.body:
- **First-order**: MR = MC. **Second-order**: MC must cut MR from below (MC rising).
- Short run: firm may earn supernormal profit (P > ATC), normal profit (P = ATC) or loss.
- **Shutdown point**: P = minimum AVC. Below it the firm stops production, losing only fixed cost.
- Firm's short-run supply curve = MC above minimum AVC.
- **Long run**: entry/exit eliminates abnormal profit ⇒ P = MR = MC = minimum LAC (normal profit only).

steps.title: Solved: firm's output
steps.body:
P = ₹40. TC = 100 + 4Q + Q², so MC = 4 + 2Q.

1. MR = MC: 40 = 4 + 2Q ⇒ **Q = 18**
2. TR = 720; TC = 100 + 72 + 324 = 496
3. **Profit = ₹224** (supernormal)

AVC = 4 + Q, minimum at Q → 0 is ₹4, so the shutdown price here is ₹4.

steps.title: Solved: shutdown decision
steps.body:
P = ₹15, AVC = ₹18, AFC = ₹5 at the best output.

Price does not cover AVC, so producing loses ₹8 per unit (vs ₹5 if closed) ⇒ **shut down**. If P were ₹20 (above AVC, below ATC ₹23), it should **continue** in the short run.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using P = ATC as the shutdown rule — it is P = minimum AVC.
- Forgetting the second-order condition when MC cuts MR twice.

activity.prompt: Market price is ₹60 and MC = 10 + 5Q. What is the profit-maximising output?

quiz.q: A perfectly competitive firm's demand curve is:
quiz.why: The firm can sell any quantity at the given market price, so its demand curve is horizontal.

quiz.q: In the long run a competitive firm earns:
quiz.why: Free entry and exit push price to minimum LAC, leaving only normal profit.

quiz.q: The firm shuts down in the short run if price is below:
quiz.why: If price cannot cover average variable cost, producing adds to the loss beyond fixed cost.

scenes.text: Indian Railways charges different fares for sleeper, AC 3-tier and AC 2-tier on the same train.
Selling the same journey at different prices to groups with different elasticity is price discrimination.

steps.title: Monopoly
steps.body:
- Single seller, no close substitutes, strong barriers to entry (patents, licences, control of inputs, natural monopoly).
- Price maker: faces the downward-sloping market demand; MR < AR.
- Equilibrium: MR = MC with MC cutting MR from below; price read off the AR curve.
- A monopolist always produces on the **elastic** part of demand (MR > 0).
- **Lerner index** of monopoly power = (P − MC)/P.

steps.title: Solved: monopoly equilibrium
steps.body:
Demand P = 100 − 2Q, MC = AC = ₹20.

1. TR = 100Q − 2Q² ⇒ MR = 100 − 4Q
2. MR = MC: 100 − 4Q = 20 ⇒ **Q = 20**
3. P = 100 − 40 = **₹60**
4. Profit = (60 − 20) × 20 = **₹800**
5. Lerner index = (60 − 20)/60 ≈ **0.67**

Under perfect competition P = MC = 20 ⇒ Q = 40: monopoly restricts output.

steps.title: Price discrimination
steps.body:
- **First degree**: each unit at the buyer's maximum price.
- **Second degree**: price by quantity blocks (electricity slabs).
- **Third degree**: different prices in separate markets.

Conditions: separable markets, no resale, different elasticities. Equilibrium: **MR1 = MR2 = MC**; the less elastic market pays more.

steps.title: Solved: third-degree discrimination
steps.body:
MC = ₹30, |e1| = 2, |e2| = 4. MR = P(1 − 1/|e|).

- Market 1: P1(1 − 1/2) = 30 ⇒ **P1 = ₹60**
- Market 2: P2(1 − 1/4) = 30 ⇒ **P2 = ₹40**

The less elastic market 1 is charged more.

steps.title: Equilibrium
steps.body:
- **Short run**: MR = MC; may earn supernormal profit or loss.
- **Long run**: entry pushes each firm's AR down until it is **tangent to LAC** ⇒ P = AC, normal profit only.
- Tangency lies on the falling part of LAC ⇒ output below minimum-cost level: **excess capacity** (a key criticism).

steps.title: Examples

steps.title: Kinked demand curve (Sweezy)
steps.body:
- Rivals match a price **cut** but ignore a price **rise**.
- So demand is elastic above the prevailing price and inelastic below it ⇒ a kink.
- MR has a **vertical gap (discontinuity)** at the kink; MC can move within the gap without changing price or output ⇒ explains **price rigidity**.
- Limitation: does not explain how the initial price is set.

steps.title: Solved: prisoners' dilemma
steps.body:
Firms A and B choose High or Low price. Profits (A, B) in ₹ crore:

- Both High: (10, 10)
- A Low, B High: (14, 4)
- A High, B Low: (4, 14)
- Both Low: (6, 6)

Whatever B does, Low gives A more (14 > 10, 6 > 4) ⇒ Low is A's **dominant strategy**; same for B. **Nash equilibrium = (Low, Low) = (6, 6)**, though both would gain by colluding at High.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

scenes.text: An e-commerce warehouse in Bhiwandi pays packers ₹600 a day. A new packer would pack 40 more parcels earning ₹20 each.
₹800 of extra revenue beats ₹600 of wage, so the manager hires.

steps.title: Marginal productivity theory
steps.body:
- **MPP** = extra physical output from one more worker.
- **MRP** = MPP × MR (under perfect competition in the product market, VMP = MPP × P = MRP).
- A firm hires labour until **MRP = wage** (and MRP is falling).
- The falling part of the MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labour.
- Criticisms: assumes perfect competition, homogeneous labour, full employment, measurable marginal product.

steps.title: Wage concepts
steps.body:
- **Nominal (money) wage** vs **real wage** = what money wages buy (money wage ÷ price index).
- Wage differences arise from skill, risk, training costs, trade unions, location and discrimination.
- **Collective bargaining** can raise wages above the competitive level; a **monopsony** employer can pay below MRP.

steps.title: Solved: hiring decision
steps.body:
Product price ₹5. MPP of workers 1–5: 30, 26, 20, 14, 8. Wage ₹100.

- MRP = 150, 130, 100, 70, 40
- Hire while MRP ≥ wage ⇒ **3 workers** (MRP of the 3rd = 100 = wage).

steps.title: Solved: real wage
steps.body:
Money wage rises from ₹20,000 to ₹22,000 while CPI rises from 100 to 115.

- Real wage = 22,000 × 100/115 ≈ **₹19,130**
- Real wage **fell** by about 4.3% despite the raise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing MPP (units) directly with the wage (₹).
- Treating a money-wage rise as a real-wage rise without checking prices.

quiz.why: Real wage measures the goods and services a money wage can buy at current prices.

quiz.why: A monopsony is a market with a single buyer, here of labour.

scenes.text: Fertile valley land gives 40 quintals per acre; hill-slope land just barely covers costs at 25 quintals.
Ricardo said the valley's 15 extra quintals are economic rent.

steps.title: Rent
steps.body:
- **Ricardian rent**: surplus of produce of superior land over that of **marginal (no-rent) land**, due to differences in fertility and location; land is fixed in supply.
- **Modern theory**: rent = earnings of any factor above its **transfer earnings** (opportunity cost).
- **Quasi-rent** (Marshall): short-run surplus of a man-made fixed factor = TR − TVC; disappears in the long run.

steps.title: Interest and profit
steps.body:
**Interest**
- Classical: set by saving (supply) and investment (demand).
- **Loanable funds** (neo-classical): supply = savings + bank credit + dishoarding + disinvestment; demand = investment + hoarding + consumption loans.
- **Liquidity preference** (Keynes): interest is the reward for parting with liquidity; demand for money from transactions, precautionary and speculative motives; supply fixed by the central bank.

**Profit**
- Risk theory (Hawley), **uncertainty-bearing** (Knight: only non-insurable risk earns profit), **innovation** theory (Schumpeter), dynamic theory (Clark).

steps.title: Solved: Ricardian rent
steps.body:
Grades A, B, C yield 40, 32, 25 quintals per acre with equal cost; C is marginal.

- Rent of A = 40 − 25 = **15 quintals**
- Rent of B = 32 − 25 = **7 quintals**
- Rent of C = **0**

steps.title: Solved: quasi-rent and transfer earnings
steps.body:
A machine earns TR ₹5,000 a month with TVC ₹3,500 ⇒ quasi-rent = **₹1,500**.

An engineer earns ₹1,20,000; her next best offer is ₹90,000 ⇒ economic rent = **₹30,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating economic rent with contract rent paid to a landlord.
- Saying Knight's profit arises from insurable risk — insurable risk is a cost.

quiz.why: Marshall's quasi-rent is the short-run surplus over variable cost earned by a fixed man-made factor.

quiz.why: Keynes explained interest as the reward for parting with liquidity.

quiz.why: Schumpeter argued profit rewards entrepreneurs who introduce innovations, and lasts until imitators catch up.

steps.title: Demand and elasticity
steps.body:
- Equilibrium: Qd = Qs
- Ep = %ΔQ/%ΔP; arc Ep = (ΔQ/avg Q)/(ΔP/avg P)
- Ey = %ΔQ/%ΔY; Exy = %ΔQx/%ΔPy
- MR = AR(1 − 1/|e|)
- Consumer surplus = Σ willingness to pay − P×Q
- Equi-marginal: MUx/Px = MUy/Py; ordinal: MRSxy = Px/Py; budget slope = −Px/Py

steps.title: Production and cost
steps.body:
- AP = TP/L; MP = ΔTP/ΔL; Cobb–Douglas RTS from a + b
- Least cost: MPL/w = MPK/r
- TC = TFC + TVC; ATC = AFC + AVC; MC = ΔTC/ΔQ
- BEP units = FC/(P − AVC); target units = (FC + profit)/(P − AVC)

steps.title: Markets and factors
steps.body:
- Profit max: MR = MC, MC rising
- Shutdown: P < min AVC; competitive long run: P = min LAC
- Monopoly: price from AR; Lerner = (P − MC)/P
- Discrimination: MR1 = MR2 = MC
- Hire labour till MRP = w; quasi-rent = TR − TVC; economic rent = earnings − transfer earnings

steps.title: Q1 Equilibrium with tax
steps.body:
Qd = 150 − 3P, Qs = −30 + 6P. A tax of ₹3 per unit is imposed on sellers. Find old and new equilibrium.

**Solution**: Old: 150 − 3P = −30 + 6P ⇒ 9P = 180 ⇒ P = 20, Q = 90. New supply: −30 + 6(P − 3) = −48 + 6P. 150 − 3P = −48 + 6P ⇒ 9P = 198 ⇒ **P = 22, Q = 84**. Buyers bear ₹2 of the ₹3 tax.

steps.title: Q2 Elasticity and revenue
steps.body:
A firm sells 500 units at ₹40. If price falls to ₹36, sales rise to 600. Is demand elastic? What happens to revenue?

**Solution**: %ΔQ = 20%, %ΔP = −10% ⇒ |Ep| = 2 (elastic). TR rises from ₹20,000 to ₹21,600.

steps.title: Q3 Cost function
steps.body:
TC = 200 + 10Q + Q². Find AFC, AVC, ATC and MC at Q = 10.

**Solution**: AFC = 20; AVC = 10 + Q = 20; ATC = 40; MC = 10 + 2Q = **30**.

steps.title: Q4 Monopoly
steps.body:
P = 60 − Q, TC = 10Q + 100. Find profit-maximising Q, P and profit.

**Solution**: MR = 60 − 2Q = 10 ⇒ Q = 25, P = 35. TR = 875, TC = 350 ⇒ **profit ₹525**.

scenes.text: A supermarket chain in Hyderabad wants to know how much its customers spend per visit.
It can ask every customer (census) or a well-chosen sample of 500 — and must then organise the answers.

steps.title: Meaning, functions, limitations
steps.body:
- **Statistics** (plural): numerical facts systematically collected. (Singular): the science of collecting, organising, analysing and interpreting data.
- Functions: simplifies complexity, enables comparison, helps forecasting and policy.
- Limitations: studies aggregates not individuals, results true only on average, can be misused, needs homogeneous data.

steps.title: Collection of data
steps.body:
- **Primary data**: collected first-hand — direct personal interview, indirect investigation, questionnaires (mailed or by enumerators), local correspondents.
- **Secondary data**: already collected by others — RBI bulletins, Census of India, NSSO/MoSPI reports, company annual reports. Check reliability, suitability, adequacy.
- **Census** covers every unit; **sampling** studies a part. Methods: simple random, stratified, systematic, cluster (random); judgement, quota, convenience (non-random).

steps.title: Classification and presentation
steps.body:
- Classification: geographical, chronological, qualitative, quantitative.
- **Frequency distribution**: class intervals, class limits, mid-points, frequencies. **Exclusive** (10–20, 20–30) vs **inclusive** (10–19, 20–29) classes.
- Sturges' rule for number of classes: k ≈ 1 + 3.322 log10 N.
- Diagrams: bar, sub-divided bar, pie. Graphs: **histogram**, frequency polygon, **ogive** (cumulative frequency curve, used to locate median graphically).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing an upper-limit value (30) in the lower class in an exclusive table.
- Drawing a histogram with gaps between bars — bars must touch.
- Using secondary data without checking its definitions and period.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Raw data: x̄ = Σx/N
- Discrete series: x̄ = Σfx/N
- Continuous series (direct): x̄ = Σfm/N, m = mid-point
- **Step-deviation**: x̄ = A + (Σfd′/N) × h, where d′ = (m − A)/h
- **Weighted mean**: x̄w = Σwx/Σw
- **Combined mean**: x̄12 = (N1x̄1 + N2x̄2)/(N1 + N2)

Properties: Σ(x − x̄) = 0; Σ(x − x̄)² is minimum.

steps.title: Median and partitions
steps.body:
- **Median**: middle value of ordered data. Raw: the ((N + 1)/2)th item.
- Grouped: **Median = L + ((N/2 − cf)/f) × h**, where L = lower limit of median class, cf = cumulative frequency before it, f = its frequency, h = width.
- **Quartiles**: Q1 at N/4, Q3 at 3N/4 using the same formula. Deciles and percentiles likewise.

steps.title: Mode
steps.body:
- **Mode**: most frequently occurring value.
- Grouped: **Mode = L + ((f1 − f0)/(2f1 − f0 − f2)) × h**, f1 = modal class frequency, f0 and f2 = preceding and succeeding frequencies.
- **Empirical relation** (moderately skewed data): Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the cf of the median class itself instead of the one before it.
- Not converting inclusive classes to exclusive before applying formulas.
- Choosing the modal class by cumulative frequency.
