steps.title: GM and HM
steps.body:
- **Geometric mean** GM = (x1·x2·…·xn)^(1/n); log form: GM = antilog(Σlog x / n). Used for **rates of growth**, ratios and index numbers.
- **Harmonic mean** HM = N / Σ(1/x). Used for **rates** such as speed or price per unit when the numerator quantity is constant.
- For positive unequal values: **AM > GM > HM**; for two values GM² = AM × HM.

steps.title: Solved: average growth
steps.body:
Growth factors 1.10 and 1.30.

- GM = √(1.10 × 1.30) = √1.43 ≈ **1.1958** ⇒ average growth ≈ 19.58% per year (not 20%).
- Check: 1.1958² ≈ 1.43 ✓

steps.title: Solved: average speed
steps.body:
Equal distances at 40 and 60 km/h.

- HM = 2/(1/40 + 1/60) = 2/(5/120) = **48 km/h**
- Check: 60 km takes 1.5 h + 1 h = 2.5 h for 120 km ⇒ 48 km/h ✓
- For two values: AM = 50, GM = √2400 ≈ 48.99, HM = 48 ⇒ AM > GM > HM ✓

steps.title: Choosing an average
steps.body:
- Mean: symmetric data, further algebra needed.
- Median: skewed data (incomes, house prices), open-ended classes.
- Mode: most common size (shoe sizes, fashion).
- GM: growth rates, index numbers.
- HM: rates with constant numerator (speed over equal distances, equal rupees spent at different prices).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Averaging growth percentages arithmetically.
- Using HM when equal times (not equal distances) are given — then AM is correct.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Dispersion, skewness and kurtosis
courses.summary: Absolute and relative measures of dispersion — range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, standard deviation and coefficient of variation — followed by Karl Pearson's and Bowley's skewness, moments and kurtosis.
outcomes: Compute range, quartile deviation and mean deviation with their coefficients
Calculate standard deviation for raw and grouped data by the step-deviation method

lessons.title: Range, quartile deviation and mean deviation

scenes.text: Two batsmen both average 50 runs. One scores 45–55 every match; the other swings between 0 and 120.
Dispersion measures that difference in consistency.

steps.title: Absolute vs relative measures
steps.body:
- **Absolute** measures are in the units of the data (₹, kg); **relative** ones (coefficients) are unit-free and used for comparison.
- **Range** R = L − S; coefficient = (L − S)/(L + S). Simple but depends only on extremes.
- **Quartile deviation** QD = (Q3 − Q1)/2; coefficient = (Q3 − Q1)/(Q3 + Q1). Ignores the top and bottom 25%.
- **Mean deviation** MD = Σ|x − A|/N, taken about the mean or median (minimum about the median); coefficient = MD/A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the absolute-value signs in mean deviation (the signed sum about the mean is always zero).
- Comparing absolute measures across series in different units.

activity.prompt: Highest price ₹180, lowest ₹120. Find the coefficient of range.

quiz.why: Coefficients are ratios with no units, so they are relative measures.

lessons.title: Standard deviation and coefficient of variation

scenes.text: Supplier A delivers in a mean of 50 hours with SD 5; supplier B in 60 hours with SD 9.
The coefficient of variation shows which is relatively more consistent.

steps.title: Standard deviation
steps.body:
Karl Pearson's **standard deviation** σ = √(Σ(x − x̄)²/N) — the root-mean-square deviation from the mean.

- Shortcut: σ = √(Σx²/N − (Σx/N)²)
- Step-deviation (grouped): **σ = h × √(Σfd′²/N − (Σfd′/N)²)**
- **Variance** = σ²
- Properties: independent of change of origin, depends on change of scale; combined SD uses both group SDs and mean differences.

steps.title: Coefficient of variation
steps.body:
**CV = (σ / x̄) × 100**

- Lower CV ⇒ more consistent / less variable / more uniform.
- Used to compare share returns, worker output, rainfall across regions with different units or means.

steps.title: Solved: comparing consistency
steps.body:
- Supplier A: CV = 5/50 × 100 = **10%**
- Supplier B: CV = 9/60 × 100 = **15%**

A is **more consistent** although it is compared on a different mean.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the square root before dividing by N.
- Choosing the series with the smaller SD as more consistent when means differ — compare CVs.
- Forgetting to multiply by h in the step-deviation formula.

activity.prompt: Mean monthly sales ₹80,000 with SD ₹12,000. Find the coefficient of variation (%).

quiz.why: SD is unaffected by a change of origin because all deviations from the mean stay the same.

quiz.q: Multiplying every value by 3 changes SD to:
quiz.why: SD changes with scale in the same ratio, so it triples (variance becomes 9 times).

quiz.q: Share X: mean return 12%, σ 3%. Share Y: mean 15%, σ 4.5%. More consistent:
quiz.why: CV of X is 25% and of Y is 30%, so X varies less relative to its mean.

steps.title: Skewness
steps.body:
- **Symmetric**: mean = median = mode.
- **Positive (right) skew**: mean > median > mode, long right tail.
- **Negative (left) skew**: mean < median < mode.
- **Karl Pearson**: Sk = (Mean − Mode)/σ, or 3(Mean − Median)/σ when mode is ill-defined; usually between −3 and +3.
- **Bowley**: Sk = (Q3 + Q1 − 2 Median)/(Q3 − Q1), between −1 and +1; useful for open-ended data.

steps.title: Moments and kurtosis
steps.body:
- Central moments μr = Σ(x − x̄)^r/N; μ1 = 0, μ2 = variance.
- β1 = μ3²/μ2³ (skewness), **β2 = μ4/μ2²** (kurtosis).
- β2 = 3 **mesokurtic** (normal); β2 > 3 **leptokurtic** (peaked); β2 < 3 **platykurtic** (flat).

steps.title: Solved: kurtosis
steps.body: μ2 = 4, μ4 = 60 ⇒ β2 = 60/16 = **3.75 > 3** ⇒ leptokurtic (more peaked than normal).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing dispersion (spread) with skewness (asymmetry).
- Forgetting that Bowley's measure must lie between −1 and +1 — a larger result signals an arithmetic error.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Correlation and regression
courses.summary: Types of correlation and scatter diagrams, Karl Pearson's coefficient with probable error, Spearman's rank correlation including tied ranks, and the two lines of regression with prediction.
outcomes: Identify positive, negative, linear and non-linear correlation from a scatter diagram

scenes.text: A detergent brand notices that months with higher TV ad spending usually show higher sales.
Correlation measures how closely two variables move together — but not why.

steps.title: Meaning and types
steps.body:
- **Correlation**: the degree and direction of association between two variables.
- **Positive**: both move in the same direction (price and supply). **Negative**: opposite directions (price and demand).
- **Linear** vs **non-linear (curvilinear)**: constant vs changing ratio of change.
- **Simple** (two variables), **partial** and **multiple** (more variables).

steps.title: Scatter diagram
steps.body:
Plot each (X, Y) pair as a dot.

- Dots rising close to a line ⇒ high positive correlation.
- Falling close to a line ⇒ high negative.
- No pattern ⇒ no correlation.

Merit: simple, visual, shows non-linearity. Limitation: gives no exact numerical degree.

steps.title: Correlation is not causation
steps.body:
- **Spurious (nonsense) correlation**: ice-cream sales and drowning cases rise together because both rise in summer.
- A third variable, chance, or mutual influence can create correlation without cause and effect.

steps.title: Range of r
steps.body: Karl Pearson's coefficient r lies between −1 and +1. r = +1 perfect positive, r = −1 perfect negative, r = 0 no linear correlation (a non-linear relation may still exist).

activity.prompt: Classify the likely correlation between each pair.

scenes.text: An HR manager records training hours (X) and daily output (Y) for five workers.
She computes r to see how strongly training relates to output.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**r = Σdxdy / √(Σdx² · Σdy²)**, where dx = X − X̄, dy = Y − Ȳ.

Alternative: r = Cov(X,Y)/(σx σy), Cov = Σdxdy/N.

**Probable error** PE = 0.6745 × (1 − r²)/√N.
- If r < PE: not significant. If r > 6 PE: significant.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by Σdx² × Σdy² without the square root.
- Getting |r| > 1 — always a sign of an arithmetic slip.
- Using N − 1 in PE.

quiz.why: A coefficient smaller than its probable error could easily be due to chance.

scenes.text: Two judges rank five dance teams at a college fest.
Rank correlation shows how far their judgements agree.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**R = 1 − 6Σd² / (n(n² − 1))**, d = difference between ranks of each item.

- Used for qualitative attributes (beauty, honesty) or when only ranks are available.
- **Tied ranks**: give each tied item the average rank, and add **m(m² − 1)/12** to Σd² for every tie group of size m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting Σd = 0 as a check before squaring.
- Using n² instead of n(n² − 1) in the denominator.

steps.title: Two regression lines
steps.body:
- **Y on X** (to estimate Y): Y − Ȳ = byx(X − X̄), byx = Σdxdy/Σdx² = r σy/σx
- **X on Y** (to estimate X): X − X̄ = bxy(Y − Ȳ), bxy = Σdxdy/Σdy² = r σx/σy
- **r = ±√(byx × bxy)** with the sign of the coefficients; both coefficients have the same sign and their product ≤ 1.
- Both lines pass through (X̄, Ȳ); they coincide when r = ±1 and are perpendicular when r = 0.

steps.title: Solved: fitting both lines
steps.body:
From the Pearson lab: Σdxdy = 6, Σdx² = 10, Σdy² = 6, X̄ = 3, Ȳ = 4.

- byx = 6/10 = 0.6 ⇒ Y − 4 = 0.6(X − 3) ⇒ **Y = 2.2 + 0.6X**
- bxy = 6/6 = 1 ⇒ X − 3 = 1(Y − 4) ⇒ **X = Y − 1**
- r = √(0.6 × 1) = **0.775** ✓ (matches the Pearson lab)
- Estimate Y at X = 6: 2.2 + 3.6 = **5.8 units**

steps.title: Solved: means from two lines
steps.body:
Lines: 2X + 3Y = 26 and 6X + Y = 30.

- Solve: from the second, Y = 30 − 6X ⇒ 2X + 90 − 18X = 26 ⇒ 16X = 64 ⇒ **X̄ = 4**, **Ȳ = 6**.

steps.body:

- Taking r = byx × bxy without the square root.

lessons.title: Index numbers: meaning and simple methods

story.title: How much dearer is the thali?

scenes.text: A canteen thali cost ₹60 in 2020 and ₹84 in 2025.
An index number expresses that change as 140 with 2020 = 100.

steps.title: Meaning and uses
steps.body:
- An **index number** is a statistical measure of the relative change in a variable or group of variables over time or place, with the **base** = 100.
- Types: price, quantity, value indices.
- Uses: measure inflation (CPI, WPI), deflate values, adjust wages (DA), guide policy.
- Problems: choice of base year (normal year), items, prices, weights, formula and average.

steps.title: Simple (unweighted) methods
steps.body:
- **Simple aggregative**: P01 = (Σp1/Σp0) × 100
- **Simple average of price relatives**: P01 = Σ(p1/p0 × 100)/N (AM or GM)
- **Chain base**: link relative = (current/previous) × 100; chain index = (link relative × previous chain index)/100

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Simple aggregative index is distorted by units (price per kg vs per tonne) — relatives avoid this.
- Choosing an abnormal year (drought, pandemic) as base.

quiz.why: By convention the base period is set to 100.

quiz.why: A chain index is built by linking each period to the one before it.

scenes.text: An analyst compares a household's basket in the base and current years, with both prices and quantities changing.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Laspeyres** (base-year quantities): L = Σp1q0/Σp0q0 × 100
- **Paasche** (current quantities): P = Σp1q1/Σp0q1 × 100
- **Fisher's ideal** = √(L × P)
- **Time-reversal test**: P01 × P10 = 1. **Factor-reversal test**: P01 × Q01 = Σp1q1/Σp0q0. Fisher's index satisfies both, hence 'ideal'.

steps.title: Bias
steps.body: Laspeyres tends to **overstate** price rise (ignores substitution to cheaper goods); Paasche tends to **understate**. Fisher lies between them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing q0 and q1 between numerator and denominator.
- Taking the arithmetic mean of L and P instead of the geometric mean for Fisher.

steps.title: Cost-of-living (consumer price) index
steps.body:
Measures the change in the cost of a fixed basket for a specific group.

- **Aggregate expenditure method**: Σp1q0/Σp0q0 × 100 (Laspeyres)
- **Family budget method**: Σ(I × W)/ΣW, where I = price relative and W = base-year expenditure weight (p0q0)
- Uses: wage negotiation, DA, deflating, measuring purchasing power (= 100/CPI).

steps.title: Solved: deflating
steps.body:
Real wage = money wage / CPI × 100.

- Before: 30,000/100 × 100 = 30,000
- After: 36,000/125 × 100 = **₹28,800**
- Purchasing power of a rupee = 100/125 = **₹0.80**

steps.body:

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
- **Secular trend (T)**: long-term movement
- **Seasonal (S)**: regular within-year pattern (festival sales)
- **Cyclical (C)**: business cycles of several years
- **Irregular (I)**: random shocks (floods, strikes)

Models: additive Y = T + S + C + I; multiplicative Y = T × S × C × I.

steps.title: Measuring trend
steps.body:
- Free-hand, semi-averages, **moving averages**, **least squares**.
- Least squares Y = a + bX with X coded so ΣX = 0: **a = ΣY/N, b = ΣXY/ΣX²**.
- For odd N code X = …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2; for even N use −5, −3, −1, 1, 3, 5 (half-years).

steps.body:
- Forgetting to state the origin and unit of X with the trend equation.
- Centring an even-period moving average without a second (2-period) averaging step.

courses.summary: Classical and empirical probability, addition and multiplication theorems, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem; binomial, Poisson and normal distributions; and a full-subject formula sheet with practice problems and exam.
outcomes: Apply the addition and multiplication theorems of probability
Use Bayes' theorem to revise probabilities

scenes.text: Machine A makes 60% of a factory's bolts with 2% defective; machine B makes 40% with 5% defective.
A bolt is found defective. Bayes' theorem tells the chance it came from B.

steps.title: Basic concepts
steps.body:
- **Random experiment**, **sample space** S, **event** A ⊆ S.
- **Classical**: P(A) = favourable cases / total equally likely cases.
- **Empirical (relative frequency)**: P(A) = lim (m/n).
- **Axiomatic**: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, P(S) = 1, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) for mutually exclusive events.
- Mutually exclusive: cannot occur together. Independent: one does not affect the other.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
- **Addition**: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
- **Multiplication**: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B|A); for independent events P(A) × P(B)
- **Conditional**: P(B|A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A)
- **Complement**: P(A′) = 1 − P(A)
- **Bayes**: P(Ai|D) = P(Ai)P(D|Ai) / Σ P(Aj)P(D|Aj)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding probabilities of overlapping events without subtracting the intersection.
- Treating mutually exclusive events as independent — exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are dependent.

activity.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of at least one head? (decimal)

quiz.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, independent. P(A ∩ B) =
quiz.why: For independent events P(A ∩ B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2.

quiz.why: Bayes' theorem revises prior probabilities after observing an outcome.

scenes.text: A bank's help desk gets on average 2 calls per minute.
Poisson tells the chance of a silent minute; binomial handles yes/no trials like defective items in a box.

steps.title: Binomial
steps.body:
n independent trials, each success with probability p (q = 1 − p).

- **P(X = r) = nCr p^r q^(n−r)**, r = 0, 1, …, n
- Mean = **np**, variance = **npq**, SD = √(npq)
- Mean > variance always (since q < 1).

steps.title: Poisson
steps.body:
Rare events in a large number of trials (n large, p small, m = np).

- **P(X = r) = e^(−m) m^r / r!**
- Mean = variance = **m**
- Examples: printing errors per page, accidents per day, calls per minute. e^(−2) ≈ 0.1353.

steps.title: Solved: binomial
steps.body:
4 fair coins tossed. P(exactly 2 heads)?

- 4C2 (0.5)²(0.5)² = 6 × 1/16 = **0.375**
- Mean = 4 × 0.5 = 2; variance = 4 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 1

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using binomial when trials are not independent (sampling without replacement from a small lot).
- Claiming Poisson variance = m² — it equals m.

scenes.text: A mill fills 1 kg packs; actual weights are normal with mean 1,000 g and SD 10 g.
The bell curve tells what share of packs are underweight.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- Bell-shaped, symmetric about the mean; mean = median = mode.
- Total area = 1; tails approach but never touch the X-axis.
- **z = (X − μ)/σ** converts to the standard normal (mean 0, SD 1).
- Empirical areas: μ ± 1σ ≈ **68.27%**, μ ± 2σ ≈ **95.45%**, μ ± 3σ ≈ **99.73%**.
- Quartile deviation ≈ 0.6745σ; mean deviation ≈ 0.7979σ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting areas on opposite sides of the mean instead of adding them.
- Forgetting that table areas are usually from 0 to z, not cumulative.

uni-bcom-corporate-accounting.title: B.Com · Corporate Accounting (full paper)
uni-bcom-corporate-accounting.description: The complete Corporate Accounting paper unit by unit: issue, forfeiture and reissue of shares, debentures and buy-back, company final accounts under Schedule III, valuation of goodwill and shares, amalgamation, internal reconstruction and consolidation basics, with solved numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Issue, forfeiture and reissue of shares
courses.summary: Kinds of share capital and the structure of capital in a company's balance sheet, uses of securities premium, issue of shares at par and premium in instalments, calls in arrears and in advance, over-subscription and pro-rata allotment, and forfeiture and reissue of shares with transfer to capital reserve.
outcomes: Explain authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital
State the permitted uses of securities premium under Section 52
Journalise issue of shares payable in instalments, including premium
Handle over-subscription with pro-rata allotment
Record forfeiture and reissue of shares and compute the capital reserve

scenes.text: Three founders convert their partnership into a private limited company to raise money from many investors.
Its memorandum fixes the maximum capital it may issue – the authorised capital.

steps.title: Capital structure
steps.body:
- **Authorised (nominal)** – maximum stated in the memorandum
- **Issued** – part offered to the public
- **Subscribed** – part taken up by investors (subscribed and fully paid; subscribed but not fully paid)
- **Called-up** – part of face value demanded so far
- **Paid-up** – called-up less calls in arrears

In the balance sheet (Schedule III), share capital appears under **Shareholders' funds / Equity**, with details in a note.

steps.title: Kinds of shares
steps.body:
Under Section 43 of the Companies Act, 2013:
- **Equity shares** – with voting rights, or with differential rights as to dividend/voting
- **Preference shares** – preferential right to fixed dividend and to repayment of capital on winding up; may be cumulative/non-cumulative, participating/non-participating, redeemable, convertible

Issue of shares at a **discount** is prohibited (Section 53), except sweat equity shares.

steps.title: Securities premium – Section 52
steps.body:
Premium is credited to **Securities Premium A/c** and may be used only to:
1. issue fully paid bonus shares
2. write off preliminary expenses of the company
3. write off expenses of, commission paid or discount allowed on, any issue of shares or debentures
4. provide for premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures
5. buy back its own shares or securities under Section 68

It cannot be used to pay dividend.

steps.title: Solved: capital note
steps.body:
Authorised 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10. Issued and subscribed 60,000. Called up ₹8 per share. Calls in arrears ₹4,000.

- Authorised: ₹10,00,000
- Issued & subscribed: ₹6,00,000 (face value)
- Called-up: 60,000 × 8 = ₹4,80,000
- **Paid-up: 4,80,000 − 4,000 = ₹4,76,000**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Showing authorised capital in the balance sheet total (it is shown only in the note).
- Adding securities premium to share capital (it goes under Reserves and Surplus / Other Equity).
- Using securities premium to pay dividends.

activity.prompt: Is this a permitted use of securities premium under Section 52?

items.text: Issue of fully paid bonus shares
Premium payable on redemption of debentures
Writing off a loss on sale of machinery

quiz.q: The maximum capital a company can issue is its:
quiz.why: Authorised capital, stated in the memorandum, is the ceiling on issue.

quiz.q: Issue of shares at a discount is prohibited by:
quiz.why: Section 53 bans issue of shares at a discount, except sweat equity shares.

quiz.q: Called-up capital ₹5,00,000, calls in arrears ₹6,000. Paid-up capital:
quiz.why: Paid-up = called-up − calls in arrears = ₹4,94,000.

quiz.q: Preference shareholders have preference regarding:
quiz.why: Preference shares carry a preferential right to dividend and to repayment of capital on winding up.

lessons.title: Issue of shares at par and premium

scenes.text: A Pune engineering company issues 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 at a premium of ₹2.
Investors pay in three instalments: application, allotment and a final call.

steps.title: Journal pattern
steps.body:
For each instalment:
1. **Bank A/c Dr / To Share Application A/c** (money received)
2. **Share Application A/c Dr / To Share Capital A/c** (transfer)
3. **Share Allotment A/c Dr / To Share Capital, To Securities Premium** (amount due)
4. **Bank A/c Dr / To Share Allotment A/c**
5. Same for each call.

Premium is usually collected with allotment.

steps.title: Solved: issue at premium
steps.body:
10,000 shares of ₹10 at ₹12: application ₹3, allotment ₹5 (including premium ₹2), first and final call ₹4. All money received.

- Application: Bank Dr 30,000 / To Share Application 30,000; transfer to Share Capital 30,000
- Allotment due: Share Allotment Dr 50,000 / To Share Capital 30,000, To Securities Premium 20,000
- Call due: Share First & Final Call Dr 40,000 / To Share Capital 40,000
- **Share capital = ₹1,00,000; Securities premium = ₹20,000; Bank = ₹1,20,000**

steps.title: Calls in arrears and in advance
steps.body:
- **Calls in arrears**: amount called but unpaid. Debit Calls in Arrears A/c; deducted from called-up capital in the note. Interest (if articles adopt Table F) up to 10% p.a.
- **Calls in advance**: amount received before it is called. Credit Calls in Advance A/c – shown as **other current liability**; interest under Table F up to 12% p.a.

steps.title: Solved: arrears
steps.body:
In the above issue, Ravi holding 200 shares does not pay the final call.

- Bank receives 40,000 − 800 = 39,200 on the call
- **Calls in Arrears A/c Dr 800**
- Paid-up capital = 1,00,000 − 800 = ₹99,200

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Crediting premium to Share Capital.
- Showing calls in advance as part of share capital.
- Forgetting that called-up capital includes calls in arrears until deducted.

activity.prompt: A company issues 20,000 shares of ₹10 at a premium of ₹3, payable ₹2 on application, ₹6 on allotment (including premium) and ₹5 on first and final call. All money is received except the call on 500 shares. Total cash received (₹)?

quiz.q: Securities premium collected on allotment is credited to:
quiz.why: Premium is credited to a separate Securities Premium account.

quiz.q: Calls in advance are shown in the balance sheet as:
quiz.why: Money received before it is called is owed back to shareholders until called, so it is a liability.

quiz.q: Under Table F, interest on calls in arrears may be charged up to:
quiz.why: Table F allows interest on unpaid calls at a rate not exceeding 10% p.a.

quiz.q: 10,000 shares of ₹10 issued at ₹11, fully paid. Securities premium:
quiz.why: Premium ₹1 × 10,000 shares = ₹10,000.

scenes.text: A popular issue of 10,000 shares receives applications for 15,000.
The board allots pro rata and adjusts the extra application money against allotment.

steps.title: Three ways to handle excess
steps.body:
1. **Reject** some applications fully – refund their money.
2. **Pro-rata allotment** – allot fewer shares than applied; excess application money is adjusted towards allotment (and calls, if the articles allow), balance refunded.
3. Combination of rejection and pro-rata.

steps.title: Solved: pro-rata
steps.body:
10,000 shares offered; applications for 15,000; all applicants allotted pro rata (2 shares for every 3 applied). Application ₹3, allotment ₹5.

- Application money received = 15,000 × 3 = 45,000
- Required for 10,000 shares = 30,000 → **excess ₹15,000** adjusted towards allotment
- Allotment due = 10,000 × 5 = 50,000 → **cash received on allotment = 35,000**

Entry: Share Application Dr 45,000 / To Share Capital 30,000, To Share Allotment 15,000.

steps.title: Solved: individual shareholder
steps.body:
An applicant applied for 1,500 shares and received 1,000.

- Paid on application 1,500 × 3 = 4,500; needed 3,000; excess 1,500
- Allotment due 1,000 × 5 = 5,000
- **Pays on allotment 5,000 − 1,500 = ₹3,500**

If he defaults on allotment, his arrears are 3,500, not 5,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Refunding excess money that should be adjusted against allotment.
- Computing arrears on allotment without deducting the excess application money.
- Adjusting excess beyond the allotment amount when articles do not permit adjustment against calls.

activity.prompt: Shares of ₹10: application ₹3, allotment ₹4. An investor applied for 900 shares and was allotted 600 under pro-rata allotment. How much does he pay on allotment (₹)?

quiz.q: Under pro-rata allotment, excess application money is usually:
quiz.why: Excess money is adjusted against amounts due on allotment, with any balance refunded.

quiz.q: 20,000 shares offered, applications 30,000, all allotted pro rata, application ₹2. Excess application money:
quiz.why: Received 60,000, needed 40,000, so ₹20,000 is excess.

quiz.q: Applications for 25,000 shares; 5,000 rejected; the rest allotted 20,000 shares fully. This is:
quiz.why: Rejected applicants are refunded and the remaining applications receive full allotment.

quiz.q: Minimum subscription in a public issue protects:
quiz.why: If minimum subscription is not received, money must be refunded, so investors are not left in an under-funded company.

scenes.text: Despite reminders, a shareholder holding 100 shares does not pay the final call.
The board forfeits his shares, keeps the money already paid, and later reissues the shares to someone else.

steps.title: Forfeiture entry
steps.body:
**Share Capital A/c Dr** (amount called up on forfeited shares)
**Securities Premium A/c Dr** (only if premium was due and not received)
**To Calls in Arrears / Unpaid calls**
**To Share Forfeiture A/c** (amount actually received)

Share forfeiture balance is shown under share capital until reissue.

steps.title: Solved: forfeiture and reissue (par)
steps.body:
100 shares of ₹10 fully called; holder paid ₹7 and failed to pay the final call of ₹3. Shares forfeited and reissued at ₹8 fully paid.

- Forfeiture: Share Capital Dr 1,000 / To Final Call 300, To Share Forfeiture 700
- Reissue: Bank Dr 800, Share Forfeiture Dr 200 / To Share Capital 1,000
- **Capital reserve = 700 − 200 = ₹500**: Share Forfeiture Dr 500 / To Capital Reserve 500

steps.title: Solved: premium already received
steps.body:
50 shares of ₹10 issued at ₹12; holder paid application ₹3 and allotment ₹5 (including ₹2 premium), defaulted on final call ₹4.

- Premium was received, so it is **not** reversed
- Share Capital Dr 500 / To Final Call 200, To Share Forfeiture 300
- (Forfeited amount = money received less premium = 3 + 3 = ₹6 per share)

steps.title: Reissue limit
steps.body: Discount on reissue cannot exceed the amount forfeited on those shares. Only the forfeited amount on **reissued** shares is transferred to capital reserve; the balance on shares not yet reissued stays in Share Forfeiture A/c.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Debiting Securities Premium on forfeiture when the premium was already received.
- Transferring the forfeited amount on all forfeited shares to capital reserve when only some are reissued.
- Allowing a reissue discount larger than the forfeited amount.

activity.prompt: 200 shares of ₹10 (issued at par) were forfeited for non-payment of the final call of ₹4; ₹6 per share had been paid. 150 of these shares were reissued at ₹7 per share fully paid. Amount transferred to capital reserve (₹)?

quiz.q: On forfeiture, Share Capital is debited with:
quiz.why: Share capital is cancelled to the extent called up on the forfeited shares.

quiz.q: Securities Premium is debited on forfeiture only when:
options: premium was due but not received
quiz.why: Premium once received is never reversed; only unreceived premium is cancelled.

quiz.q: Forfeited ₹600 on 100 shares; reissued at a discount of ₹2 each. Capital reserve:
The balance in Share Forfeiture A/c on shares not yet reissued is shown:
options: added to share capital in the note
quiz.why: Until reissue, the forfeited amount is shown with share capital in the notes.

questions.q: Kinds of share capital are specified in Section:
questions.why: Section 43 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides for equity and preference share capital.

questions.q: Securities premium can be used for:
options: writing off discount on issue of debentures
questions.why: Section 52 permits writing off discount on issue of shares or debentures.

questions.q: Authorised ₹20,00,000; issued ₹12,00,000; called up ₹9,00,000; arrears ₹15,000. Paid-up capital:
Shares of ₹10 at ₹15 issued; premium credited per share:
questions.why: Premium is the excess over face value: ₹5.

questions.q: Calls in advance carry interest under Table F up to:
questions.why: Table F allows interest on calls in advance not exceeding 12% p.a.

questions.q: 30,000 shares offered; applied 45,000; pro rata to all; application ₹2, allotment ₹3. Cash received on allotment (no default):
questions.why: Excess application money is 30,000; allotment due 90,000; cash = ₹60,000.

questions.q: An applicant got 400 shares for 600 applied; application ₹2, allotment ₹4. If he fails to pay allotment, arrears are:
questions.why: Excess paid is 400; allotment due 1,600; arrears = ₹1,200.

questions.q: Share forfeiture A/c is credited with:
options: amount received on forfeited shares (excluding premium received)
questions.why: The forfeiture account records money actually received towards capital on those shares.

questions.q: Maximum discount on reissue of forfeited shares is limited to:
options: the amount forfeited on those shares
questions.why: Discount on reissue cannot exceed the amount already forfeited on the reissued shares.

questions.q: 300 shares of ₹10 forfeited after ₹8 paid; all reissued at ₹9 fully paid. Capital reserve:
questions.why: Forfeited 2,400; discount 300 × 1 = 300; capital reserve = ₹2,100.

questions.q: A shareholder of 100 shares (₹10 at ₹13) paid application ₹2 only and defaulted on allotment ₹5 (incl. premium ₹3); shares forfeited before the call of ₹6. Entry debits:
questions.why: Called up capital is ₹4 per share (₹400) and premium ₹300 was due but unpaid, so both are debited.

questions.q: Capital reserve from reissue of forfeited shares is shown under:
questions.why: It is a capital profit shown under reserves.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Debentures, bonus issue, buy-back and redemption
courses.summary: Issue of debentures at par, premium and discount with redemption terms, interest and debenture redemption reserve, redemption by purchase in the open market, bonus shares and rights issues, buy-back of shares under Section 68 and redemption of preference shares with the capital redemption reserve.
outcomes: Record the six standard combinations of debenture issue and redemption
Explain DRR and record redemption including open-market purchase
Record a bonus issue from permitted sources
Apply the main conditions of buy-back and record it with CRR
Compute the transfer to CRR on redemption of preference shares

scenes.text: A cement company needs ₹1 crore for a new kiln but does not want to dilute ownership.
It issues 9% debentures – a loan from the public, carrying fixed interest whether or not it earns profit.

steps.title: Debentures vs shares
steps.body:
- A debenture is an acknowledgement of **debt**; debenture-holders are creditors, shares make holders owners.
- Interest is a **charge** against profit; dividend is an appropriation.
- Debentures can be issued at a discount (shares cannot, except sweat equity); usually secured by a charge on assets.
- Types: secured/unsecured, redeemable/irredeemable, convertible/non-convertible, registered/bearer.

steps.title: Solved: issue at discount, redeemable at premium
steps.body:
1,000 9% debentures of ₹100 issued at ₹95, redeemable at ₹105.

**Bank A/c Dr 95,000
Loss on Issue of Debentures A/c Dr 10,000
To 9% Debentures A/c 1,00,000
To Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c 5,000**

Loss = discount 5,000 + redemption premium 5,000. It is written off over the life of the debentures, first from securities premium, then from P&L.

steps.title: Collateral security
steps.body: Debentures issued as collateral for a loan: either no entry (shown as a note below the loan) or **Debenture Suspense A/c Dr / To Debentures A/c**, shown as a deduction. No interest is paid on collateral debentures.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Crediting premium on redemption to Securities Premium (it is a liability: Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c).
- Treating debenture interest as an appropriation of profit.
- Paying interest on debentures issued as collateral.

activity.prompt: 2,000 debentures of ₹100 are issued at a 4% discount and are redeemable at a 5% premium. Loss on issue of debentures (₹)?

quiz.q: Debenture-holders are the company's:
quiz.why: A debenture is a loan to the company, so its holders are creditors.

quiz.q: Premium payable on redemption of debentures is credited to:
options: Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c
quiz.why: It is a future liability, so a separate Premium on Redemption account is credited.

quiz.q: Debentures issued at ₹98 and redeemable at par give a loss on issue per debenture of:
quiz.why: The only loss is the ₹2 discount on issue.

quiz.q: Interest on debentures is:
quiz.why: Interest is a contractual cost payable even in a loss year.

lessons.title: Interest, DRR and redemption of debentures

scenes.text: The cement company's debentures fall due for repayment.
Because it built a reserve and set aside liquid funds each year, it repays without a cash crisis.

steps.title: Interest entries
steps.body:
- Interest due: **Debenture Interest A/c Dr / To Debenture-holders A/c, To TDS Payable A/c**
- Payment: Debenture-holders Dr / To Bank
- Year end: P&L Dr / To Debenture Interest

Interest is on face value, not issue price.

steps.title: Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR)
steps.body: Under Section 71 and the share-capital and debentures rules, companies covered must create a DRR out of profits (10% of outstanding debentures for the covered classes, e.g. unlisted companies other than NBFCs/HFCs), and invest or deposit at least 15% of debentures maturing in the year before 30 April of that year. After the 2019 amendment, listed companies and certain financial companies are exempt from DRR. Rules change – check the current text before applying.

steps.title: Solved: redemption at premium out of profits
steps.body:
1,000 debentures of ₹100 redeemed at 5% premium.

- Debentures Dr 1,00,000, Premium on Redemption Dr 5,000 / To Debenture-holders 1,05,000
- Debenture-holders Dr / To Bank 1,05,000
- DRR no longer needed: DRR Dr / To General Reserve

steps.title: Solved: purchase in the open market
steps.body:
Company buys 500 of its own ₹100 debentures at ₹97 for cancellation.

- Own Debentures Dr 48,500 / To Bank 48,500
- Cancellation: Debentures Dr 50,000 / To Own Debentures 48,500, To Profit on Cancellation 1,500
- Profit on cancellation is a capital profit → **Capital Reserve**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calculating interest on issue price.
- Treating profit on cancellation of own debentures as revenue profit.
- Transferring DRR to P&L instead of General Reserve after redemption.

activity.prompt: A company buys 800 of its own 10% debentures of ₹100 at ₹96 each and cancels them. Profit on cancellation (₹)?

quiz.q: Debenture interest is calculated on:
quiz.why: The coupon rate applies to the nominal (face) value.

quiz.q: After redemption, the DRR balance is transferred to:
quiz.why: The DRR is a free reserve again once its purpose is over, so it goes to General Reserve.

quiz.q: Profit on cancellation of own debentures is credited to:
quiz.why: It arises from a capital transaction, so it goes to Capital Reserve.

quiz.q: ₹5,00,000 10% debentures; annual interest:

scenes.text: A profitable FMCG company has large reserves but wants to conserve cash.
It issues one bonus share for every four held – capitalising reserves instead of paying a cash dividend.

steps.title: Bonus issue
steps.body:
Under Section 63, fully paid bonus shares may be issued out of:
- free reserves
- securities premium account
- capital redemption reserve

Not out of revaluation reserve. Bonus issue must be authorised by the articles and cannot be in lieu of dividend.

steps.title: Solved: bonus entry
steps.body:
40,000 equity shares of ₹10; bonus 1 for every 4 held, out of General Reserve.

- Bonus shares = 10,000 → ₹1,00,000
- **General Reserve Dr 1,00,000 / To Bonus to Shareholders 1,00,000**
- **Bonus to Shareholders Dr / To Equity Share Capital 1,00,000**

steps.title: Rights issue
steps.body:
Under Section 62, further shares are first offered to existing shareholders in proportion to holdings, usually at a price below market. Theoretical value of a right:

**Value of right = (Market price − Ex-right price)**, where Ex-right price = (MP × old shares + issue price × new shares) ÷ total shares.

E.g. MP ₹50, 1 for 4 at ₹40: ex-right = (200 + 40) ÷ 5 = ₹48; value of right per old share = ₹2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using revaluation reserve for bonus shares.
- Debiting P&L directly with bonus (use the reserve).
- Treating a rights issue as free – shareholders pay for rights shares.

activity.prompt: A company has 60,000 equity shares of ₹10 and issues bonus shares in the ratio 2:5 (2 bonus for every 5 held) out of securities premium. Amount capitalised (₹)?

quiz.q: Bonus shares cannot be issued out of:
quiz.why: Section 63 does not permit revaluation reserve, an unrealised gain, to fund bonus shares.

quiz.q: Rights shares are offered first to:
quiz.why: Section 62 requires further issue to be offered to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings.

quiz.q: MP ₹60; rights 1 for 2 at ₹45. Ex-right price:
Bonus issue increases:
options: share capital but not total equity
quiz.why: Reserves are converted into share capital, so total shareholders' funds stay the same.

lessons.title: Buy-back and redemption of preference shares

scenes.text: An IT company with idle cash buys back some of its shares from shareholders.
The law protects creditors: buy-back must come from specified sources, and capital bought out of reserves is replaced by a capital redemption reserve.

steps.title: Buy-back – Section 68 (main conditions)
steps.body:
- Sources: free reserves, securities premium, or proceeds of an issue of **different** kind of shares/securities
- Authorised by articles; board resolution up to 10% of paid-up equity + free reserves; special resolution up to 25%
- Equity buy-back in a year ≤ 25% of paid-up equity capital
- Post buy-back **debt–equity ratio ≤ 2:1**
- Shares must be fully paid
- **Section 69**: if bought out of free reserves or securities premium, transfer nominal value to **Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR)**

steps.title: Solved: buy-back entries
steps.body:
10,000 equity shares of ₹10 bought back at ₹15 out of free reserves.

- Equity Share Capital Dr 1,00,000
- Premium on Buy-back Dr 50,000 / To Equity Shareholders 1,50,000
- Securities Premium (or General Reserve) Dr 50,000 / To Premium on Buy-back 50,000
- **General Reserve Dr 1,00,000 / To CRR 1,00,000**
- Shareholders Dr / To Bank 1,50,000

steps.title: Solved: redemption of preference shares
steps.body:
Preference shares ₹5,00,000 redeemed at par. Fresh issue of equity shares ₹2,00,000 at par for the purpose.

- Section 55: preference shares redeemed out of profits or a fresh issue
- Part not covered by fresh issue = 5,00,000 − 2,00,000 = 3,00,000
- **Transfer to CRR = ₹3,00,000** from divisible profits

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the securities premium on the fresh issue as 'proceeds' for CRR purposes (only the nominal value of the fresh issue counts for CRR).
- Funding a buy-back of equity shares out of a fresh issue of equity shares.
- Forgetting the CRR when buy-back is out of free reserves.

activity.prompt: ₹6,00,000 preference shares are redeemed at par. The company issues 25,000 equity shares of ₹10 at a premium of ₹2 to finance it. Amount to be transferred to CRR (₹)?

quiz.q: Post buy-back, the debt–equity ratio must not exceed:
quiz.why: Section 68 requires debt to be at most twice the paid-up capital and free reserves after buy-back.

quiz.q: A buy-back of equity shares cannot be financed from:
options: a fresh issue of equity shares
a fresh issue of preference shares
quiz.why: Proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares cannot fund the buy-back.

quiz.q: CRR can be used to:
quiz.why: Capital redemption reserve may be applied only in paying up unissued shares as fully paid bonus shares.

quiz.q: Buy-back of shares must be of shares that are:
quiz.why: Only fully paid-up shares can be bought back.

questions.q: Debentures can be issued at a discount because:
questions.why: The prohibition on discount in Section 53 applies to shares, not to debentures.

questions.q: Debentures of ₹100 issued at ₹104 redeemable at par. Credit to Securities Premium per debenture:
questions.why: The excess of issue price over face value, ₹4, is securities premium.

questions.q: 5,000 debentures of ₹100 at ₹96, redeemable at ₹110. Loss on issue:
Collateral debentures are:
options: given as additional security for a loan
questions.why: They are issued to a lender as extra security; they become enforceable only on default.

questions.q: Company buys 1,000 own debentures of ₹100 at ₹102 for cancellation. Result:
questions.why: Paying above face value gives a loss of ₹2,000 on cancellation.

questions.q: Bonus shares may be issued out of:
questions.why: Section 63 allows free reserves, securities premium and CRR.

questions.q: MP ₹100; rights 1 for 4 at ₹80. Value of right per old share:
questions.why: Ex-right = (400 + 80) ÷ 5 = 96; value of right = 100 − 96 = ₹4.

questions.q: Buy-back by board resolution alone is limited to:
questions.why: The board may approve buy-back up to 10% of paid-up equity capital and free reserves.

questions.q: 20,000 shares of ₹10 bought back at ₹12 out of general reserve. Transfer to CRR:
questions.why: CRR equals the nominal value bought back from free reserves: ₹2,00,000.

questions.q: Preference shares ₹4,00,000 redeemed; fresh equity issue ₹1,50,000 at par. CRR:
A shareholder of 1,200 shares gets bonus at 1:3. Bonus shares received:
questions.why: One for every three held: 1,200 ÷ 3 = 400.

questions.q: The debenture redemption reserve, where required, is created out of:
questions.why: DRR is an appropriation of profits that would otherwise be available for dividend.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Company final accounts under Schedule III
courses.summary: The vertical balance sheet and statement of profit and loss prescribed by Schedule III, current and non-current classification, profit prior to incorporation by time and sales ratios, managerial remuneration limits and the basic rules for declaring dividends.
outcomes: Classify items into the Schedule III balance sheet headings
Prepare a statement of profit and loss with the prescribed expense heads
Apportion profit between pre- and post-incorporation periods
Compute maximum managerial remuneration under Section 197
State the main rules for declaration of dividend

scenes.text: Neha opens the annual report of a listed company and finds a balance sheet laid out top to bottom, not in two sides.
Schedule III fixes the headings so every company's statements can be compared.

steps.title: Format (Division I – non-Ind AS companies)
steps.body:
**I. Equity and Liabilities**
1. Shareholders' funds: (a) Share capital (b) Reserves and surplus
2. Share application money pending allotment
3. Non-current liabilities: long-term borrowings, deferred tax liabilities, other long-term liabilities, long-term provisions
4. Current liabilities: short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities, short-term provisions

**II. Assets**
1. Non-current assets: property, plant and equipment; intangible assets; capital work-in-progress; non-current investments; long-term loans and advances
2. Current assets: current investments, inventories, trade receivables, cash and cash equivalents, short-term loans and advances, other current assets

(Division II for Ind AS companies uses 'Equity' and 'Other equity' instead.)

steps.title: Current vs non-current
steps.body:
An asset or liability is **current** if it is expected to be realised/settled within **12 months** after the reporting date or within the company's **operating cycle**, or is held primarily for trading. Everything else is non-current.

The current portion of a long-term loan (instalments due within 12 months) is shown under 'Other current liabilities'.

steps.title: Solved: where does it go?
steps.body:
- Calls in advance → Other current liabilities
- Unpaid dividend → Other current liabilities
- Proposed dividend → not a liability (disclosed in notes, under AS 4 revised)
- Loose tools → Inventories
- 10% Debentures repayable after 5 years → Long-term borrowings
- Securities premium → Reserves and surplus
- Bills receivable → Trade receivables

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Showing proposed dividend as a current liability (not after the AS 4 revision).
- Putting calls in arrears on the assets side (they are deducted from called-up capital).
- Treating the next year's loan instalment as long-term.

activity.prompt: Under which main heading of the Schedule III balance sheet does each item fall?

quiz.q: Calls in advance are shown under:
quiz.why: Money received before being called is repayable or adjustable soon, so it is a current liability.

quiz.q: The normal cut-off for current classification is:
quiz.why: Items realised or settled within 12 months or the operating cycle are current.

quiz.q: Loose tools are shown under:
quiz.why: Schedule III lists loose tools as a sub-head of inventories.

quiz.q: Goodwill appears under:
quiz.why: Goodwill is a non-current intangible asset.

scenes.text: A component maker reports ₹10 lakh revenue from operations for the year.
Schedule III makes it show its expenses under fixed heads so analysts can see what drives profit.

steps.title: Format
steps.body:
I. Revenue from operations
II. Other income
III. Total income (I + II)
IV. Expenses: cost of materials consumed; purchases of stock-in-trade; **changes in inventories** of FG, WIP and stock-in-trade; employee benefits expense; finance costs; depreciation and amortisation; other expenses
V. Profit before exceptional items and tax … tax expense … **profit for the period**, then earnings per share.

steps.title: Solved: statement of P&L
steps.body:
Revenue from operations 10,00,000; other income 50,000; cost of materials 4,00,000; finished goods: opening 80,000, closing 1,00,000; employee benefits 1,50,000; finance costs 30,000; depreciation 60,000; other expenses 1,20,000; tax 25%.

- Change in inventories = 80,000 − 1,00,000 = **−20,000**
- Total expenses = 4,00,000 − 20,000 + 1,50,000 + 30,000 + 60,000 + 1,20,000 = 7,40,000
- PBT = 10,50,000 − 7,40,000 = **3,10,000**
- Tax = 77,500 → **Profit = ₹2,32,500**

steps.title: Where items go
steps.body:
- Interest on debentures and loans → finance costs
- Salaries, PF contribution, staff welfare → employee benefits
- Dividend/interest received, profit on sale of investments → other income
- Rent, audit fees, advertising, repairs → other expenses (details in notes)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding the change in inventories with the wrong sign (an increase reduces expenses).
- Showing interest income in revenue from operations for a non-finance company.
- Deducting dividends paid in the statement of P&L (dividends are appropriations, not expenses).

activity.prompt: Revenue from operations ₹8,00,000; other income ₹20,000; purchases of stock-in-trade ₹3,50,000; stock-in-trade opening ₹60,000, closing ₹40,000; employee benefits ₹1,20,000; finance costs ₹25,000; depreciation ₹35,000; other expenses ₹90,000. Profit before tax (₹)?

quiz.q: Interest on debentures is shown under:
quiz.why: Schedule III requires interest and other borrowing costs under finance costs.

quiz.q: Opening FG ₹50,000, closing FG ₹70,000. Change in inventories in the statement of P&L:
quiz.why: Opening minus closing is −20,000, which reduces total expenses.

quiz.q: Dividend received on investments is:
quiz.why: For a non-investment company, dividend received is not from main operations, so it is other income.

quiz.q: Contribution to provident fund is part of:
quiz.why: PF contribution is a cost of employing staff.

story.title: A company takes over a running business

scenes.text: Shree Ltd takes over a proprietor's business from 1 April but is incorporated only on 1 August.
Profit for April–July is earned before the company exists, so it is a capital profit, not available for dividend.

steps.title: Ratios
steps.body:
- **Time ratio**: months before and after incorporation
- **Sales ratio**: sales before and after incorporation

Apportion:
- Gross profit, selling expenses (commission, carriage outwards, advertisement, bad debts) → **sales ratio**
- Fixed/time-based expenses (salaries, rent, office expenses, depreciation, interest to vendor) → **time ratio**
- Wholly pre: interest to vendor up to incorporation
- Wholly post: directors' fees, preliminary expenses, debenture interest, formation-related costs

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Business taken over 1 April 2025; incorporated 1 August 2025; year ends 31 March 2026. Sales 12,00,000 of which 3,00,000 up to 31 July. GP 3,60,000; salaries 72,000; rent 36,000; selling commission 24,000; directors' fees 12,000.

- Time ratio 4:8 = 1:2; sales ratio 3:9 = 1:3
- GP: 90,000 | 2,70,000
- Salaries: 24,000 | 48,000; Rent 12,000 | 24,000
- Commission: 6,000 | 18,000; Directors' fees: – | 12,000
- **Pre-incorporation profit = 48,000** (to Capital Reserve)
- **Post-incorporation profit = 1,68,000** (to P&L)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the time ratio for gross profit.
- Distributing pre-incorporation profit as dividend.
- Splitting directors' fees across both periods.

activity.prompt: Gross profit for the year ₹2,40,000; sales ratio pre:post = 1:3. Time-based expenses ₹48,000; time ratio pre:post = 1:3. No other expenses. Pre-incorporation profit (₹)?

quiz.q: Pre-incorporation profit is transferred to:
quiz.why: It is earned before the company exists, so it is a capital profit.

quiz.q: Gross profit is apportioned in the:
quiz.why: Gross profit arises from sales, so it follows the sales ratio.

quiz.q: Directors' fees are charged to:
quiz.why: Directors exist only after incorporation, so their fees are wholly post-incorporation.

quiz.q: Rent for the year is apportioned on:
quiz.why: Rent accrues with time, so the time ratio is used.

story.title: How much can the MD be paid?

scenes.text: A public company's board wants to raise its managing director's pay.
Section 197 sets percentage ceilings based on profits computed under Section 198.

steps.title: Section 197 limits (public companies)
steps.body:
On net profit computed under Section 198:
- Total managerial remuneration: **11%**
- One managing/whole-time director or manager: **5%**; more than one: **10%** in all
- Non-executive directors: **1%** if there is an MD/WTD/manager, otherwise **3%**

Higher amounts are possible with shareholders' approval by special resolution (and lender consent where applicable). Sitting fees are excluded.

steps.title: Solved: ceilings
steps.body:
Net profit u/s 198 = ₹50,00,000.

- Overall ceiling: 11% = **₹5,50,000**
- If one MD: 5% = **₹2,50,000**
- If there is an MD, non-executive directors together: 1% = **₹50,000**

steps.title: Dividend basics – Section 123
steps.body:
- Declared out of profits of the year (after depreciation) or undistributed profits of earlier years, or out of money provided by government guarantee
- Transfer to reserves before dividend is optional (at the board's discretion)
- Interim dividend may be declared by the board
- Dividend must be deposited in a separate bank account within 5 days of declaration and paid within 30 days
- Unpaid dividend goes to an Unpaid Dividend Account; amounts unclaimed for 7 years go to the IEPF

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing remuneration on profit after tax (Section 198 profit is a specially adjusted figure, before managerial remuneration and tax).
- Paying dividend out of capital profits or revaluation gains.
- Treating sitting fees as part of the 11% limit.

activity.prompt: A public company's net profit computed under Section 198 is ₹80,00,000. It has two whole-time directors. Maximum remuneration payable to them together without special approval (₹)?

quiz.q: The overall limit of managerial remuneration for a public company is:
quiz.why: Section 197 caps total managerial remuneration at 11% of net profit, unless approved otherwise.

quiz.q: With one MD, the limit for that MD alone is:
quiz.why: A single managing or whole-time director or manager is limited to 5%.

quiz.q: Unpaid dividend must be transferred to a separate account within:
options: 7 days of the 30-day payment period ending
quiz.why: Dividend not paid within 30 days is moved to an Unpaid Dividend Account within 7 days.

quiz.q: Interim dividend is declared by the:
quiz.why: The board may declare interim dividend between AGMs.

questions.q: Under Schedule III, trade receivables are part of:
questions.why: Debtors and bills receivable are current assets.

questions.q: Capital work-in-progress appears under:
questions.why: Assets under construction are shown under non-current assets.

questions.q: Instalment of a term loan due within 12 months is shown as:
questions.why: Current maturities of long-term debt go under other current liabilities.

questions.q: Revenue ₹12,00,000; other income ₹30,000; total expenses ₹9,10,000. PBT:
Closing WIP higher than opening WIP by ₹15,000 makes total expenses:
questions.why: An increase in inventories is a negative change, reducing total expenses.

questions.q: Year from 1 April; incorporated 1 July. Time ratio:
questions.why: 3 months pre and 9 months post gives 3:9 = 1:3.

questions.q: Sales ₹10,00,000 of which ₹2,00,000 before incorporation; GP ₹3,00,000. Pre-incorporation GP:
Bad debts are apportioned in the:
questions.why: Bad debts arise from sales, so they follow the sales ratio.

questions.q: Preliminary expenses are charged to:
questions.why: They relate to the company's formation and are treated as post-incorporation.

questions.q: Net profit u/s 198 ₹40,00,000; company has an MD. Non-executive directors' total commission ceiling:
questions.why: With an MD, non-executive directors get at most 1%: ₹40,000.

questions.q: Dividend amounts unclaimed for 7 years are transferred to:
questions.why: Unclaimed dividends after 7 years go to the Investor Education and Protection Fund.

questions.q: Dividend may be declared out of:
questions.why: Section 123 requires dividend out of profits after depreciation, or past undistributed profits.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Valuation of goodwill and shares
courses.summary: Need for valuation, capital employed and future maintainable profit, goodwill by super-profit and capitalisation methods, and valuation of shares by the net assets (intrinsic) method, the yield method, the earnings (P/E) approach and fair value.
outcomes: Compute capital employed and future maintainable profit
Value goodwill by super profit and capitalisation methods
Value equity shares by the net assets method
Value shares by dividend yield and earnings yield methods
Compute the fair value of a share and explain when each method suits

scenes.text: A larger firm offers to acquire a profitable family-owned pharmaceutical company.
The sellers argue that their brand earns more than a normal return – that excess earning power is goodwill.

steps.title: Building blocks
steps.body:
- **Capital employed** = Total assets at current values (excluding goodwill, fictitious assets and non-trade investments) − Outside liabilities. Average capital employed = closing − ½ of current year's profit (after tax) or (opening + closing) ÷ 2.
- **Future maintainable profit (FMP)** = average past profit adjusted for non-recurring items, abnormal losses/gains, income from non-trade investments, changes expected in future (e.g. new salary), and tax.
- **Normal rate of return (NRR)**: return expected by investors in similar businesses.

steps.title: Solved: goodwill
steps.body:
Assets (at current value, excl. goodwill) 12,00,000; outside liabilities 3,00,000 → capital employed **9,00,000**. FMP 1,35,000; NRR 12%.

- Normal profit = 12% × 9,00,000 = 1,08,000
- Super profit = 27,000
- 4 years' purchase of super profit = **₹1,08,000**
- Capitalisation of super profit = 27,000 × 100/12 = **₹2,25,000**
- Capitalisation of average profit = 1,35,000 × 100/12 − 9,00,000 = 11,25,000 − 9,00,000 = **₹2,25,000** (same as above, as expected)

steps.title: Adjusting past profits
steps.body: Typical adjustments to arrive at FMP: add back abnormal losses (fire, strike), deduct abnormal gains (profit on sale of a fixed asset), deduct income from non-trade investments, adjust for under- or over-valued stock, deduct proposed increase in managerial salary, and deduct tax at the current rate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including non-trade investments in capital employed but deducting their income from profit (or vice versa) – treat consistently.
- Forgetting to deduct tax from FMP when the question gives a tax rate.
- Including existing goodwill in capital employed.

activity.prompt: Future maintainable profit ₹2,00,000; capital employed ₹15,00,000; normal rate of return 10%. Goodwill at 3 years' purchase of super profit (₹)?

quiz.q: Capital employed excludes:
quiz.why: Goodwill is what we are trying to value, so existing goodwill is excluded from capital employed.

quiz.q: Abnormal loss due to fire in a past year is:
quiz.why: An abnormal loss will not recur, so it is added back to find maintainable profit.

quiz.q: FMP ₹90,000; NRR 15%; capital employed ₹5,00,000. Super profit:
quiz.why: Normal profit 75,000; super profit 90,000 − 75,000 = ₹15,000.

quiz.q: Capitalised value of average profit minus capital employed gives:
quiz.why: The excess of the business's capitalised earning value over its net assets is goodwill.

scenes.text: An investor wants to know how much each share would be worth if all assets were sold and debts paid.
That 'break-up' value divided by the number of equity shares is the intrinsic value.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
**Net assets for equity** = Assets at realisable/current values (including goodwill at its valuation, excluding fictitious assets) − Outside liabilities − Preference share capital (and arrears of preference dividend if payable)

**Intrinsic value per equity share = Net assets for equity ÷ Number of equity shares**

Partly-paid shares: add notional calls to net assets, divide by number of shares, then deduct unpaid calls per share.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Assets at revalued figures (incl. goodwill 1,00,000) ₹15,00,000; outside liabilities ₹4,00,000; 10% preference capital ₹1,00,000; 50,000 equity shares of ₹10.

- Net assets for equity = 15,00,000 − 4,00,000 − 1,00,000 = 10,00,000
- **Value per share = ₹20**

steps.title: Solved: partly paid shares
steps.body:
Net assets ₹4,50,000. 20,000 shares of ₹10 fully paid and 10,000 shares of ₹10 with ₹7 paid.

- Add notional call 10,000 × 3 = 30,000 → 4,80,000
- Per fully paid share = 4,80,000 ÷ 30,000 = **₹16**
- Per partly paid share = 16 − 3 = **₹13**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including preliminary expenses or debit balance of P&L as assets.
- Forgetting to deduct preference capital.
- Dividing by authorised rather than issued equity shares.

activity.prompt: Assets at realisable value ₹11,00,000 (no fictitious assets); outside liabilities ₹2,60,000; no preference shares; 40,000 equity shares. Intrinsic value per share (₹)?

quiz.q: The net assets method is also called:
quiz.why: It measures the asset backing (intrinsic value) of each share.

quiz.q: Preliminary expenses in the balance sheet are:
quiz.why: Fictitious assets have no realisable value, so they are excluded.

quiz.q: Net assets ₹6,00,000; preference capital ₹1,00,000; 25,000 equity shares. Value per share:
For partly paid shares, the value is found by:
options: adding notional calls then deducting unpaid amount per share
quiz.why: Notional calls equalise all shares; then each partly paid share is reduced by its unpaid amount.

scenes.text: A small investor buys 500 shares; she cannot control the company or its assets.
What matters to her is the dividend she can expect – so the yield method suits her.

steps.title: Dividend yield
steps.body:
**Value per share = (Expected rate of dividend ÷ Normal rate of return) × Paid-up value per share**

Expected rate of dividend = Profit available for equity dividend (after tax, transfers to reserves and preference dividend) ÷ Paid-up equity capital × 100.

Suited to small/minority holdings.

steps.title: Solved: dividend yield
steps.body:
Profit after tax ₹1,50,000; transfer to reserves 20%; equity capital 1,00,000 shares of ₹10; NRR 10%; no preference shares.

- Available for dividend = 1,50,000 − 30,000 = 1,20,000
- Expected rate = 1,20,000 ÷ 10,00,000 = **12%**
- Value = 12/10 × 10 = **₹12 per share**

steps.title: Earnings yield and P/E
steps.body:
- **Earnings yield** value = (Earnings rate ÷ NRR) × paid-up value, where earnings rate = profit available for equity (before transfer to reserves) ÷ equity capital.
- **P/E approach**: Value = EPS × P/E ratio of comparable companies. E.g. EPS ₹5 and P/E 14 → ₹70.

Suited to controlling holdings where retained earnings matter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using profit before tax for the expected rate.
- Forgetting to deduct preference dividend.
- Using face value when shares are partly paid (use paid-up value).

activity.prompt: Expected rate of dividend 15%; normal rate of return 12%; paid-up value ₹10 per share. Value per share by dividend yield (₹)?

quiz.q: Yield method is most suitable for valuing:
quiz.why: Minority holders mainly get dividends, so the dividend yield best reflects their value.

quiz.q: Expected dividend 18%, NRR 12%, paid-up ₹100. Value:
EPS ₹8; P/E ratio 12. Value per share:
quiz.why: Value = EPS × P/E = 8 × 12 = ₹96.

quiz.q: Before computing expected rate of dividend, deduct:
options: preference dividend and transfer to reserves
quiz.why: Only profit left after preference dividend and reserves is available to equity holders.

lessons.title: Fair value and choosing a method

scenes.text: Two branches of a family disagree on the price at which one will buy the other's shares.
A valuer blends asset backing and earning power into a 'fair value'.

steps.title: Fair value
steps.body:
**Fair value = (Intrinsic value + Yield value) ÷ 2**

It balances the security of assets with the return on investment. Commonly used in negotiated transfers and in exam questions where both methods are asked.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Intrinsic value ₹30; yield value ₹24.

- **Fair value = (30 + 24) ÷ 2 = ₹27**

steps.title: Which method when?
steps.body:
- **Net assets**: liquidation, amalgamation share-exchange ratios, asset-heavy companies
- **Dividend yield**: minority shareholdings
- **Earnings yield / P/E**: controlling interest, listed comparables available
- **Fair value**: compromise when both asset and earnings views matter

In amalgamation, exchange ratio = value of transferor share ÷ value of transferee share.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Averaging values computed on different paid-up amounts.
- Using market value of a thinly-traded share as 'fair value'.
- Forgetting to round the exchange ratio to the terms given.

activity.prompt: A share has intrinsic value ₹46 and yield value ₹38. Its fair value (₹)?

quiz.q: Fair value is the average of:
quiz.why: Fair value is the simple average of the net-assets and yield values.

quiz.q: For valuing a controlling interest, the preferred basis is:
quiz.why: A controlling holder can decide retention, so total earnings matter more than dividends.

quiz.q: Transferor share value ₹60, transferee share value ₹40. Exchange ratio:
quiz.why: 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5, i.e. 3 transferee shares for every 2 transferor shares.

quiz.q: The net assets method is most suitable when:
quiz.why: In liquidation, shareholders receive asset proceeds, so asset backing is the right measure.

questions.q: Normal profit = ?
questions.why: Normal profit is the return expected on capital employed at the normal rate.

questions.q: Capital employed ₹8,00,000; NRR 10%; FMP ₹1,04,000. Goodwill by capitalising super profit:
Profit on sale of machinery included in past profits is:
questions.why: It is non-recurring, so it is removed from maintainable profit.

questions.q: Average past profit ₹1,00,000 before tax; tax 30%; FMP after tax:
Net assets ₹9,00,000; preference capital ₹2,00,000; 35,000 equity shares. Intrinsic value:
Net assets ₹3,40,000; 10,000 shares fully paid ₹10 and 10,000 shares paid ₹8. Value of a partly paid share:
questions.why: Add notional call 20,000 → 3,60,000 ÷ 20,000 = 18 per fully paid; partly paid = 18 − 2 = ₹17.

questions.q: PAT ₹2,00,000; preference dividend ₹20,000; reserves transfer ₹30,000; equity capital ₹10,00,000. Expected dividend rate:
Expected dividend 15%, NRR 10%, paid-up ₹10: value:
EPS ₹12.50; industry P/E 16. Value:
Intrinsic ₹55, yield ₹45. Fair value:
Which is NOT included in capital employed for goodwill?
options: non-trade investments (when their income is excluded)
questions.why: If income from non-trade investments is excluded from profit, the investments are excluded from capital employed too.

questions.q: Exchange ratio when A Ltd share = ₹36 and B Ltd (transferee) share = ₹24:
questions.why: 36 ÷ 24 = 1.5, so 3 B shares for every 2 A shares.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Amalgamation, internal reconstruction and consolidation
courses.summary: Amalgamation in the nature of merger and purchase under AS 14, methods of computing purchase consideration, entries in transferor and transferee books, internal reconstruction through capital reduction, and the basics of consolidating a holding company with its subsidiary under AS 21.
outcomes: Distinguish merger and purchase types of amalgamation
Compute purchase consideration by net assets and share exchange methods
Close transferor books and record goodwill or capital reserve in the transferee
Record a capital reduction scheme and its use to write off losses
Compute goodwill on consolidation and minority interest

scenes.text: Two regional dairies agree that one will take over the other's business.
First they must agree the price – the purchase consideration – that the transferor's shareholders will receive.

steps.title: AS 14: two types
steps.body:
**Amalgamation in the nature of merger** – all five conditions: all assets and liabilities transferred; holders of at least 90% of equity (by value) become shareholders of the transferee; consideration only in equity shares (cash only for fractions); business intended to continue; book values carried over (only uniform-policy adjustments). Accounted by **pooling of interests** method.

**Amalgamation in the nature of purchase** – any condition not met. Accounted by **purchase method**: assets/liabilities at book or fair values; difference vs consideration → goodwill or capital reserve.

steps.title: Purchase consideration (AS 14)
steps.body:
PC is the aggregate of shares and other securities issued and payments in cash or other assets made by the transferee **to the shareholders** of the transferor.

Methods: lump sum; **net assets** (agreed assets − agreed liabilities taken over); **net payment** (sum of payments to shareholders); **share exchange** (intrinsic value based ratio). Payments to debenture-holders or creditors are **not** part of PC under AS 14.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Transferee takes over assets ₹10,00,000 (agreed values) and liabilities ₹2,00,000.

- Net assets method: **PC = ₹8,00,000**
- Discharged by issuing 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 at ₹20 = ₹8,00,000 (share capital 4,00,000; securities premium 4,00,000)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including payment to the transferor's debenture-holders in PC.
- Using pooling of interests when consideration includes significant cash.
- Taking fictitious assets into net assets.

activity.prompt: The transferor has 20,000 equity shares. For every 2 of its shares, the transferee issues 3 equity shares of ₹10 at ₹12 each, and also pays ₹2 in cash per transferor share. Purchase consideration (₹)?

quiz.why: AS 14 requires pooling of interests for amalgamations in the nature of merger.

story.title: Closing one set of books, opening another

scenes.text: The transferor closes its books through a realisation account.
The transferee records the assets and liabilities it acquired and the shares it issued.

steps.title: Transferor company
steps.body:
1. Realisation A/c Dr / To Assets (book values)
2. Liabilities Dr / To Realisation A/c (liabilities taken over)
3. Transferee Co. Dr / To Realisation A/c (PC)
4. Shares in Transferee + Bank Dr / To Transferee Co.
5. Share capital + reserves Dr / To Equity Shareholders A/c
6. Realisation profit/loss to Equity Shareholders A/c
7. Equity Shareholders Dr / To Shares in Transferee, To Bank

steps.title: Solved: transferee (purchase method)
steps.body:
PC ₹8,00,000 in shares. Net assets acquired at fair value ₹7,40,000.

**Business Purchase A/c Dr 8,00,000 / To Liquidator of Transferor 8,00,000**
**Assets Dr (fair values) and Goodwill Dr 60,000 / To Liabilities, To Business Purchase 8,00,000**
**Liquidator Dr 8,00,000 / To Equity Share Capital, To Securities Premium**

If net assets exceeded PC, the excess would be **capital reserve**.

steps.title: Statutory reserves
steps.body: Under the purchase method, statutory reserves of the transferor (e.g. export profit reserve) that must be preserved are recorded by: **Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve A/c Dr / To Statutory Reserve A/c**. Formation expenses of the transferee may be debited to P&L or written off from securities premium.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Carrying the transferor's general reserve into the transferee under the purchase method (only under pooling).
- Recording goodwill in transferor books.
- Forgetting to cancel inter-company debts after amalgamation.

activity.prompt: Purchase consideration ₹6,50,000. The transferee takes over assets at fair value ₹8,20,000 and liabilities ₹2,00,000. Under the purchase method, what is the goodwill (₹)? (Enter a negative number if it is a capital reserve.)

quiz.q: In the transferor's books, PC is credited to:
quiz.why: The PC is the sale price of the business, credited to Realisation.

quiz.q: Excess of net assets over PC in the transferee's books is:
quiz.why: A bargain purchase gives a capital reserve.

quiz.q: Under the purchase method, the transferor's general reserve is:
quiz.why: Only identifiable assets and liabilities are recorded; free reserves are not carried over.

quiz.q: Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve is used to:
quiz.why: It records statutory reserves that must be maintained by the transferee under the purchase method.

scenes.text: Years of losses leave a textile company with a large debit balance in P&L and worthless goodwill on its books.
Shareholders agree to reduce the face value of their shares so the losses can be written off and a clean balance sheet presented.

steps.title: Meaning and legal basis
steps.body:
Internal reconstruction reorganises capital **without liquidating** the company and without forming a new one.
- Alteration of share capital (consolidation, sub-division, conversion) – Section 61
- **Reduction of share capital** – Section 66, by special resolution and confirmation of the Tribunal (NCLT)
- Compromise with creditors/debenture-holders – Sections 230–232

steps.title: Solved: capital reduction
steps.body:
50,000 equity shares of ₹10 fully paid reduced to ₹4 each. Write off P&L debit balance ₹2,20,000, goodwill ₹50,000 and preliminary expenses ₹10,000.

- **Equity Share Capital (₹10) Dr 5,00,000 / To Equity Share Capital (₹4) 2,00,000, To Capital Reduction 3,00,000**
- **Capital Reduction Dr 2,80,000 / To P&L 2,20,000, To Goodwill 50,000, To Preliminary Expenses 10,000**
- Balance 20,000 → **Capital Reserve**

steps.title: Other uses of Capital Reduction A/c
steps.body: Write down overvalued assets (machinery, stock), write off discount on issue of debentures, and provide for contingent liabilities. Any gain from creditors' sacrifice is also credited to Capital Reduction. The balance left over is capital reserve – never a revenue profit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Crediting the balance of Capital Reduction to P&L.
- Reducing liabilities to outsiders without their consent.
- Forgetting to change the 'Name of Company and Reduced' disclosure in the balance sheet where required.

activity.prompt: 80,000 equity shares of ₹10 are reduced to ₹6 each. The amount is used to write off P&L debit balance ₹2,40,000 and goodwill ₹60,000, and to reduce machinery by ₹15,000. Balance transferred to capital reserve (₹)?

quiz.q: Reduction of share capital requires confirmation of the:
quiz.why: Section 66 requires a special resolution confirmed by the Tribunal.

quiz.q: The balance of Capital Reduction A/c after write-offs goes to:
quiz.why: Any surplus from reduction is a capital profit and goes to capital reserve.

quiz.q: Internal reconstruction involves:
options: reorganising capital of the same company
quiz.why: The same company continues; only its capital structure changes.

quiz.q: Consolidating ₹10 shares into ₹100 shares falls under:
quiz.why: Consolidation and sub-division of shares are alterations under Section 61.

scenes.text: H Ltd owns 80% of S Ltd. Their separate balance sheets do not show the group's real position.
Consolidation combines them line by line and shows the 20% outside holders' share as minority interest.

steps.title: Key terms (AS 21)
steps.body:
- **Holding company**: controls the composition of the board or holds more than half the voting power of another company (Companies Act definition uses more than one-half of total share capital).
- **Cost of control / goodwill**: cost of investment − holding company's share of subsidiary's net assets (equity) on the date of acquisition. Negative → capital reserve.
- **Pre-acquisition profits**: capital profits, used in computing cost of control.
- **Post-acquisition profits**: revenue profits; holding company's share added to consolidated reserves.
- **Minority interest**: outsiders' share in subsidiary's share capital + all reserves (pre and post).

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
H buys 80% of S (share capital ₹1,00,000) for ₹1,50,000 when S's reserves are ₹50,000. At the balance sheet date S's reserves are ₹80,000.

- Net assets at acquisition = 1,50,000; H's share 1,20,000
- **Goodwill = 1,50,000 − 1,20,000 = ₹30,000**
- Post-acquisition profit = 30,000; H's share **24,000** to consolidated reserves
- **Minority interest = 20% × (1,00,000 + 80,000) = ₹36,000**

steps.title: Eliminations
steps.body: Cancel inter-company balances (debtors/creditors, loans, bills), and remove unrealised profit on inter-company stock (holding company's share, or full amount as per question) from consolidated reserves and stock.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing minority interest only on share capital.
- Adding all of the subsidiary's reserves to group reserves.
- Forgetting to eliminate inter-company debts on both sides.

quiz.why: Profits earned before acquisition are bought with the shares, so they are capital profits.

questions.why: Amalgamations in the nature of purchase use the purchase method.

questions.why: Sacrifices under the scheme are pooled in Capital Reduction A/c.

courses.summary: Key-point and formula sheet for the whole paper, a practical on preparing a Schedule III balance sheet from balances, a practical on EPS and dividend capacity, previous-year-style questions with answer plans, and a 15-question paper-level exam.
outcomes: Recall the section numbers, formulas and rules used across the paper

scenes.text: Aditi folds the whole Corporate Accounting syllabus into one revision sheet.
She tests herself on every line before the exam.

steps.title: Shares and debentures
steps.body:
- Sec 43 kinds of capital; Sec 52 securities premium uses; Sec 53 no discount issue (except sweat equity)
- Paid-up = Called-up − Calls in arrears; calls in advance = other current liability
- Forfeiture: Dr Share Capital (called up) / Cr unpaid calls, Cr Forfeiture (received)
- Capital reserve on reissue = forfeited amount on reissued shares − discount on reissue
- Loss on issue of debentures = discount + premium on redemption

steps.title: Buy-back, bonus, redemption
steps.body:
- Bonus (Sec 63): free reserves, securities premium, CRR – not revaluation reserve
- Buy-back (Sec 68): ≤ 25% (10% by board), D/E ≤ 2:1 after, fully paid shares; CRR (Sec 69) = nominal value bought from free reserves/premium
- Preference redemption (Sec 55): CRR = nominal value redeemed − nominal value of fresh issue

steps.title: Final accounts and valuation
steps.body:
- Current: within 12 months or operating cycle
- Change in inventories = opening − closing
- Pre-incorporation: GP and selling expenses by sales ratio; fixed costs by time ratio; result to capital reserve
- Sec 197: 11% overall; 5% one MD; 10% for more; 1% / 3% non-executive
- Goodwill = Super profit × years, or Super profit × 100 ÷ NRR
- Intrinsic value = (Net assets − preference capital) ÷ equity shares
- Yield value = Expected rate ÷ NRR × paid-up value; Fair value = average of the two

steps.title: Amalgamation, reconstruction, consolidation
steps.body:
- AS 14 PC = consideration to shareholders only; merger → pooling, else purchase
- PC > net assets → goodwill; < → capital reserve
- Capital reduction (Sec 66) surplus → capital reserve
- Goodwill on consolidation = cost − share of (capital + pre-acquisition reserves)
- Minority interest = minority % × (capital + all reserves)
